In Troy, there lies the scene. From isles of Greece / The princes orgulous, their high blood chaf'd, / Have to the port of Athens sent their ships / Fraught with the ministers and instruments / Of cruel war. Sixty and nine that wore / Their crownets regal from the Athenian bay / Put forth toward Phrygia; and their vow is made / To ransack Troy, within whose strong immures / The ravish'd Helen, Menelaus' queen, / With wanton Paris sleeps—and that's the quarrel. / To Tenedos they come, / And the deep-drawing barks do there disgorge / Their war-like fraughtage. Now on Dardan plains / The fresh and yet unbruised Greeks do pitch / Their brave pavilions: Priam's six-gated city, / Dardan, and Tymbria, Ilias, Chetas, Troien, / And Antenorides, with massy staples / And corresponsive and fulfilling bolts, / Stir up the sons of Troy. / Now expectation, tickling skittish spirits / On one and other side, Trojan and Greek, / Sets all on hazard. And hither am I come / A prologue arm'd, but not in confidence / Of author's pen or actor's voice, but suited / In like conditions as our argument, / To tell you, fair beholders, that our play / Leaps o'er the vaunt and firstlings of those broils, / Beginning in the middle; starting thence away, / To what may be digested in a play. / Like or find fault; do as your pleasures are; / Now good or bad, 'tis but the chance of war.

Our scene is Troy. Proud princes from the islands of Greece, their noble blood inflamed, have sent their ships to the port of Athens, loaded with the men and weapons of cruel war. Sixty-nine kings wearing royal crowns set sail from the bay of Athens towards Phrygia, sworn to sack Troy, where, behind strong walls, Helen, Menelaus' stolen queen, sleeps with the lustful Paris. That is the quarrel. They land at Tenedos, and the heavy ships unload their warlike cargo there. Now the fresh Greeks, not yet bruised by fighting, pitch their splendid tents on the plains of Troy, while Priam's city, with its six gates (Dardan, Tymbria, Ilias, Chetas, Troien and Antenorides), barred with massive staples and close-fitting bolts, shuts in the sons of Troy. Now anticipation, teasing the nervous spirits of both sides, Trojan and Greek, puts everything at risk. And I have come here as a prologue in armour, not because I am confident in the author's pen or the actors' voices, but dressed to suit our subject, to tell you, fair audience, that our play skips the boasts and opening skirmishes of this war and begins in the middle, going on from there to whatever can be fitted into a play. Like it or find fault; do as you please. Good or bad, it is only the luck of war.

Call here my varlet; I'll unarm again. / Why should I war without the walls of Troy / That find such cruel battle here within? / Each Trojan that is master of his heart, / Let him to field; Troilus, alas! hath none.

Call my servant here; I'm taking my armour off again. Why should I fight outside the walls of Troy when I am suffering such a cruel battle in here, inside myself? Let every Trojan who is master of his own heart go to the battlefield. Troilus, alas, has no heart left.
Will this gear ne'er be mended?
Will this business never be put right?

The Greeks are strong, and skilful to their strength, / Fierce to their skill, and to their fierceness valiant; / But I am weaker than a woman's tear, / Tamer than sleep, fonder than ignorance, / Less valiant than the virgin in the night, / And skilless as unpractis'd infancy.

The Greeks are strong, and skilful as well as strong, fierce as well as skilful, and brave as well as fierce. But I am weaker than a woman's tear, tamer than sleep, more foolish than ignorance, less brave than a virgin at night, and as unskilled as an inexperienced child.
Well, I have told you enough of this; for my part, I'll not meddle nor make no farther. He that will have a cake out of the wheat must tarry the grinding.
Well, I have told you enough about this. For my part, I won't interfere or have anything more to do with it. Whoever wants a cake made from the wheat must wait for the grinding.
Ay, the grinding; but you must tarry the bolting.
Yes, for the grinding, but you must also wait for the sifting.
Ay, the bolting; but you must tarry the leavening.
Yes, for the sifting, but you must wait for the rising.

Ay, to the leavening; but here's yet in the word 'hereafter' the kneading, the making of the cake, the heating of the oven, and the baking; nay, you must stay the cooling too, or you may chance burn your lips.

Yes, for the rising, but in the word "afterwards" there is still the kneading, the shaping of the cake, the heating of the oven and the baking. And you must wait for it to cool down too, or you might burn your lips.

Patience herself, what goddess e'er she be, / Doth lesser blench at suff'rance than I do. / At Priam's royal table do I sit; / And when fair Cressid comes into my thoughts, / So, traitor! 'when she comes'! when she is thence?

Patience herself, whatever goddess she is, flinches less at suffering than I do. I sit at Priam's royal table, and when lovely Cressida comes into my thoughts... Traitor that I am! "When she comes"! When is she ever out of them?
Well, she look'd yesternight fairer than ever I saw her look, or any woman else.
Well, she looked lovelier last night than I have ever seen her look, or any other woman.

I was about to tell thee: when my heart, / As wedged with a sigh, would rive in twain, / Lest Hector or my father should perceive me, / I have, as when the sun doth light a storm, / Buried this sigh in wrinkle of a smile. / But sorrow that is couch'd in seeming gladness / Is like that mirth fate turns to sudden sadness.

I was going to tell you: when my heart felt as if a sigh had been wedged into it and would split it in two, I buried that sigh in a wrinkled smile, like the sun shining through a storm, so that Hector or my father would not notice. But sorrow hidden under a show of happiness is like the cheerfulness that fate suddenly turns to sadness.

An her hair were not somewhat darker than Helen's, well, go to, there were no more comparison between the women. But, for my part, she is my kinswoman; I would not, as they term it, praise her, but I would somebody had heard her talk yesterday, as I did. I will not dispraise your sister Cassandra's wit; but—

If her hair weren't a bit darker than Helen's, well, there'd be no comparing the two women. But, for my part, she's my relative, so I wouldn't, as they say, praise her. But I wish someone had heard her talking yesterday, as I did. I won't run down your sister Cassandra's intelligence, but...

O Pandarus! I tell thee, Pandarus, / When I do tell thee there my hopes lie drown'd, / Reply not in how many fathoms deep / They lie indrench'd. I tell thee I am mad / In Cressid's love. Thou answer'st 'She is fair'; / Pour'st in the open ulcer of my heart / Her eyes, her hair, her cheek, her gait, her voice, / Handlest in thy discourse. O! that her hand, / In whose comparison all whites are ink / Writing their own reproach; to whose soft seizure / The cygnet's down is harsh, and spirit of sense / Hard as the palm of ploughman! This thou tell'st me, / As true thou tell'st me, when I say I love her; / But, saying thus, instead of oil and balm, / Thou lay'st in every gash that love hath given me / The knife that made it.

Oh Pandarus! I tell you, Pandarus, when I tell you that my hopes are drowned there, don't answer by telling me how many fathoms deep they lie. I tell you I am mad with love for Cressida. You answer, "She's beautiful," and pour into the open wound of my heart her eyes, her hair, her cheek, her walk, her voice. You go on and on about them. Oh, her hand, next to which every white thing looks like ink writing its own disgrace, and compared to whose soft touch a young swan's down is rough and the most delicate sense of touch is as hard as a ploughman's palm! You tell me this, and it is true, when I say I love her. But by saying it, instead of oil and soothing ointment, you lay in every wound that love has given me the knife that made it.
I speak no more than truth.
I speak nothing but the truth.
Thou dost not speak so much.
You don't speak even as much as the truth.
Faith, I'll not meddle in't. Let her be as she is: if she be fair, 'tis the better for her; and she be not, she has the mends in her own hands.
Honestly, I won't interfere. Let her be as she is. If she's beautiful, so much the better for her; if she isn't, she can do something about it herself.
Good Pandarus! What's the matter, Pandarus?
I have had my labour for my travail, ill thought on of her and ill thought on of you; gone between and between, but small thanks for my labour.
I've had nothing but trouble for my efforts, been badly thought of by her and badly thought of by you. I've gone back and forth between you, and got little thanks for my work.
What! art thou angry, Pandarus? What! with me?
What! Are you angry, Pandarus? What! With me?

Because she's kin to me, therefore she's not so fair as Helen. And she were not kin to me, she would be as fair on Friday as Helen is on Sunday. But what care I? I care not and she were a blackamoor; 'tis all one to me.

Because she's related to me, she's not as beautiful as Helen. If she weren't related to me, she'd look as good in her weekday clothes as Helen does in her Sunday best. But what do I care? I wouldn't care if she were black as a Moor; it's all the same to me.
Say I she is not fair?
Did I say she isn't beautiful?

I do not care whether you do or no. She's a fool to stay behind her father. Let her to the Greeks; and so I'll tell her the next time I see her. For my part, I'll meddle nor make no more i' the matter.

I don't care whether you do or not. She's a fool to stay behind when her father has gone. Let her go to the Greeks, and I'll tell her so next time I see her. For my part, I won't interfere or meddle any more in the matter.
Pray you, speak no more to me: I will leave all as I found it, and there an end.
Please, don't say any more to me. I'll leave everything as I found it, and that's the end of it.

Peace, you ungracious clamours! Peace, rude sounds! / Fools on both sides! Helen must needs be fair, / When with your blood you daily paint her thus. / I cannot fight upon this argument; / It is too starv'd a subject for my sword. / But Pandarus, O gods! how do you plague me! / I cannot come to Cressid but by Pandar; / And he's as tetchy to be woo'd to woo / As she is stubborn-chaste against all suit. / Tell me, Apollo, for thy Daphne's love, / What Cressid is, what Pandar, and what we? / Her bed is India; there she lies, a pearl; / Between our Ilium and where she resides / Let it be call'd the wild and wandering flood; / Ourself the merchant, and this sailing Pandar / Our doubtful hope, our convoy, and our bark.

Quiet, you ugly noises! Quiet, you rough sounds! Fools on both sides! Helen must be beautiful when you paint her red with your blood every day. I can't fight for this cause; it's too thin a subject for my sword. But Pandarus! Oh gods, how you torment me! I can't get to Cressida except through Pandarus, and he is as touchy about being persuaded to do the wooing as she is stubbornly chaste against every suitor. Tell me, Apollo, for the love of your Daphne, what Cressida is, what Pandarus is, and what we are. Her bed is India; she lies there like a pearl. Let the space between our palace in Troy and where she lives be called the wild and stormy sea. I am the merchant, and this drifting Pandarus is my uncertain hope, my escort and my ship.
How now, Prince Troilus! Wherefore not afield?
Hello, Prince Troilus! Why aren't you on the battlefield?
Because not there. This woman's answer sorts, / For womanish it is to be from thence. / What news, Aeneas, from the field today?
Because I'm not there. That is a woman's answer, and it fits, because it is womanish to stay away from there. What news from the battlefield today, Aeneas?
That Paris is returned home, and hurt.
That Paris has come home wounded.
Let Paris bleed: 'tis but a scar to scorn; / Paris is gor'd with Menelaus' horn.
Let Paris bleed. It's only a scratch, nothing to worry about. Paris has been gored by Menelaus' horn. (Menelaus is the cuckold, with a cuckold's horns.)
Hark what good sport is out of town today!
Listen to the fine sport going on outside the town today!
Better at home, if 'would I might' were 'may.' / But to the sport abroad. Are you bound thither?
There would be better sport at home, if "I wish I might" could become "I may." But let's go to the sport out there. Are you heading there?
Come on, then, let's go together.
Who were those people who went by?

Up to the eastern tower, / Whose height commands as subject all the vale, / To see the battle. Hector, whose patience / Is as a virtue fix'd, today was mov'd. / He chid Andromache, and struck his armourer; / And, like as there were husbandry in war, / Before the sun rose he was harness'd light, / And to the field goes he; where every flower / Did as a prophet weep what it foresaw / In Hector's wrath.

Up to the eastern tower, which is high enough to look down over the whole valley, to watch the battle. Hector, whose patience is as steady as a virtue, was angry today. He scolded Andromache and hit his armourer, and, as if war were a matter of good housekeeping, he put on his light armour before sunrise and went out to the battlefield, where every flower wept with dew, like a prophet foreseeing what Hector's anger would do.
What was his cause of anger?
The noise goes, this: there is among the Greeks / A lord of Trojan blood, nephew to Hector; / They call him Ajax.
The rumour goes like this: there is a lord among the Greeks who has Trojan blood, Hector's nephew. They call him Ajax.
They say he is a very man per se / And stands alone.
They say he is a man unique in himself, and stands alone.
So do all men, unless they are drunk, sick, or have no legs.
So do all men, unless they are drunk, sick, or have no legs.

This man, lady, hath robb'd many beasts of their particular additions: he is as valiant as the lion, churlish as the bear, slow as the elephant—a man into whom nature hath so crowded humours that his valour is crush'd into folly, his folly sauced with discretion. There is no man hath a virtue that he hath not a glimpse of, nor any man an attaint but he carries some stain of it; he is melancholy without cause and merry against the hair; he hath the joints of everything; but everything so out of joint that he is a gouty Briareus, many hands and no use, or purblind Argus, all eyes and no sight.

This man, lady, has stolen from many animals their special qualities. He is as brave as the lion, as surly as the bear, as slow as the elephant. He is a man into whom nature has crammed so many moods that his courage is crushed into foolishness, and his foolishness is seasoned with a little sense. There is no man with a virtue that he doesn't have a glimpse of, and no man with a fault that he doesn't share a trace of. He is gloomy for no reason and cheerful at the wrong time. He has the parts of everything, but everything is so out of joint that he is like a gouty Briareus, with many hands and no use of them, or a half-blind Argus, all eyes and no sight.
But how should this man, that makes me smile, make Hector angry?
But how could this man, who makes me smile, make Hector angry?
They say he yesterday cop'd Hector in the battle and struck him down, the disdain and shame whereof hath ever since kept Hector fasting and waking.
They say that yesterday he met Hector in the battle and knocked him down, and the disgust and shame of it have kept Hector from eating or sleeping ever since.
As may be in the world, lady.
As fine as any in the world, lady.
Good morrow, cousin Cressid. What do you talk of?—Good morrow, Alexander.—How do you, cousin? When were you at Ilium?
Good morning, niece Cressida. What are you talking about? Good morning, Alexander. How are you, niece? When were you at the palace?
What were you talking of when I came? Was Hector arm'd and gone ere you came to Ilium? Helen was not up, was she?
What were you talking about when I arrived? Had Hector armed and gone before you got to the palace? Helen wasn't up, was she?
Hector was gone; but Helen was not up.
Hector had gone, but Helen wasn't up.
E'en so. Hector was stirring early.
Just so. Hector was up early.
That were we talking of, and of his anger.
That's what we were talking about, and about his anger.
True, he was so; I know the cause too; he'll lay about him today, I can tell them that. And there's Troilus will not come far behind him; let them take heed of Troilus, I can tell them that too.
That's true, he was. I know the reason too. He'll lay into them today, I can tell them that. And Troilus won't be far behind him. Let them watch out for Troilus, I can tell them that too.
Who, Troilus? Troilus is the better man of the two.
Who, Troilus? Troilus is the better man of the two.
What, not between Troilus and Hector? Do you know a man if you see him?
What, not between Troilus and Hector? Do you know a real man when you see one?
Ay, if I ever saw him before and knew him.
Yes, if I've seen him before and know who he is.
Well, I say Troilus is Troilus.
Well, I say Troilus is Troilus.
Then you say as I say, for I am sure he is not Hector.
Then you're saying what I'm saying, because I'm sure he isn't Hector.
No, nor Hector is not Troilus in some degrees.
No, and Hector isn't Troilus in some ways.
'Tis just to each of them: he is himself.
That's fair to both of them: each is himself.
Himself! Alas, poor Troilus! I would he were!
Himself! Alas, poor Troilus! I wish he were!
Condition I had gone barefoot to India.
And if he is, I'll walk barefoot to India.

Himself! no, he's not himself. Would a' were himself! Well, the gods are above; time must friend or end. Well, Troilus, well! I would my heart were in her body! No, Hector is not a better man than Troilus.

Himself! No, he's not himself. I wish he were himself! Well, the gods are above us; time will either help or finish things. Well, Troilus, well! I wish my heart were in her body! No, Hector is not a better man than Troilus.
Th'other's not come to't; you shall tell me another tale when th'other's come to't. Hector shall not have his wit this year.
The other one hasn't reached his age yet. You'll tell a different story when the other one has. Hector won't have his brains this year.
He shall not need it if he have his own.
He won't need them if he has his own.
'Twould not become him: his own's better.
They wouldn't suit him: his own are better.
You have no judgement, niece. Helen herself swore th'other day that Troilus, for a brown favour, for so 'tis, I must confess—not brown neither—
You have no judgement, niece. Helen herself swore the other day that Troilus, for a dark complexion (for it is dark, I have to admit; well, not dark exactly)...
Faith, to say truth, brown and not brown.
Honestly, to tell the truth, dark and not dark.
To say the truth, true and not true.
To tell the truth, true and not true.
She prais'd his complexion above Paris.
She praised his complexion above Paris's.

Then Troilus should have too much. If she prais'd him above, his complexion is higher than his; he having colour enough, and the other higher, is too flaming a praise for a good complexion. I had as lief Helen's golden tongue had commended Troilus for a copper nose.

Then Troilus must have too much. If she praised his colour above Paris's, his colour is higher than Paris's. If Paris has enough colour and Troilus has more, that's too fiery a compliment for a good complexion. I'd rather Helen's golden tongue had praised Troilus for having a red nose.
I swear to you I think Helen loves him better than Paris.
I swear to you, I think Helen loves him more than Paris.
Then she's a merry Greek indeed.
Then she's a merry Greek indeed (a loose woman).
Nay, I am sure she does. She came to him th'other day into the compass'd window—and you know he has not past three or four hairs on his chin—
No, I'm sure she does. She came up to him the other day in the bay window, and you know he hasn't more than three or four hairs on his chin...
Indeed a tapster's arithmetic may soon bring his particulars therein to a total.
Indeed, a barman's arithmetic could soon add up his hairs.
Why, he is very young, and yet will he within three pound lift as much as his brother Hector.
Why, he's very young, and yet he can lift almost as much as his brother Hector, within three pounds.
Is he so young a man and so old a lifter?
Is he such a young man and such an old lifter (thief)?
But to prove to you that Helen loves him: she came and puts me her white hand to his cloven chin—
But to prove to you that Helen loves him: she came and put her white hand to his cleft chin...
Juno have mercy! How came it cloven?
Juno have mercy! How did it get split?
Why, you know, 'tis dimpled. I think his smiling becomes him better than any man in all Phrygia.
Why, you know, it's dimpled. I think smiling suits him better than any man in all Troy.
O yes, an 'twere a cloud in autumn!
Oh yes, like a cloud in autumn!
Why, go to, then! But to prove to you that Helen loves Troilus—
Oh, come on! But to prove to you that Helen loves Troilus...
Troilus will stand to the proof, if you'll prove it so.
Troilus will stand up to the test, if you can prove it.
Troilus! Why, he esteems her no more than I esteem an addle egg.
Troilus! Why, he thinks no more of her than I think of a rotten egg.
If you love an addle egg as well as you love an idle head, you would eat chickens i' th' shell.
If you loved a rotten egg as much as you love an empty head, you'd eat chickens still in the shell.
I cannot choose but laugh to think how she tickled his chin. Indeed, she has a marvell's white hand, I must needs confess.
I can't help laughing to think how she tickled his chin. She really does have a marvellously white hand, I have to admit.
Without being forced on the rack to admit it.
And she takes upon her to spy a white hair on his chin.
And she claimed to spot a white hair on his chin.
Alas, poor chin! Many a wart is richer.
Alas, poor chin! Plenty of warts have more hair.
But there was such laughing! Queen Hecuba laugh'd that her eyes ran o'er.
But there was such laughing! Queen Hecuba laughed until her eyes ran over.
With millstones (she'd be as likely to cry millstones).
But there was a more temperate fire under the pot of her eyes. Did her eyes run o'er too?
But there was a cooler fire under the pot of her eyes. Did her eyes run over too?
At what was all this laughing?
Marry, at the white hair that Helen spied on Troilus' chin.
Why, at the white hair Helen spotted on Troilus' chin.
And't had been a green hair I should have laugh'd too.
If it had been a green hair, I'd have laughed too.
They laugh'd not so much at the hair as at his pretty answer.
They didn't laugh so much at the hair as at his clever answer.
Quoth she 'Here's but two and fifty hairs on your chin, and one of them is white.'
She said, "There are only fifty-two hairs on your chin, and one of them is white."

That's true; make no question of that. 'Two and fifty hairs,' quoth he 'and one white. That white hair is my father, and all the rest are his sons.' 'Jupiter!' quoth she 'which of these hairs is Paris my husband?' 'The forked one,' quoth he, 'pluck't out and give it him.' But there was such laughing! and Helen so blush'd, and Paris so chaf'd; and all the rest so laugh'd that it pass'd.

That's true, no question about it. "Fifty-two hairs," he said, "and one white one. That white hair is my father, and all the rest are his sons." "Jupiter!" she said, "which of these hairs is my husband Paris?" "The forked one," he said. "Pluck it out and give it to him." But there was such laughing! And Helen blushed so much, and Paris got so annoyed, and everyone else laughed so much, it was beyond anything.
So let it now; for it has been a great while going by.
Then let it pass now, because it's been passing for a long time.
Well, cousin, I told you a thing yesterday; think on't.
Well, niece, I told you something yesterday. Think about it.
I'll be sworn 'tis true; he will weep you, and 'twere a man born in April.
I swear it's true. He'll weep for you like a man born in rainy April.
And I'll spring up in his tears, an 'twere a nettle against May.
And I'll spring up in his tears like a nettle before May.
Hark! they are coming from the field. Shall we stand up here and see them as they pass toward Ilium? Good niece, do, sweet niece Cressida.
Listen! They're coming back from the battlefield. Shall we stand up here and watch them as they pass towards the palace? Do, dear niece, sweet niece Cressida.
Here, here, here's an excellent place; here we may see most bravely. I'll tell you them all by their names as they pass by; but mark Troilus above the rest.
Here, here, here's an excellent spot. We can see beautifully from here. I'll tell you all their names as they go past, but watch out for Troilus above all.
That's Aeneas. Is not that a brave man? He's one of the flowers of Troy, I can tell you. But mark Troilus; you shall see anon.
That's Aeneas. Isn't he a fine man? He's one of the flowers of Troy, I can tell you. But watch for Troilus; you'll see him soon.

That's Antenor. He has a shrewd wit, I can tell you; and he's a man good enough; he's one o' th' soundest judgements in Troy, whosoever, and a proper man of person. When comes Troilus? I'll show you Troilus anon. If he see me, you shall see him nod at me.

That's Antenor. He's very shrewd, I can tell you, and he's a good enough man. He has one of the soundest judgements in Troy, whoever you compare him with, and he's a handsome man. When is Troilus coming? I'll show you Troilus soon. If he sees me, you'll see him nod at me.
Will he give you the nod?
Will he give you the nod (call you a fool)?
If he do, the rich shall have more.
If he does, the rich will have more (you have plenty of foolishness already).
That's Hector, that, that, look you, that; there's a fellow! Go thy way, Hector! There's a brave man, niece. O brave Hector! Look how he looks. There's a countenance! Is't not a brave man?
That's Hector, that one, that one, look, that one. There's a man for you! Go on, Hector! There's a brave man, niece. Oh brave Hector! Look how he looks. What a face! Isn't he a brave man?

Is a' not? It does a man's heart good. Look you what hacks are on his helmet! Look you yonder, do you see? Look you there. There's no jesting; there's laying on; take't off who will, as they say. There be hacks.

Isn't he? It does your heart good. Look at the dents on his helmet! Look over there, do you see? Look there. That's no joke; that's hard fighting. Let anyone take that off who can, as they say. Those are real dents.
Swords! anything, he cares not; and the devil come to him, it's all one. By God's lid, it does one's heart good. Yonder comes Paris, yonder comes Paris.
Swords! Anything, he doesn't care. If the devil himself came at him, it would be all the same. By God's eyelid, it does your heart good. Here comes Paris, here comes Paris.

Look ye yonder, niece; is't not a gallant man too, is't not? Why, this is brave now. Who said he came hurt home today? He's not hurt. Why, this will do Helen's heart good now, ha! Would I could see Troilus now! You shall see Troilus anon.

Look over there, niece. Isn't he a fine man too, isn't he? Why, this is splendid. Who said he came home wounded today? He's not hurt. Why, this will do Helen's heart good, ha! I wish I could see Troilus now! You'll see Troilus soon.
That's Helenus. I marvel where Troilus is. That's / Helenus. I think he went not forth today. That's Helenus.
That's Helenus. I wonder where Troilus is. That's Helenus. I don't think he went out today. That's Helenus.
Helenus! no. Yes, he'll fight indifferent well. I marvel where Troilus is. Hark! do you not hear the people cry 'Troilus'?—Helenus is a priest.
Helenus! No. Yes, he fights reasonably well. I wonder where Troilus is. Listen! Can't you hear the people shouting "Troilus"? Helenus is a priest.
Who's that sneaky-looking fellow over there?
Where? yonder? That's Deiphobus. 'Tis Troilus. There's a man, niece. Hem! Brave Troilus, the prince of chivalry!
Where? Over there? That's Deiphobus. No, it's Troilus! There's a man, niece. Ahem! Brave Troilus, the prince of knighthood!

Mark him; note him. O brave Troilus! Look well upon him, niece; look you how his sword is bloodied, and his helm more hack'd than Hector's; and how he looks, and how he goes! O admirable youth! he never saw three and twenty. Go thy way, Troilus, go thy way. Had I a sister were a grace or a daughter a goddess, he should take his choice. O admirable man! Paris? Paris is dirt to him; and, I warrant, Helen, to change, would give an eye to boot.

Watch him, take note of him. Oh brave Troilus! Look at him carefully, niece. Look how bloody his sword is, and his helmet more dented than Hector's. And look how he looks, and how he walks! Oh admirable young man! He isn't even twenty-three yet. Go on, Troilus, go on. If I had a sister who was one of the Graces, or a daughter who was a goddess, he could take his pick. Oh admirable man! Paris? Paris is dirt next to him, and I bet Helen would give an eye to make the exchange.

Asses, fools, dolts! chaff and bran, chaff and bran! porridge after meat! I could live and die in the eyes of Troilus. Ne'er look, ne'er look; the eagles are gone. Crows and daws, crows and daws! I had rather be such a man as Troilus than Agamemnon and all Greece.

Donkeys, fools, idiots! Chaff and bran, chaff and bran! Porridge after the meat! I could live and die gazing into Troilus' eyes. Don't bother looking, don't bother looking; the eagles have gone. Crows and jackdaws, crows and jackdaws! I'd rather be a man like Troilus than Agamemnon and all of Greece.
There is amongst the Greeks Achilles, a better man than Troilus.
Among the Greeks there's Achilles, a better man than Troilus.
Achilles? A drayman, a porter, a very camel!
Achilles? A carthorse driver, a porter, a real camel!

Well, well! Why, have you any discretion? Have you any eyes? Do you know what a man is? Is not birth, beauty, good shape, discourse, manhood, learning, gentleness, virtue, youth, liberality, and such like, the spice and salt that season a man?

Well, well! Why, have you no judgement? Have you no eyes? Do you know what a man is? Aren't good birth, beauty, a good figure, conversation, manliness, learning, gentleness, virtue, youth, generosity and so on the spice and salt that season a man?
Ay, a minc'd man; and then to be bak'd with no date in the pie, for then the man's date is out.
Yes, a minced man, then baked in a pie with no dates in it, because then the man's date has run out (he is past it).
You are such a woman! A man knows not at what ward you lie.
You're such a woman! A man never knows what guard you're keeping.

Upon my back, to defend my belly; upon my wit, to defend my wiles; upon my secrecy, to defend mine honesty; my mask, to defend my beauty; and you, to defend all these; and at all these wards I lie, at a thousand watches.

On my back, to defend my belly; on my wit, to defend my tricks; on my secrecy, to defend my chastity; my mask, to defend my looks; and you, to defend all of these. I keep all these guards, and a thousand watches.
Tell me one of your watches.

Nay, I'll watch you for that; and that's one of the chiefest of them too. If I cannot ward what I would not have hit, I can watch you for telling how I took the blow; unless it swell past hiding, and then it's past watching.

No, I'll watch you for that, and that's one of the most important ones. If I can't guard what I don't want hit, I can watch to stop you telling how I took the blow, unless it swells too big to hide, and then it's past watching (unless I get pregnant).
Sir, my lord would instantly speak with you.
Sir, my lord wants to speak to you at once.
At your own house; there he unarms him.
At your house. He's taking his armour off there.
Good boy, tell him I come. [Exit Boy] I doubt he be hurt. Fare ye well, good niece.
Good boy, tell him I'm coming. (The Boy leaves.) I'm afraid he's been wounded. Goodbye, good niece.
I will be with you, niece, by and by.
I'll be with you soon, niece.
Yes, a love token from Troilus.

By the same token, you are a bawd. / Words, vows, gifts, tears, and love's full sacrifice, / He offers in another's enterprise; / But more in Troilus thousand-fold I see / Than in the glass of Pandar's praise may be, / Yet hold I off. Women are angels, wooing: / Things won are done; joy's soul lies in the doing. / That she belov'd knows naught that knows not this: / Men prize the thing ungain'd more than it is. / That she was never yet that ever knew / Love got so sweet as when desire did sue; / Therefore this maxim out of love I teach: / 'Achievement is command; ungain'd, beseech.' / Then though my heart's content firm love doth bear, / Nothing of that shall from mine eyes appear.

By that same token, you are a pimp. He offers words, vows, gifts, tears, and the whole sacrifice of love on another man's behalf. But I see a thousand times more in Troilus than the mirror of Pandarus' praise can show. Still I hold back. Women are angels while they are being wooed. Once a thing is won, it is finished; the soul of joy is in the chase. A woman who is loved knows nothing if she doesn't know this: men value what they haven't won more than it is worth. No woman has ever known love to be as sweet once it is gained as when desire was still pleading. So love teaches me this rule: "Once won, men command; while unwon, they beg." So although my heart is full of steady love, none of it will show in my eyes.

Princes, / What grief hath set these jaundies o'er your cheeks? / The ample proposition that hope makes / In all designs begun on earth below / Fails in the promis'd largeness; checks and disasters / Grow in the veins of actions highest rear'd, / As knots, by the conflux of meeting sap, / Infects the sound pine, and diverts his grain / Tortive and errant from his course of growth. / Nor, princes, is it matter new to us / That we come short of our suppose so far / That after seven years' siege yet Troy walls stand; / Sith every action that hath gone before, / Whereof we have record, trial did draw / Bias and thwart, not answering the aim, / And that unbodied figure of the thought / That gave't surmised shape. Why then, you princes, / Do you with cheeks abash'd behold our works / And call them shames, which are, indeed, naught else / But the protractive trials of great Jove / To find persistive constancy in men; / The fineness of which metal is not found / In fortune's love? For then the bold and coward, / The wise and fool, the artist and unread, / The hard and soft, seem all affin'd and kin. / But in the wind and tempest of her frown / Distinction, with a broad and powerful fan, / Puffing at all, winnows the light away; / And what hath mass or matter by itself / Lies rich in virtue and unmingled.

Princes, what trouble has spread this yellow sickness over your faces? The great promises that hope makes at the start of every plan on earth fall short of what was promised. Setbacks and disasters grow inside the highest undertakings, just as knots, caused by the sap meeting, infect the healthy pine and twist its grain off its straight course of growth. And it is nothing new to us, princes, that we have fallen so far short of our expectations that after seven years of siege the walls of Troy still stand. Every action in the past that we have records of went crooked and wrong when it was put to the test, and did not match the aim or the imagined shape that the thought first gave it. So why, princes, do you look at our efforts with embarrassed faces and call them shameful? They are really nothing but the drawn-out tests of great Jove, to find out which men have lasting endurance. The quality of that metal is not found when fortune is kind, because then the brave and the cowardly, the wise and the foolish, the learned and the ignorant, the hard and the soft, all seem alike and related. But in the wind and storm of fortune's frown, the difference between them, like a broad and powerful fan, blows on everything and winnows the light chaff away, and what has real weight and substance lies there rich in virtue and pure.

With due observance of thy godlike seat, / Great Agamemnon, Nestor shall apply / Thy latest words. In the reproof of chance / Lies the true proof of men. The sea being smooth, / How many shallow bauble boats dare sail / Upon her patient breast, making their way / With those of nobler bulk! / But let the ruffian Boreas once enrage / The gentle Thetis, and anon behold / The strong-ribb'd bark through liquid mountains cut, / Bounding between the two moist elements / Like Perseus' horse. Where's then the saucy boat, / Whose weak untimber'd sides but even now / Co-rivall'd greatness? Either to harbour fled / Or made a toast for Neptune. Even so / Doth valour's show and valour's worth divide / In storms of fortune; for in her ray and brightness / The herd hath more annoyance by the breeze / Than by the tiger; but when the splitting wind / Makes flexible the knees of knotted oaks, / And flies fled under shade—why, then the thing of courage, / As rous'd with rage, with rage doth sympathise, / And with an accent tun'd in self-same key / Retorts to chiding fortune.

With due respect to your godlike throne, great Agamemnon, Nestor will apply your last words. The true test of men lies in how they stand up to bad luck. When the sea is calm, how many flimsy little boats dare to sail on her patient surface, keeping pace with much larger ships! But let the rough north wind once stir up the gentle sea, and soon you see the strong-ribbed ship cutting through mountains of water, leaping between the sea and the sky like Perseus' winged horse. Where is the cheeky little boat then, whose weak, flimsy sides a moment ago rivalled greatness? Either it has fled to harbour or it has been swallowed by Neptune like toast in wine. In the same way, the appearance of courage and real courage separate in the storms of fortune. In fortune's bright sunshine the herd is more troubled by the gadfly than by the tiger, but when the splitting wind bends the knees of knotted oaks, and the flies have run for shelter, then the courageous creature, roused to anger, matches the storm's rage and answers back to scolding fortune in the same key.

Agamemnon, / Thou great commander, nerve and bone of Greece, / Heart of our numbers, soul and only spirit / In whom the tempers and the minds of all / Should be shut up—hear what Ulysses speaks. / Besides th'applause and approbation / The which, [To Agamemnon] most mighty, for thy place and sway, / [To Nestor] And, thou most reverend, for thy stretch'd-out life, / I give to both your speeches—which were such / As Agamemnon and the hand of Greece / Should hold up high in brass; and such again / As venerable Nestor, hatch'd in silver, / Should with a bond of air, strong as the axle-tree / On which heaven rides, knit all the Greekish ears / To his experienc'd tongue—yet let it please both, / Thou great, and wise, to hear Ulysses speak.

Agamemnon, great commander, nerve and bone of Greece, heart of our army, soul and single spirit in whom the temperaments and minds of all of us should be contained: listen to what Ulysses says. Besides the applause and approval that I give to both your speeches (to you, most mighty, for your rank and power, and to you, most reverend, for your long life), speeches which Agamemnon and the hand of Greece should engrave in brass, and which venerable Nestor, silver-haired, should use to bind all Greek ears to his experienced tongue with a bond of breath as strong as the axle on which heaven turns: still, may it please you both, great and wise, to hear Ulysses speak.

Speak, Prince of Ithaca; and be't of less expect / That matter needless, of importless burden, / Divide thy lips than we are confident, / When rank Thersites opes his mastic jaws, / We shall hear music, wit, and oracle.
Speak, Prince of Ithaca. We are less likely to hear useless, unimportant things from your lips than we are to hear music, wit and prophecy when foul Thersites opens his jaws.

Troy, yet upon his basis, had been down, / And the great Hector's sword had lack'd a master, / But for these instances: / The specialty of rule hath been neglected; / And look how many Grecian tents do stand / Hollow upon this plain, so many hollow factions. / When that the general is not like the hive, / To whom the foragers shall all repair, / What honey is expected? Degree being vizarded, / Th'unworthiest shows as fairly in the mask. / The heavens themselves, the planets, and this centre, / Observe degree, priority, and place, / Insisture, course, proportion, season, form, / Office, and custom, in all line of order; / And therefore is the glorious planet Sol / In noble eminence enthron'd and spher'd / Amidst the other, whose med'cinable eye / Corrects the influence of evil planets, / And posts, like the commandment of a king, / Sans check, to good and bad. But when the planets / In evil mixture to disorder wander, / What plagues and what portents, what mutiny, / What raging of the sea, shaking of earth, / Commotion in the winds! Frights, changes, horrors, / Divert and crack, rend and deracinate, / The unity and married calm of states / Quite from their fixture! O, when degree is shak'd, / Which is the ladder of all high designs, / The enterprise is sick! How could communities, / Degrees in schools, and brotherhoods in cities, / Peaceful commerce from dividable shores, / The primogenity and due of birth, / Prerogative of age, crowns, sceptres, laurels, / But by degree stand in authentic place? / Take but degree away, untune that string, / And hark what discord follows! Each thing melts / In mere oppugnancy: the bounded waters / Should lift their bosoms higher than the shores, / And make a sop of all this solid globe; / Strength should be lord of imbecility, / And the rude son should strike his father dead; / Force should be right; or, rather, right and wrong— / Between whose endless jar justice resides— / Should lose their names, and so should justice too. / Then everything includes itself in power, / Power into will, will into appetite; / And appetite, an universal wolf, / So doubly seconded with will and power, / Must make perforce an universal prey, / And last eat up himself. Great Agamemnon, / This chaos, when degree is suffocate, / Follows the choking. / And this neglection of degree it is / That by a pace goes backward, with a purpose / It hath to climb. The general's disdain'd / By him one step below, he by the next, / That next by him beneath; so every step, / Exampl'd by the first pace that is sick / Of his superior, grows to an envious fever / Of pale and bloodless emulation. / And 'tis this fever that keeps Troy on foot, / Not her own sinews. To end a tale of length, / Troy in our weakness stands, not in her strength.

Troy would have fallen by now, still on its foundations, and great Hector's sword would have lost its master, if not for these reasons. The proper order of command has been neglected. Look how many Greek tents stand empty on this plain: there are just as many empty factions. When the general is not like the hive that all the foraging bees return to, what honey can be expected? When rank is disguised, the most unworthy man looks as good as anyone behind the mask. The heavens themselves, the planets, and the earth at the centre keep to rank, priority and place, regularity, course, proportion, season, form, function and custom, all in order. That is why the glorious sun is enthroned in noble majesty among the other planets, and its healing eye corrects the influence of evil planets and moves without hindrance, like a king's command, to good and bad alike. But when the planets wander into disorder in a bad combination, what plagues and omens, what rebellion, what raging of the sea, earthquakes, storms of wind! Terrors, upheavals and horrors twist and crack, tear and uproot the unity and wedded calm of states right off their foundations! Oh, when rank is shaken, which is the ladder to all high undertakings, the whole enterprise falls sick! How could communities, ranks in universities, guilds in cities, peaceful trade between distant shores, the rights of the eldest son, the privileges of age, crowns, sceptres and laurels keep their rightful place except through rank? Just take away rank, put that string out of tune, and listen to the discord that follows! Everything would clash in pure conflict. The seas would rise higher than the shores and turn the whole solid globe into a soggy mess. The strong would rule the weak, and the brutal son would strike his father dead. Might would be right; or rather, right and wrong, between whose endless quarrel justice lives, would lose their names, and so would justice. Then everything would be reduced to power, power to will, and will to appetite. And appetite, a universal wolf, backed up by both will and power, would have to make the whole world its prey, and finally eat itself. Great Agamemnon, this chaos follows the choking of rank. It is this neglect of rank that makes us go backwards when we mean to climb. The general is scorned by the man one step below him, that man by the next, and that one by the man below him. So every step, following the example of the first one that grew sick of its superior, grows into a jealous fever of pale, bloodless rivalry. It is this fever that keeps Troy standing, not her own strength. To finish a long story: Troy stands because of our weakness, not her strength.
Most wisely hath Ulysses here discover'd / The fever whereof all our power is sick.
Ulysses has very wisely uncovered the fever that our whole army is sick with.
The nature of the sickness found, Ulysses, / What is the remedy?
Now that you have found what the sickness is, Ulysses, what is the cure?

The great Achilles, whom opinion crowns / The sinew and the forehand of our host, / Having his ear full of his airy fame, / Grows dainty of his worth, and in his tent / Lies mocking our designs; with him Patroclus / Upon a lazy bed the livelong day / Breaks scurril jests; / And with ridiculous and awkward action— / Which, slanderer, he imitation calls— / He pageants us. Sometime, great Agamemnon, / Thy topless deputation he puts on; / And like a strutting player whose conceit / Lies in his hamstring, and doth think it rich / To hear the wooden dialogue and sound / 'Twixt his stretch'd footing and the scaffoldage— / Such to-be-pitied and o'er-wrested seeming / He acts thy greatness in; and when he speaks / 'Tis like a chime a-mending; with terms unsquar'd, / Which, from the tongue of roaring Typhon dropp'd, / Would seem hyperboles. At this fusty stuff / The large Achilles, on his press'd bed lolling, / From his deep chest laughs out a loud applause; / Cries 'Excellent! 'Tis Agamemnon right! / Now play me Nestor; hem, and stroke thy beard, / As he being drest to some oration.' / That's done—as near as the extremest ends / Of parallels, as like as Vulcan and his wife; / Yet god Achilles still cries 'Excellent! / 'Tis Nestor right. Now play him me, Patroclus, / Arming to answer in a night alarm.' / And then, forsooth, the faint defects of age / Must be the scene of mirth: to cough and spit / And, with a palsy fumbling on his gorget, / Shake in and out the rivet. And at this sport / Sir Valour dies; cries 'O, enough, Patroclus; / Or give me ribs of steel! I shall split all / In pleasure of my spleen.' And in this fashion / All our abilities, gifts, natures, shapes, / Severals and generals of grace exact, / Achievements, plots, orders, preventions, / Excitements to the field or speech for truce, / Success or loss, what is or is not, serves / As stuff for these two to make paradoxes.

The great Achilles, whom public opinion crowns as the muscle and front line of our army, has had his ears filled with his windy fame and has become fussy about his own worth. He lies in his tent mocking our plans. Patroclus lies with him on a lazy bed all day long cracking crude jokes, and with ridiculous, clumsy gestures, which the slanderer calls imitation, he acts us out. Sometimes, great Agamemnon, he puts on your supreme authority, and like a strutting actor whose talent is all in his legs, who thinks it wonderful to hear the wooden echo of his stamping on the stage, he acts your greatness in an over-strained performance that deserves pity. When he speaks, it sounds like a chime being repaired, with crooked words that would seem exaggerated even from the mouth of the roaring giant Typhon. At this stale stuff, the large Achilles, lolling on his crushed bed, lets out loud applause from his deep chest, crying, "Excellent! That's Agamemnon exactly! Now play Nestor for me. Clear your throat and stroke your beard, like him getting ready to make a speech." That is done, as close to the real thing as two parallel lines are to each other, as alike as Vulcan and his wife Venus. Yet god Achilles still cries, "Excellent! That's Nestor exactly! Now play him for me, Patroclus, arming himself to answer a night attack." And then, if you please, the weaknesses of old age become the comic scene: coughing and spitting, and shaking the rivets in and out of his neck armour with trembling fingers. At this game Sir Courage dies laughing and cries, "Oh, enough, Patroclus, or give me ribs of steel! I'll split my sides laughing." And in this way all our abilities, gifts, characters, appearances, our individual and shared qualities, our achievements, plans, orders, precautions, calls to battle or speeches for truce, success or loss, what is and what is not, all become material for these two to make jokes about.

And in the imitation of these twain— / Who, as Ulysses says, opinion crowns / With an imperial voice—many are infect. / Ajax is grown self-will'd and bears his head / In such a rein, in full as proud a place / As broad Achilles; keeps his tent like him; / Makes factious feasts; rails on our state of war / Bold as an oracle, and sets Thersites, / A slave whose gall coins slanders like a mint, / To match us in comparisons with dirt, / To weaken and discredit our exposure, / How rank soever rounded in with danger.

And many have been infected by copying these two, whom, as Ulysses says, opinion crowns with an emperor's authority. Ajax has become self-willed and holds his head as high and proudly as big Achilles. He keeps to his tent like him, holds rebellious feasts, and criticises our conduct of the war as boldly as an oracle. And he sets Thersites, a slave whose bile turns out slanders like a mint turns out coins, to compare us to dirt, to weaken and discredit our position, however badly we are surrounded by danger.

They tax our policy and call it cowardice, / Count wisdom as no member of the war, / Forestall prescience, and esteem no act / But that of hand. The still and mental parts / That do contrive how many hands shall strike / When fitness calls them on, and know, by measure / Of their observant toil, the enemies' weight— / Why, this hath not a finger's dignity: / They call this bed-work, mapp'ry, closet-war; / So that the ram that batters down the wall, / For the great swinge and rudeness of his poise, / They place before his hand that made the engine, / Or those that with the fineness of their souls / By reason guide his execution.

They criticise our strategy and call it cowardice. They don't count wisdom as part of the war. They reject foresight and value no action except physical fighting. The quiet thinking that plans how many soldiers should strike when the moment is right, and that works out the enemy's strength through careful observation, isn't worth a finger to them. They call it bed-work, map-making, war in a study. So they rate the battering ram that knocks down the wall, because of the great swing and force of its weight, above the man who made the machine, or above those who guide its use by reason and subtle intelligence.
Let this be granted, and Achilles' horse / Makes many Thetis' sons.
Once we grant this, Achilles' horse is worth many Achilles (sons of Thetis).
What trumpet is that? Look, Menelaus.
What would you fore our tent?
What do you want in front of our tent?
Is this great Agamemnon's tent, I pray you?
Is this great Agamemnon's tent, please?
May one that is a herald and a prince / Do a fair message to his kingly eyes?
May someone who is both a herald and a prince deliver an honourable message to his royal eyes?
With surety stronger than Achilles' arm / Fore all the Greekish heads, which with one voice / Call Agamemnon head and general.
Yes, with a guarantee of safety stronger than Achilles' arm, in front of all the Greek leaders, who all agree in calling Agamemnon their head and general.
Fair leave and large security. How may / A stranger to those most imperial looks / Know them from eyes of other mortals?
Generous permission and great safety. How can a stranger to those most imperial looks tell them apart from the eyes of other mortals?

Ay; / I ask, that I might waken reverence, / And bid the cheek be ready with a blush / Modest as morning when she coldly eyes / The youthful Phoebus. / Which is that god in office, guiding men? / Which is the high and mighty Agamemnon?

Yes. I ask so that I can stir up my respect and tell my cheeks to be ready with a blush as modest as the dawn when she looks shyly at the young sun god. Which one is that god in power, guiding men? Which one is the high and mighty Agamemnon?
This Trojan scorns us, or the men of Troy / Are ceremonious courtiers.
This Trojan is mocking us, or else the men of Troy are very formal courtiers.

Courtiers as free, as debonair, unarm'd, / As bending angels; that's their fame in peace. / But when they would seem soldiers, they have galls, / Good arms, strong joints, true swords; and, Jove's accord, / Nothing so full of heart. But peace, Aeneas, / Peace, Trojan; lay thy finger on thy lips. / The worthiness of praise distains his worth, / If that the prais'd himself bring the praise forth; / But what the repining enemy commends, / That breath fame blows; that praise, sole pure, transcends.

Courtiers as open and gracious, when unarmed, as bowing angels; that is their reputation in peace. But when they want to be soldiers, they have spirit, good weapons, strong limbs, true swords, and, with Jove's help, nothing is so full of courage. But quiet, Aeneas, quiet, Trojan; put your finger to your lips. Praise loses its worth if the man praised praises himself. But what an unwilling enemy praises, that is what fame spreads; that praise alone is pure and goes beyond everything.
Sir, you of Troy, call you yourself Aeneas?
Sir, from Troy, do you call yourself Aeneas?
Ay, Greek, that is my name.
Yes, Greek, that is my name.
What's your affairs, I pray you?
Excuse me, sir, it is for Agamemnon's ears.
He hears naught privately that comes from Troy.
He hears nothing in private that comes from Troy.
Nor I from Troy come not to whisper with him; / I bring a trumpet to awake his ear, / To set his sense on the attentive bent, / And then to speak.
And I haven't come from Troy to whisper with him. I bring a trumpet to wake his ear and make him pay attention, and then I will speak.
Speak frankly as the wind; / It is not Agamemnon's sleeping hour. / That thou shalt know, Trojan, he is awake, / He tells thee so himself.
Speak as freely as the wind. It is not Agamemnon's bedtime. So that you know he is awake, Trojan, he tells you so himself.
Trumpet, blow loud, / Send thy brass voice through all these lazy tents; / And every Greek of mettle, let him know / What Troy means fairly shall be spoke aloud.
Trumpet, blow loud. Send your brass voice through all these lazy tents, and let every Greek with any spirit know that what Troy honourably intends will be spoken aloud.

We have, great Agamemnon, here in Troy / A prince called Hector—Priam is his father— / Who in this dull and long-continued truce / Is resty grown; he bade me take a trumpet / And to this purpose speak: Kings, princes, lords! / If there be one among the fair'st of Greece / That holds his honour higher than his ease, / That feeds his praise more than he fears his peril, / That knows his valour and knows not his fear, / That loves his mistress more than in confession / With truant vows to her own lips he loves, / And dare avow her beauty and her worth / In other arms than hers—to him this challenge. / Hector, in view of Trojans and of Greeks, / Shall make it good or do his best to do it: / He hath a lady wiser, fairer, truer, / Than ever Greek did couple in his arms; / And will tomorrow with his trumpet call / Mid-way between your tents and walls of Troy / To rouse a Grecian that is true in love. / If any come, Hector shall honour him; / If none, he'll say in Troy, when he retires, / The Grecian dames are sunburnt and not worth / The splinter of a lance. Even so much.

Great Agamemnon, we have here in Troy a prince called Hector, Priam's son, who has grown restless in this dull, long truce. He told me to bring a trumpeter and say this: "Kings, princes, lords! If there is one among the best of Greece who values his honour more than his comfort, who seeks praise more than he fears danger, who knows his courage and does not know fear, who loves his lady more than in idle vows spoken to her own lips, and dares to defend her beauty and worth in other arms than hers, to him this challenge. Hector, in sight of Trojans and Greeks, will prove, or do his best to prove, that he has a lady wiser, more beautiful and more faithful than any Greek ever held in his arms. Tomorrow he will call with his trumpet, halfway between your tents and the walls of Troy, to rouse a Greek who is true in love. If anyone comes, Hector will honour him. If no one comes, he will say in Troy, when he goes back, that the Greek ladies are sunburnt and not worth a splinter of a lance." That is all.

This shall be told our lovers, Lord Aeneas. / If none of them have soul in such a kind, / We left them all at home. But we are soldiers; / And may that soldier a mere recreant prove / That means not, hath not, or is not in love. / If then one is, or hath, or means to be, / That one meets Hector; if none else, I am he.

This will be told to our lovers, Lord Aeneas. If none of them has that kind of spirit, we left them all at home. But we are soldiers, and may any soldier prove a total coward who doesn't intend to be, hasn't been, or isn't in love. So if anyone is, or has been, or intends to be, that one will meet Hector. If no one else will, I'll be the one.

Tell him of Nestor, one that was a man / When Hector's grandsire suck'd. He is old now; / But if there be not in our Grecian host / A noble man that hath one spark of fire / To answer for his love, tell him from me / I'll hide my silver beard in a gold beaver, / And in my vambrace put this wither'd brawns, / And meeting him, will tell him that my lady / Was fairer than his grandam, and as chaste / As may be in the world. His youth in flood, / I'll prove this troth with my three drops of blood.

Tell him about Nestor, a man who was grown up when Hector's grandfather was still a baby. He is old now, but if there isn't a single nobleman in our Greek army with one spark of fire to defend his love, tell him from me that I'll hide my silver beard in a gold visor, put these withered arms into armour, and when I meet him tell him that my lady was more beautiful than his grandmother, and as chaste as anyone in the world. Against his youth in full flood I'll prove this truth with my three drops of blood.
Now heavens forfend such scarcity of youth!
Heaven forbid there should be such a shortage of young men!

Fair Lord Aeneas, let me touch your hand; / To our pavilion shall I lead you, sir. / Achilles shall have word of this intent; / So shall each lord of Greece, from tent to tent. / Yourself shall feast with us before you go, / And find the welcome of a noble foe.

Fair Lord Aeneas, let me take your hand. I will lead you to our tent, sir. Achilles will be told of this plan, and so will every lord of Greece, from tent to tent. You will feast with us before you go, and find the welcome a noble enemy deserves.
I have a young conception in my brain; / Be you my time to bring it to some shape.
I have a new idea in my brain. Be the time that helps it grow into some shape.

This 'tis: / Blunt wedges rive hard knots. The seeded pride / That hath to this maturity blown up / In rank Achilles must or now be cropp'd / Or, shedding, breed a nursery of like evil / To overbulk us all.

This is it: blunt wedges split hard knots. The pride that has been sown and has grown to full ripeness in swollen Achilles must either be cut down now or, scattering its seeds, breed a crop of similar evil that will overgrow us all.
This challenge that the gallant Hector sends, / However it is spread in general name, / Relates in purpose only to Achilles.
This challenge that brave Hector sends, however widely it is addressed, is really aimed only at Achilles.

True. The purpose is perspicuous even as substance / Whose grossness little characters sum up; / And, in the publication, make no strain / But that Achilles, were his brain as barren / As banks of Libya—though, Apollo knows, / 'Tis dry enough—will with great speed of judgement, / Ay, with celerity, find Hector's purpose / Pointing on him.

True. The aim is as clear as a total made up of small numbers. When it is announced, there is no doubt that Achilles, even if his brain were as barren as the shores of Libya (and Apollo knows it's dry enough), will very quickly, yes, at once, see that Hector's challenge is aimed at him.
And wake him to the answer, think you?
And you think it will rouse him to answer?

Why, 'tis most meet. Who may you else oppose / That can from Hector bring those honours off, / If not Achilles? Though 't be a sportful combat, / Yet in this trial much opinion dwells / For here the Trojans taste our dear'st repute / With their fin'st palate; and trust to me, Ulysses, / Our imputation shall be oddly pois'd / In this vile action; for the success, / Although particular, shall give a scantling / Of good or bad unto the general; / And in such indexes, although small pricks / To their subsequent volumes, there is seen / The baby figure of the giant mass / Of things to come at large. It is suppos'd / He that meets Hector issues from our choice; / And choice, being mutual act of all our souls, / Makes merit her election, and doth boil, / As 'twere from forth us all, a man distill'd / Out of our virtues; who miscarrying, / What heart receives from hence a conquering part, / To steel a strong opinion to themselves? / Which entertain'd, limbs are his instruments, / In no less working than are swords and bows / Directive by the limbs.

Why, that would be most fitting. Who else could you put up against him who could come away from Hector with honour, if not Achilles? Although it is a friendly fight, a lot of reputation depends on this trial. Here the Trojans will taste our dearest reputation with their finest palate, and believe me, Ulysses, our standing will be strangely balanced on this petty action, because its outcome, though only a single fight, will give a sample of good or bad for the whole army. And in such indexes, though they are small marks compared with the volumes that follow, you can see a baby version of the giant mass of things to come. People will assume that the man who meets Hector is our chosen one, and choice, being the agreed act of all our souls, picks by merit and boils out of us all, as it were, one man distilled from our virtues. If he fails, what encouragement will the winning side take from that to strengthen their opinion of themselves? Once they believe that, their limbs become its tools, just as swords and bows are directed by limbs.

Give pardon to my speech. Therefore 'tis meet / Achilles meet not Hector. Let us, like merchants, / First show foul wares, and think perchance they'll sell; / If not, the lustre of the better shall exceed / By showing the worse first. Do not consent / That ever Hector and Achilles meet; / For both our honour and our shame in this / Are dogg'd with two strange followers.

Excuse me for saying so, but that is why Achilles must not meet Hector. Let's be like merchants: show the shoddy goods first and see if they might sell. If not, the shine of the better goods will look even brighter after showing the worse. Don't agree to Hector and Achilles ever meeting, because both our honour and our shame in this are followed by two strange companions.
I see them not with my old eyes. What are they?
I can't see them with my old eyes. What are they?

What glory our Achilles shares from Hector, / Were he not proud, we all should share with him; / But he already is too insolent; / And it were better parch in Afric sun / Than in the pride and salt scorn of his eyes, / Should he scape Hector fair. If he were foil'd, / Why, then we do our main opinion crush / In taint of our best man. No, make a lott'ry; / And, by device, let blockish Ajax draw / The sort to fight with Hector. Among ourselves / Give him allowance for the better man; / For that will physic the great Myrmidon, / Who broils in loud applause, and make him fall / His crest, that prouder than blue Iris bends. / If the dull brainless Ajax come safe off, / We'll dress him up in voices; if he fail, / Yet go we under our opinion still / That we have better men. But, hit or miss, / Our project's life this shape of sense assumes— / Ajax employ'd plucks down Achilles' plumes.

Whatever glory our Achilles wins from Hector, we would all share with him if he weren't proud. But he is already too arrogant, and it would be better to be scorched in the African sun than in the pride and bitter scorn of his eyes if he came away from Hector well. If he were beaten, then we would crush our main reputation by disgracing our best man. No, let's hold a lottery, and rig it so that thick-headed Ajax draws the lot to fight Hector. Among ourselves, let's treat him as the better man, because that will be good medicine for the great leader of the Myrmidons, who basks in loud applause, and make him lower his crest, which curves more proudly than the rainbow. If the dull, brainless Ajax comes off safely, we'll dress him up in praise. If he fails, we can still keep our reputation that we have better men. But hit or miss, the life of our plan comes down to this: using Ajax will pluck Achilles' feathers.

Now, Ulysses, I begin to relish thy advice; / And I will give a taste thereof forthwith / To Agamemnon. Go we to him straight. / Two curs shall tame each other: pride alone / Must tarre the mastiffs on, as 'twere their bone.

Now, Ulysses, I begin to like the taste of your advice, and I'll give Agamemnon a taste of it at once. Let's go to him straight away. Two dogs will tame each other. Pride alone must set the mastiffs fighting, as if it were their bone.
Agamemnon—how if he had boils, full, all over, generally?
Agamemnon: what if he had boils, full ones, all over him, everywhere?
And those boils did run—say so. Did not the general run then? Were not that a botchy core?
And what if those boils ran? Suppose they did. Wouldn't the general be running then? Wouldn't that be a pus-filled sore?
Then there would come some matter from him; / I see none now.
Then some matter (pus, or sense) would come out of him. I see none now.
Thou bitch-wolf's son, canst thou not hear? Feel, then.
You son of a she-wolf, can't you hear? Then feel.
The plague of Greece upon thee, thou mongrel beef-witted lord!
May the plague of Greece fall on you, you mongrel lord with a brain of beef!
Speak, then, thou unsalted leaven, speak. I will beat thee into handsomeness.
Speak, then, you stale lump of dough, speak. I'll beat you into good looks.

I shall sooner rail thee into wit and holiness; but I think thy horse will sooner con an oration than thou learn a prayer without book. Thou canst strike, canst thou? A red murrain o' thy jade's tricks!

I'll sooner nag you into wisdom and holiness. But I think your horse will learn a speech by heart sooner than you will learn a prayer without reading it. You can hit, can you? A red plague on your nag's tricks!
Toadstool, find out the proclamation for me.
Dost thou think I have no sense, thou strikest me thus?
Do you think I have no feeling, that you hit me like this?
Thou art proclaim'd fool, I think.
You've been proclaimed a fool, I think.
Do not, porpentine, do not; my fingers itch.
Don't, porcupine, don't. My fingers are itching.
I would thou didst itch from head to foot and I had the scratching of thee; I would make thee the loathsomest scab in Greece. When thou art forth in the incursions, thou strikest as slow as another.
I wish you itched from head to foot and I had the job of scratching you. I'd make you the most disgusting scab in Greece. When you're out on raids, you strike as slowly as anyone else.
Thou grumblest and railest every hour on Achilles; and thou art as full of envy at his greatness as Cerberus is at Proserpina's beauty—ay, that thou bark'st at him.
You grumble and rant about Achilles every hour, and you are as full of envy of his greatness as Cerberus is of Proserpina's beauty. Yes, that's why you bark at him.
He would pun thee into shivers with his fist, as a sailor breaks a biscuit.
He'd pound you to bits with his fist, the way a sailor breaks a biscuit.

Ay, do, do; thou sodden-witted lord! Thou hast no more brain than I have in mine elbows; an asinico may tutor thee. You scurvy valiant ass! Thou art here but to thrash Trojans, and thou art bought and sold among those of any wit like a barbarian slave. If thou use to beat me, I will begin at thy heel and tell what thou art by inches, thou thing of no bowels, thou!

Yes, go on, go on, you soggy-brained lord! You have no more brain than I have in my elbows; a little donkey could teach you. You scabby, brave donkey! You're only here to beat Trojans, and anyone with any sense buys and sells you like a foreign slave. If you make a habit of beating me, I'll start at your heel and say what you are inch by inch, you heartless thing, you!
Mars his idiot! Do, rudeness; do, camel; do, do.
Mars's idiot! Go on, brute; go on, camel; go on, go on.
Why, how now, Ajax! Wherefore do ye thus? / How now, Thersites! What's the matter, man?
Why, what's this, Ajax? Why are you doing this? What's going on, Thersites? What's the matter, man?
You see him there, do you?
You see him there, do you?
So I do. What's the matter?
No, but look at him carefully.
But yet you look not well upon him; for whosomever you take him to be, he is Ajax.
But you're still not looking at him properly, because whatever you take him for, he is Ajax (a jakes, a toilet).
Ay, but that fool knows not himself.
Yes, but that fool doesn't know himself.

Lo, lo, lo, lo, what modicums of wit he utters! His evasions have ears thus long. I have bobb'd his brain more than he has beat my bones. I will buy nine sparrows for a penny, and his pia mater is not worth the ninth part of a sparrow. This lord, Achilles—Ajax, who wears his wit in his belly and his guts in his head—I'll tell you what I say of him.

Look, look, look, look, what tiny scraps of wit he comes out with! His answers have donkey's ears this long. I've hit his brain more than he's beaten my bones. I can buy nine sparrows for a penny, and his brain isn't worth a ninth of a sparrow. This lord, Achilles, Ajax, who wears his brains in his belly and his guts in his head, I'll tell you what I say about him.
No, I have to hold you back.
As will stop the eye of Helen's needle, for whom he comes to fight.
...to fill the eye of Helen's needle, and she's the one he's come to fight for.
I would have peace and quietness, but the fool will not— he there; that he; look you there.
I'd like peace and quiet, but the fool won't let me: him there, that one, look there.
O thou damned cur! I shall—
Will you set your wit to a fool's?
Will you match your wits against a fool's?
No, I warrant you, the fool's will shame it.
No, I promise you, the fool's will put his to shame.
I bade the vile owl go learn me the tenour of the proclamation, and he rails upon me.
I told the nasty owl to go and find out what the proclamation said, and he insults me.
I serve here as a volunteer.
Your last service was suff'rance; 'twas not voluntary. No man is beaten voluntary. Ajax was here the voluntary, and you as under an impress.
Your last service was putting up with a beating; that wasn't voluntary. No one gets beaten voluntarily. Ajax was the volunteer here, and you were the one press-ganged.

E'en so; a great deal of your wit too lies in your sinews, or else there be liars. Hector shall have a great catch and knock out either of your brains: a' were as good crack a fusty nut with no kernel.

Just so. A lot of your brains are in your muscles too, or else people are liars. Hector will have a great catch if he knocks out either of your brains: he might as well crack a mouldy nut with no kernel.
There's Ulysses and old Nestor—whose wit was mouldy ere your grandsires had nails on their toes—yoke you like draught oxen, and make you plough up the wars.
There's Ulysses and old Nestor, whose wits were mouldy before your grandfathers had toenails, yoking you like oxen and making you plough the wars.
Yes, good sooth. To Achilles, to Ajax, to—
Yes, truly. To Achilles, to Ajax, to...
I shall cut out your tongue.
'Tis no matter; I shall speak as much as thou afterwards.
It doesn't matter. I'll speak as much as you do afterwards.
I will hold my peace when Achilles' brach bids me, shall I?
I'm supposed to keep quiet when Achilles' bitch-hound tells me to, am I?
I will see you hang'd like clotpoles ere I come any more to your tents. I will keep where there is wit stirring, and leave the faction of fools.
I'll see you hanged like blockheads before I come to your tents again. I'll stay where there's some wit stirring and leave the party of fools.

Marry, this, sir, is proclaim'd through all our host, / That Hector, by the fifth hour of the sun, / Will with a trumpet 'twixt our tents and Troy, / Tomorrow morning, call some knight to arms / That hath a stomach; and such a one that dare / Maintain I know not what; 'tis trash. Farewell.

Well, sir, this is what has been proclaimed through our whole army: that Hector, at the fifth hour after sunrise tomorrow morning, will call out with a trumpet, between our tents and Troy, for some knight with the appetite for it to fight him, someone who dares to maintain I don't know what. It's rubbish. Goodbye.
I know not; 'tis put to lott'ry, otherwise, / He knew his man.
I don't know. It's to be decided by lottery. Otherwise he would know his man.
O, meaning you? I will go learn more of it.
Oh, meaning you? I'll go and find out more about it.

After so many hours, lives, speeches spent, / Thus once again says Nestor from the Greeks: / 'Deliver Helen, and all damage else— / As honour, loss of time, travail, expense, / Wounds, friends, and what else dear that is consum'd / In hot digestion of this cormorant war— / Shall be struck off.' Hector, what say you to't?

After so many hours, lives and speeches spent, Nestor sends this message once again from the Greeks: "Hand over Helen, and all other losses, such as honour, lost time, effort, expense, wounds, friends, and everything else precious that has been consumed in the hot stomach of this greedy war, will be cancelled." Hector, what do you say to that?

Though no man lesser fears the Greeks than I, / As far as toucheth my particular, / Yet, dread Priam, / There is no lady of more softer bowels, / More spongy to suck in the sense of fear, / More ready to cry out 'Who knows what follows?' / Than Hector is. The wound of peace is surety, / Surety secure; but modest doubt is call'd / The beacon of the wise, the tent that searches / To th' bottom of the worst. Let Helen go. / Since the first sword was drawn about this question, / Every tithe soul 'mongst many thousand dismes / Hath been as dear as Helen—I mean, of ours. / If we have lost so many tenths of ours / To guard a thing not ours, nor worth to us, / Had it our name, the value of one ten, / What merit's in that reason which denies / The yielding of her up?

Although no man fears the Greeks less than I do, as far as I personally am concerned, still, revered Priam, there is no lady with a softer heart, more ready to soak up fear, more ready to cry out "Who knows what will happen next?" than Hector. The danger of peace is overconfidence, careless overconfidence. But reasonable doubt is called the beacon of the wise, the probe that searches the worst of a wound to the bottom. Let Helen go. Since the first sword was drawn over this question, every tenth soul among many thousands of tenths has been as precious as Helen; I mean, of our people. If we have lost so many tenths of ours to keep something that is not ours, and that would not be worth one of those tenths even if it were ours, what sense is there in the argument that refuses to give her up?

Fie, fie, my brother! / Weigh you the worth and honour of a king, / So great as our dread father's, in a scale / Of common ounces? Will you with counters sum / The past-proportion of his infinite, / And buckle in a waist most fathomless / With spans and inches so diminutive / As fears and reasons? Fie, for godly shame!

Shame, shame, my brother! Do you weigh the worth and honour of a king as great as our revered father on scales meant for ordinary ounces? Will you add up his immeasurable greatness with counting tokens, and fasten a belt around a waist beyond measuring with spans and inches as tiny as fears and reasons? Shame on you, for God's sake!
No marvel though you bite so sharp of reasons, / You are so empty of them. Should not our father / Bear the great sway of his affairs with reason, / Because your speech hath none that tells him so?
No wonder you snap so sharply at reasons, you're so short of them. Should our father not govern his affairs with reason, just because your speech has no reason to tell him so?

You are for dreams and slumbers, brother priest; / You fur your gloves with reason. Here are your reasons: / You know an enemy intends you harm; / You know a sword employ'd is perilous, / And reason flies the object of all harm. / Who marvels, then, when Helenus beholds / A Grecian and his sword, if he do set / The very wings of reason to his heels / And fly like chidden Mercury from Jove, / Or like a star disorb'd? Nay, if we talk of reason, / Let's shut our gates and sleep. Manhood and honour / Should have hare hearts, would they but fat their thoughts / With this cramm'd reason. Reason and respect / Make livers pale and lustihood deject.

You are for dreams and sleeping, brother priest. You line your gloves with reason. Here are your reasons: you know an enemy means to harm you; you know a sword in use is dangerous; and reason runs from anything that can harm. So who is surprised when Helenus, seeing a Greek with his sword, fixes the wings of reason to his heels and flies off like Mercury scolded by Jove, or like a star knocked out of its orbit? No, if we're going to talk about reason, let's shut our gates and go to sleep. Manhood and honour would have the hearts of hares if they fed their thoughts on this stuffed reason. Reason and caution turn the liver pale and make vigour lose heart.
Brother, she is not worth what she doth cost the keeping.
Brother, she isn't worth what it costs to keep her.
