What is anything worth, except what it is valued at?

But value dwells not in particular will: / It holds his estimate and dignity / As well wherein 'tis precious of itself / As in the prizer. 'Tis mad idolatry / To make the service greater than the god, / And the will dotes that is attributive / To what infectiously itself affects, / Without some image of th'affected merit.

But value doesn't depend on one person's will. A thing has its worth and dignity as much in being precious in itself as in the person who prizes it. It is mad idolatry to make the worship greater than the god, and a will is foolish if it gives value to whatever it is attracted to, without any sign of real merit in the thing it desires.

I take today a wife, and my election / Is led on in the conduct of my will; / My will enkindled by mine eyes and ears, / Two traded pilots 'twixt the dangerous shores / Of will and judgement: how may I avoid, / Although my will distaste what it elected, / The wife I chose? There can be no evasion / To blench from this and to stand firm by honour. / We turn not back the silks upon the merchant / When we have soil'd them; nor the remainder viands / We do not throw in unrespective sieve, / Because we now are full. It was thought meet / Paris should do some vengeance on the Greeks; / Your breath with full consent bellied his sails; / The seas and winds, old wranglers, took a truce, / And did him service. He touch'd the ports desir'd; / And for an old aunt whom the Greeks held captive / He brought a Grecian queen, whose youth and freshness / Wrinkles Apollo's, and makes stale the morning. / Why keep we her? The Grecians keep our aunt. / Is she worth keeping? Why, she is a pearl / Whose price hath launch'd above a thousand ships, / And turn'd crown'd kings to merchants. / If you'll avouch 'twas wisdom Paris went— / As you must needs, for you all cried 'Go, go'— / If you'll confess he brought home worthy prize— / As you must needs, for you all clapp'd your hands, / And cried 'Inestimable!'—why do you now / The issue of your proper wisdoms rate, / And do a deed that never Fortune did— / Beggar the estimation which you priz'd / Richer than sea and land? O theft most base, / That we have stol'n what we do fear to keep! / But thieves unworthy of a thing so stol'n / That in their country did them that disgrace / We fear to warrant in our native place!

Suppose I take a wife today, and my choice is guided by my desire; my desire set on fire by my eyes and ears, two experienced pilots steering between the dangerous shores of desire and judgement. How could I get rid of the wife I chose, even if my desire came to dislike what it had chosen? There is no way to back out of it and still stand firm in honour. We don't give silks back to the merchant once we've dirtied them, and we don't throw leftover food into the slop bucket just because we're now full. It was thought right that Paris should take some revenge on the Greeks. Your breath, all in agreement, filled his sails. The seas and winds, old quarrellers, made a truce and helped him on his way. He reached the ports he wanted, and in exchange for an old aunt whom the Greeks held captive, he brought back a Greek queen whose youth and freshness make Apollo look wrinkled and the morning look stale. Why do we keep her? The Greeks keep our aunt. Is she worth keeping? Why, she is a pearl whose price has launched more than a thousand ships and turned crowned kings into merchants. If you agree it was wise for Paris to go (as you must, because you all cried "Go, go"), if you admit he brought home a worthy prize (as you must, because you all clapped your hands and cried "Priceless!"), why do you now criticise the result of your own wisdom, and do something Fortune never did, reduce to nothing the value of what you rated richer than sea and land? Oh, what a shameful theft, to have stolen something we are afraid to keep! We would be thieves unworthy of what we stole, if we disgraced the Greeks in their own country and are now afraid to defend it in our own.
What noise, what shriek is this?
What noise, what scream is that?
'Tis our mad sister; I do know her voice.
It's our mad sister. I know her voice.
Cry, Trojans, cry. Lend me ten thousand eyes, / And I will fill them with prophetic tears.
Weep, Trojans, weep. Lend me ten thousand eyes, and I will fill them with prophetic tears.

Virgins and boys, mid-age and wrinkled eld, / Soft infancy, that nothing canst but cry, / Add to my clamours. Let us pay betimes / A moiety of that mass of moan to come. / Cry, Trojans, cry. Practise your eyes with tears. / Troy must not be, nor goodly Ilion stand; / Our firebrand brother, Paris, burns us all. / Cry, Trojans, cry, A Helen and a woe! / Cry, cry. Troy burns, or else let Helen go.

Virgins and boys, the middle-aged and the wrinkled old, tender infants who can do nothing but cry, add to my wailing. Let's pay in advance part of the huge debt of grief to come. Weep, Trojans, weep. Train your eyes to cry. Troy will not survive, and splendid Ilium will not stand. Our brother Paris, the firebrand, is burning us all. Weep, Trojans, weep: Helen, and grief! Weep, weep. Troy burns, or else let Helen go.

Now, youthful Troilus, do not these high strains / Of divination in our sister work / Some touches of remorse? Or is your blood / So madly hot, that no discourse of reason, / Nor fear of bad success in a bad cause, / Can qualify the same?

Now, young Troilus, don't these lofty prophecies from our sister stir some feeling of remorse in you? Or is your blood so madly hot that no reasoned argument, and no fear of a bad outcome in a bad cause, can cool it?

Why, brother Hector, / We may not think the justness of each act / Such and no other than event doth form it; / Nor once deject the courage of our minds / Because Cassandra's mad. Her brain-sick raptures / Cannot distaste the goodness of a quarrel / Which hath our several honours all engag'd / To make it gracious. For my private part, / I am no more touch'd than all Priam's sons; / And Jove forbid there should be done amongst us / Such things as might offend the weakest spleen / To fight for and maintain.

Why, brother Hector, we shouldn't judge whether an action is right only by how it turns out, nor should we lose heart because Cassandra is mad. Her brain-sick fits can't spoil the goodness of a quarrel that all our honours are committed to making honourable. For my own part, I am no more involved than any of Priam's sons, and Jove forbid that we should do anything that even the weakest temper would find offensive to fight for and defend.

Else might the world convince of levity / As well my undertakings as your counsels; / But I attest the gods, your full consent / Gave wings to my propension, and cut off / All fears attending on so dire a project. / For what, alas, can these my single arms? / What propugnation is in one man's valour / To stand the push and enmity of those / This quarrel would excite? Yet I protest, / Were I alone to pass the difficulties, / And had as ample power as I have will, / Paris should ne'er retract what he hath done, / Nor faint in the pursuit.

Otherwise the world might accuse both my actions and your advice of being frivolous. But I call the gods to witness, your full agreement gave wings to my inclination and cut off all the fears that came with such a dangerous project. For what, alas, can my two arms do on their own? What defence is there in one man's courage to withstand the attack and hostility that this quarrel would stir up? Yet I swear, if I had to face the difficulties alone, and had as much power as I have will, Paris would never take back what he has done, or lose heart in following it through.
Paris, you speak / Like one besotted on your sweet delights. / You have the honey still, but these the gall; / So to be valiant is no praise at all.
Paris, you speak like someone infatuated with your own sweet pleasures. You still have the honey, but these others have the bitterness, so there's no credit at all in being brave like that.

Sir, I propose not merely to myself / The pleasures such a beauty brings with it; / But I would have the soil of her fair rape / Wip'd off in honourable keeping her. / What treason were it to the ransack'd queen, / Disgrace to your great worths, and shame to me, / Now to deliver her possession up / On terms of base compulsion! Can it be, / That so degenerate a strain as this / Should once set footing in your generous bosoms? / There's not the meanest spirit on our party / Without a heart to dare or sword to draw / When Helen is defended; nor none so noble / Whose life were ill bestow'd or death unfam'd, / Where Helen is the subject. Then, I say, / Well may we fight for her whom we know well / The world's large spaces cannot parallel.

Sir, I am not thinking only of the pleasures such a beauty brings with her. I want the stain of her abduction wiped away by keeping her honourably. What treason it would be to the stolen queen, what a disgrace to your great honour and what a shame to me, to hand her over now on terms forced on us so humiliatingly! Can such a degenerate idea ever find a foothold in your noble hearts? There isn't the lowest spirit on our side who lacks the heart to dare or the sword to draw when Helen is being defended, and no one so noble that his life would be wasted or his death unfamous when Helen is the cause. So I say we may well fight for her, since we know the whole wide world has no equal to her.

Paris and Troilus, you have both said well; / And on the cause and question now in hand / Have gloz'd, but superficially; not much / Unlike young men, whom Aristotle thought / Unfit to hear moral philosophy. / The reasons you allege do more conduce / To the hot passion of distemp'red blood / Than to make up a free determination / 'Twixt right and wrong; for pleasure and revenge / Have ears more deaf than adders to the voice / Of any true decision. Nature craves / All dues be rend'red to their owners. Now, / What nearer debt in all humanity / Than wife is to the husband? If this law / Of nature be corrupted through affection; / And that great minds, of partial indulgence / To their benumbed wills, resist the same; / There is a law in each well-order'd nation / To curb those raging appetites that are / Most disobedient and refractory. / If Helen, then, be wife to Sparta's king— / As it is known she is—these moral laws / Of nature and of nations speak aloud / To have her back return'd. Thus to persist / In doing wrong extenuates not wrong, / But makes it much more heavy. Hector's opinion / Is this, in way of truth. Yet, ne'ertheless, / My spritely brethren, I propend to you / In resolution to keep Helen still; / For 'tis a cause that hath no mean dependence / Upon our joint and several dignities.

Paris and Troilus, you have both spoken well, and you have commented on the cause and question we are discussing, but only superficially, not unlike the young men whom Aristotle thought unfit to hear moral philosophy. The reasons you give have more to do with the hot passion of disordered blood than with reaching a free judgement between right and wrong, because pleasure and revenge have ears deafer than adders to the voice of any true decision. Nature demands that everything owed be given back to its owner. Now, what closer debt is there in all humanity than a wife to her husband? If this law of nature is corrupted by passion, and great men resist it out of indulgence to their own numbed wills, there is a law in every well-ordered nation to curb those raging appetites that are most disobedient and stubborn. So if Helen is the wife of the king of Sparta, as everyone knows she is, these moral laws of nature and of nations loudly demand that she be returned. To keep on doing wrong does not lessen the wrong, but makes it much heavier. That is Hector's opinion, as a matter of truth. But nevertheless, my spirited brothers, I lean towards your decision to keep Helen, because it is a cause on which our honour, together and individually, depends heavily.

Why, there you touch'd the life of our design. / Were it not glory that we more affected / Than the performance of our heaving spleens, / I would not wish a drop of Trojan blood / Spent more in her defence. But, worthy Hector, / She is a theme of honour and renown, / A spur to valiant and magnanimous deeds, / Whose present courage may beat down our foes, / And fame in time to come canonize us; / For I presume brave Hector would not lose / So rich advantage of a promis'd glory / As smiles upon the forehead of this action / For the wide world's revenue.

Why, now you've touched the heart of our purpose. If it weren't glory that we cared about more than giving vent to our angry tempers, I wouldn't want a single drop more Trojan blood spent defending her. But, worthy Hector, she is a cause of honour and fame, a spur to brave and noble deeds, whose courage now may beat down our enemies and whose fame in times to come may make saints of us. For I assume brave Hector would not give up such a rich chance of promised glory as smiles on the face of this enterprise, not for all the wealth of the wide world.

I am yours, / You valiant offspring of great Priamus. / I have a roisting challenge sent amongst / The dull and factious nobles of the Greeks / Will strike amazement to their drowsy spirits. / I was advertis'd their great general slept, / Whilst emulation in the army crept. / This, I presume, will wake him.

I'm with you, you brave sons of great Priam. I have sent a rousing challenge among the dull, quarrelling Greek nobles that will shock their drowsy spirits. I was told their great general was asleep while rivalry crept through the army. This, I think, will wake him up.

How now, Thersites! What, lost in the labyrinth of thy fury? Shall the elephant Ajax carry it thus? He beats me, and I rail at him. O worthy satisfaction! Would it were otherwise: that I could beat him, whilst he rail'd at me! 'Sfoot, I'll learn to conjure and raise devils, but I'll see some issue of my spiteful execrations. Then there's Achilles, a rare engineer! If Troy be not taken till these two undermine it, the walls will stand till they fall of themselves. O thou great thunder-darter of Olympus, forget that thou art Jove, the king of gods, and, Mercury, lose all the serpentine craft of thy caduceus, if ye take not that little little less than little wit from them that they have! which short-arm'd ignorance itself knows is so abundant scarce, it will not in circumvention deliver a fly from a spider without drawing their massy irons and cutting the web. After this, the vengeance on the whole camp! or, rather, the Neapolitan bone-ache! for that, methinks, is the curse depending on those that war for a placket. I have said my prayers; and devil Envy say 'Amen.' What ho! my Lord Achilles!

Well, Thersites! What, lost in the maze of your fury? Is the elephant Ajax going to get away with it like this? He beats me, and I insult him. Oh, what fine satisfaction! I wish it were the other way round: that I could beat him while he insulted me. By God's foot, I'll learn to do magic and raise devils, but I'll see some result from my spiteful curses. Then there's Achilles, a fine engineer! If Troy isn't taken until these two undermine it, the walls will stand until they fall down by themselves. Oh, you great thunderbolt-thrower of Olympus, forget that you are Jove, the king of gods, and Mercury, lose all the snaky cunning of your staff, if you don't take away the little, little, less than little wit that they have! Even short-armed ignorance knows it is so scarce that it couldn't rescue a fly from a spider without drawing their heavy swords and cutting the web. After that, vengeance on the whole camp! Or rather, syphilis! Because that, I think, is the curse hanging over those who fight a war for a petticoat. I've said my prayers, and let the devil Envy say "Amen." Hey there! My Lord Achilles!
Who's there? Thersites! Good Thersites, come in and rail.
Who's there? Thersites! Good Thersites, come in and rant.

If I could a' rememb'red a gilt counterfeit, thou wouldst not have slipp'd out of my contemplation; but it is no matter; thyself upon thyself! The common curse of mankind, folly and ignorance, be thine in great revenue! Heaven bless thee from a tutor, and discipline come not near thee! Let thy blood be thy direction till thy death. Then if she that lays thee out says thou art a fair corse, I'll be sworn and sworn upon't she never shrouded any but lazars. Amen. Where's Achilles?

If I had remembered a gilded fake coin, you wouldn't have slipped out of my thoughts. But it doesn't matter: may you get what you are! The common curse of mankind, folly and ignorance, be yours in great quantity! Heaven keep you from a teacher, and may education never come near you! Let your passions guide you until you die. Then, if the woman who lays you out says you're a good-looking corpse, I'll swear and swear again that she has never wrapped any bodies but lepers'. Amen. Where's Achilles?
What, art thou devout? Wast thou in prayer?
What, are you religious? Were you praying?
Yes, may the heavens hear me!
Where, where? O, where? Art thou come? Why, my cheese, my digestion, why hast thou not served thyself in to my table so many meals? Come, what's Agamemnon?
Where, where? Oh, where? Have you come? Why, my cheese, my digestive, why haven't you served yourself up at my table for so many meals? Come on, what is Agamemnon?
Thy commander, Achilles. Then tell me, Patroclus, what's Achilles?
Your commander, Achilles. Now tell me, Patroclus, what is Achilles?
Thy lord, Thersites. Then tell me, I pray thee, what's Thersites?
Your lord, Thersites. Now tell me, please, what is Thersites?
Thy knower, Patroclus. Then tell me, Patroclus, what art thou?
The one who knows you, Patroclus. Now tell me, Patroclus, what are you?
You must say, since you know.
I'll decline the whole question. Agamemnon commands Achilles; Achilles is my lord; I am Patroclus' knower; and Patroclus is a fool.
I'll go through the whole question like a grammar lesson. Agamemnon commands Achilles; Achilles is my lord; I am the one who knows Patroclus; and Patroclus is a fool.
Peace, fool! I have not done.
He is a privileg'd man. Proceed, Thersites.
He's allowed to say anything. Carry on, Thersites.
Agamemnon is a fool; Achilles is a fool; Thersites is a fool; and, as aforesaid, Patroclus is a fool.
Agamemnon is a fool; Achilles is a fool; Thersites is a fool; and, as I said before, Patroclus is a fool.
Agamemnon is a fool to offer to command Achilles; Achilles is a fool to be commanded of Agamemnon; Thersites is a fool to serve such a fool; and this Patroclus is a fool positive.
Agamemnon is a fool to try to command Achilles; Achilles is a fool to be commanded by Agamemnon; Thersites is a fool to serve such a fool; and this Patroclus is a fool, plain and simple.
Make that demand of the Creator. It suffices me thou art. Look you, who comes here?
Ask the Creator that. It's enough for me that you are. Look, who's coming here?
Come, Patroclus, I'll speak with nobody. Come in with me, Thersites.
Come on, Patroclus, I won't speak to anyone. Come in with me, Thersites.

Here is such patchery, such juggling, and such knavery. All the argument is a whore and a cuckold—a good quarrel to draw emulous factions and bleed to death upon. Now the dry serpigo on the subject, and war and lechery confound all!

Here's such patching up, such trickery and such villainy. The whole cause is a whore and a cuckold, a fine quarrel to set rival factions against each other and bleed to death over. May a dry skin disease fall on the cause, and war and lechery destroy everything!
Within his tent; but ill-dispos'd, my lord.
In his tent, but unwell, my lord.

Let it be known to him that we are here. / He sate our messengers; and we lay by / Our appertainings, visiting of him. / Let him be told so; lest, perchance, he think / We dare not move the question of our place / Or know not what we are.

Let him know that we are here. He has insulted our messengers, and we have put aside our rank to visit him. Tell him so, in case he thinks we don't dare insist on our position, or don't know who we are.
I shall say so to him.
We saw him at the opening of his tent. / He is not sick.
We saw him at the entrance of his tent. He isn't sick.
Yes, lion-sick, sick of proud heart. You may call it melancholy, if you will favour the man; but, by my head, 'tis pride. But why, why? Let him show us a cause. A word, my lord.
Yes, lion-sick, sick with a proud heart. You can call it melancholy if you want to be kind to the man, but, by my head, it's pride. But why, why? Let him show us a reason. A word, my lord.
What moves Ajax thus to bay at him?
What makes Ajax bark at him like this?
Achilles hath inveigled his fool from him.
Achilles has lured his fool away from him.
Then will Ajax lack matter, if he have lost his argument.
Then Ajax will run short of material, if he has lost his subject.
No; you see he is his argument that has his argument, Achilles.
No; you see, his subject now is the man who has his subject: Achilles.
All the better; their fraction is more our wish than their faction. But it was a strong composure a fool could disunite!
So much the better. We want them split more than we want them united. But it was a strong alliance if a fool could break it up!
The amity that wisdom knits not, folly may easily untie.
A friendship that wisdom doesn't bind together, folly can easily untie.
The elephant hath joints, but none for courtesy; his legs are legs for necessity, not for flexure.
The elephant has joints, but none for courtesy. His legs are legs for necessity, not for bending.

Achilles bids me say he is much sorry / If any thing more than your sport and pleasure / Did move your greatness and this noble state / To call upon him; he hopes it is no other / But for your health and your digestion sake, / An after-dinner's breath.

Achilles tells me to say he is very sorry if anything more than your amusement and pleasure moved your greatness and this noble company to call on him. He hopes it is nothing more than an after-dinner stroll for the sake of your health and your digestion.

Hear you, Patroclus. / We are too well acquainted with these answers; / But his evasion, wing'd thus swift with scorn, / Cannot outfly our apprehensions. / Much attribute he hath, and much the reason / Why we ascribe it to him. Yet all his virtues, / Not virtuously on his own part beheld, / Do in our eyes begin to lose their gloss; / Yea, like fair fruit in an unwholesome dish, / Are like to rot untasted. Go and tell him / We come to speak with him; and you shall not sin / If you do say we think him over-proud / And under-honest, in self-assumption greater / Than in the note of judgement; and worthier than himself / Here tend the savage strangeness he puts on, / Disguise the holy strength of their command, / And underwrite in an observing kind / His humorous predominance; yea, watch / His course and time, his ebbs and flows, as if / The passage and whole stream of this commencement / Rode on his tide. Go tell him this, and add / That if he overhold his price so much / We'll none of him, but let him, like an engine / Not portable, lie under this report: / Bring action hither; this cannot go to war. / A stirring dwarf we do allowance give / Before a sleeping giant. Tell him so.

Listen, Patroclus. We know these answers too well, but his evasion, though it flies so fast on the wings of scorn, cannot outfly our understanding. He has many fine qualities, and many reasons why we credit him with them. Yet all his virtues, since he does not display them virtuously, are beginning to lose their shine in our eyes; yes, like good fruit on a dirty dish, they are likely to rot untasted. Go and tell him we have come to speak with him. And it won't be a sin if you tell him we think him too proud and not honest enough, greater in his own opinion than in the judgement of sensible people, and that better men than he are here waiting on the savage aloofness he puts on, hiding the sacred strength of their authority and humbly putting up with his moody dominance; yes, watching his moods and timing, his ebbs and flows, as if the whole course and current of this campaign rode on his tide. Go and tell him this, and add that if he overprices himself so much, we'll have nothing to do with him. We'll let him lie, like a siege engine too heavy to move, under this verdict: "Bring the fighting here; this cannot go to war." We value a busy dwarf above a sleeping giant. Tell him so.
I shall, and bring his answer presently.
I will, and bring his answer straight away.
In second voice we'll not be satisfied; / We come to speak with him. Ulysses, enter you.
We won't be satisfied with a go-between. We have come to speak with him. Ulysses, you go in.
What is he more than another?
What is he more than anyone else?
No more than what he thinks he is.
No more than what he thinks he is.
Is he so much? Do you not think he thinks himself a better man than I am?
Is he as much as that? Don't you think he thinks he's a better man than me?
Will you subscribe his thought and say he is?
Will you agree with his opinion and say he is?
No, noble Ajax; you are as strong, as valiant, as wise, no less noble, much more gentle, and altogether more tractable.
No, noble Ajax. You are as strong, as brave, as wise, no less noble, much more courteous, and altogether easier to deal with.
Why should a man be proud? How doth pride grow? I know not what pride is.
Why should a man be proud? How does pride grow? I don't know what pride is.

Your mind is the clearer, Ajax, and your virtues the fairer. He that is proud eats up himself. Pride is his own glass, his own trumpet, his own chronicle; and whatever praises itself but in the deed devours the deed in the praise.

Your mind is all the clearer for it, Ajax, and your virtues all the finer. A proud man eats himself up. Pride is its own mirror, its own trumpet, its own history book; and whatever praises itself except by its actions destroys the action in the praising.
I do hate a proud man as I do hate the engend'ring of toads.
I hate a proud man as much as I hate toads breeding.
[Aside] And yet he loves himself: is't not strange?
(Aside) And yet he loves himself. Isn't that strange?
Achilles will not to the field tomorrow.
Achilles won't go to the battlefield tomorrow.
He doth rely on none; / But carries on the stream of his dispose, / Without observance or respect of any, / In will peculiar and in self-admission.
He doesn't bother with one. He just follows the stream of his own mood, without paying attention or respect to anyone, with a will of his own and only his own approval.
Why will he not, upon our fair request, / Untent his person and share th'air with us?
Why won't he, when we ask him politely, come out of his tent and share the air with us?

Things small as nothing, for request's sake only, / He makes important; possess'd he is with greatness, / And speaks not to himself but with a pride / That quarrels at self-breath. Imagin'd worth / Holds in his blood such swol'n and hot discourse / That 'twixt his mental and his active parts / Kingdom'd Achilles in commotion rages, / And batters down himself. What should I say? / He is so plaguy proud that the death tokens of it / Cry 'No recovery.'

He makes things as small as nothing important, just because he is asked. He is possessed with his own greatness, and he can't even talk to himself without a pride that quarrels with its own breath. His imagined worth stirs up such a swollen, hot argument in his blood that Achilles, a kingdom in himself, rages in civil war between his mind and his actions and batters himself down. What can I say? He is so plaguily proud that the fatal spots of the disease cry "No recovery."
Let Ajax go to him. / Dear lord, go you and greet him in his tent. / 'Tis said he holds you well; and will be led / At your request a little from himself.
Let Ajax go to him. Dear lord, go and greet him in his tent. They say he thinks well of you, and he will let himself be drawn a little out of himself if you ask him.

O Agamemnon, let it not be so! / We'll consecrate the steps that Ajax makes / When they go from Achilles. Shall the proud lord / That bastes his arrogance with his own seam / And never suffers matter of the world / Enter his thoughts, save such as doth revolve / And ruminate himself—shall he be worshipp'd / Of that we hold an idol more than he? / No, this thrice worthy and right valiant lord / Shall not so stale his palm, nobly acquir'd, / Nor, by my will, assubjugate his merit, / As amply titled as Achilles is, / By going to Achilles. / That were to enlard his fat-already pride, / And add more coals to Cancer when he burns / With entertaining great Hyperion. / This lord go to him! Jupiter forbid, / And say in thunder 'Achilles go to him.'

Oh Agamemnon, don't let that happen! We will bless every step Ajax takes away from Achilles. Shall that proud lord, who bastes his arrogance in his own fat, and never lets any worldly matter enter his thoughts except what concerns himself, be worshipped by the man we idolise more than him? No, this three-times-worthy and truly brave lord must not cheapen his nobly won glory, nor, if I have anything to do with it, make his merit, which is as amply honoured as Achilles', subject to Achilles by going to him. That would be adding lard to his already fat pride, and adding more coal to the sign of Cancer when it burns with the summer sun. This lord go to him! Jupiter forbid, and say in thunder, "Achilles, go to him."
[Aside] O, this is well! He rubs the vein of him.
(Aside) Oh, this is good! He's rubbing him the right way.
[Aside] And how his silence drinks up this applause!
(Aside) And how his silence soaks up this praise!
If I go to him, with my armed fist I'll pash him o'er the face.
If I go to him, I'll smash him in the face with my armoured fist.
O, no, you shall not go.
An a' be proud with me I'll pheeze his pride. / Let me go to him.
If he's proud with me, I'll fix his pride. Let me go to him.
Not for the worth that hangs upon our quarrel.
Not for all that depends on our quarrel.
I'll bleed him to cure his moods.
[Aside] He will be the physician that should be the patient.
(Aside) He'll be the doctor when he should be the patient.
And all men were o' my mind—
If all men thought like me...
[Aside] Wit would be out of fashion.
(Aside) Wit would be out of fashion.
A' should not bear it so, a' should eat's words first. / Shall pride carry it?
He shouldn't get away with it like this; he should eat his words first. Shall pride win the day?
(Aside) If it did, you'd have half the winnings.
I will knead him, I'll make him supple.
I'll knead him, I'll make him soft.
[Aside] He's not yet through warm. Force him with praises; pour in, pour in; his ambition is dry.
(Aside) He's not warmed through yet. Stuff him with praise; pour it in, pour it in; his ambition is dry.
[To Agamemnon] My lord, you feed too much on this dislike.
(To Agamemnon) My lord, you dwell too much on this resentment.
Our noble general, do not do so.
Our noble general, don't do it.
You must prepare to fight without Achilles.
You must prepare to fight without Achilles.
Why 'tis this naming of him does him harm. / Here is a man—but 'tis before his face; / I will be silent.
Why, it's this talk about him that does the harm. Here is a man... but he's standing right here; I'll say nothing.
Wherefore should you so? / He is not emulous, as Achilles is.
Why should you? He isn't jealous of praise, the way Achilles is.
Know the whole world, he is as valiant.
Let the whole world know, he is as brave.
A whoreson dog, that shall palter with us thus! / Would he were a Trojan!
The bastard dog, to mess us around like this! I wish he were a Trojan!
What a vice were it in Ajax now—
What a fault it would be in Ajax now...
Or aloof, or in love with himself.

Thank the heavens, lord, thou art of sweet composure / Praise him that gat thee, she that gave thee suck; / Fam'd be thy tutor, and thy parts of nature / Thrice fam'd beyond, beyond all erudition; / But he that disciplin'd thine arms to fight— / Let Mars divide eternity in twain / And give him half; and, for thy vigour, / Bull-bearing Milo his addition yield / To sinewy Ajax. I will not praise thy wisdom, / Which, like a bourn, a pale, a shore, confines / Thy spacious and dilated parts. Here's Nestor, / Instructed by the antiquary times— / He must, he is, he cannot but be wise; / But pardon, father Nestor, were your days / As green as Ajax' and your brain so temper'd, / You should not have the eminence of him, / But be as Ajax.

Thank heaven, lord, you have a sweet nature. Praise your father, and your mother who nursed you. Let your teacher be famous, and your natural gifts three times more famous, beyond all learning. But as for the man who trained your arms to fight, let Mars cut eternity in two and give him half. And as for your strength, let Milo, who carried a bull, give up his title to muscular Ajax. I won't praise your wisdom, which, like a boundary, a fence, a shore, contains your wide-ranging talents. Here's Nestor, taught by ancient times. He must be wise, he is, he can't help being wise. But excuse me, father Nestor, if your days were as young as Ajax's and your brain as well balanced, you wouldn't be superior to him; you would be just like Ajax.
Be rul'd by him, Lord Ajax.

There is no tarrying here; the hart Achilles / Keeps thicket. Please it our great general / To call together all his state of war; / Fresh kings are come to Troy. Tomorrow / We must with all our main of power stand fast; / And here's a lord—come knights from east to west / And cull their flower, Ajax shall cope the best.

There's no point waiting here. The stag Achilles is hiding in the thicket. May it please our great general to call his whole war council together. New kings have come to help Troy. Tomorrow we must stand firm with all our strength. And here's a lord: let knights come from east to west and pick their best, Ajax will match the best of them.
Go we to council. Let Achilles sleep. / Light boats sail swift, though greater hulks draw deep.
Let's go to the council. Let Achilles sleep. Light boats sail fast, though bigger ships sit deeper in the water.
Friend, you—pray you, a word. Do you not follow the young Lord Paris?
Friend, you there, please, a word. Don't you follow the young Lord Paris?
Ay, sir, when he goes before me.
Yes, sir, when he walks in front of me.
You depend upon him, I mean?
I mean, you depend on him?
Sir, I do depend upon the Lord.
Sir, I depend on the Lord.
You depend upon a notable gentleman; I must needs praise him.
You depend on a remarkable gentleman. I must praise him.
You know me, do you not?
Friend, know me better: I am the Lord Pandarus.
Friend, get to know me better. I am the Lord Pandarus.
I hope I shall know your honour better.
I hope I'll know your honour better (that you'll become better).
You are in the state of grace?
Are you in a state of grace?
Grace? Not so, friend; honour and lordship are my titles. What music is this?
Grace? No, friend; "honour" and "lordship" are my titles. What music is this?
I do but partly know, sir; it is music in parts.
I only partly know, sir. It is music in parts.
At mine, sir, and theirs that love music.
At mine, sir, and at the pleasure of those who love music.
I mean at whose command, friend.
Friend, we understand not one another: I am too courtly, and thou art too cunning. At whose request do these men play?
Friend, we don't understand each other. I am too polite and you are too clever. At whose request are these men playing?
That's to't, indeed, sir. Marry, sir, at the request of Paris my lord, who is there in person; with him the mortal Venus, the heart-blood of beauty, love's invisible soul—
Now you've got to the point, sir. Well, sir, at the request of my lord Paris, who is there in person, and with him the mortal Venus, the heart's blood of beauty, love's invisible soul...
No, sir, Helen. Could not you find out that by her attributes?
No, sir, Helen. Couldn't you tell that from the description?
It should seem, fellow, that thou hast not seen the Lady Cressida. I come to speak with Paris from the Prince Troilus; I will make a complimental assault upon him, for my business seethes.
It seems, fellow, that you have never seen the Lady Cressida. I have come to speak to Paris on behalf of Prince Troilus. I'll launch a polite attack on him, because my business is boiling.
Sodden business! There's a stew'd phrase indeed!
Boiled business! That's a stewed phrase indeed! (Stews were brothels.)
Fair be to you, my lord, and to all this fair company! Fair desires, in all fair measure, fairly guide them—especially to you, fair queen! Fair thoughts be your fair pillow.
Fairness be with you, my lord, and with all this fair company! May fair desires, in all fair measure, guide them fairly, especially you, fair queen! May fair thoughts be your fair pillow.
Dear lord, you are full of fair words.
Dear lord, you are full of fair words.
You speak your fair pleasure, sweet queen. Fair prince, here is good broken music.
You're just saying what pleases you, sweet queen. Fair prince, here is some fine music in parts.
You have broke it, cousin; and by my life, you shall make it whole again; you shall piece it out with a piece of your performance.
You have broken it, cousin, and by my life you'll make it whole again; you'll patch it up with a piece of your own performance.
Rude, in sooth; in good sooth, very rude.
Rough, honestly; in all honesty, very rough.
Well said, my lord. Well, you say so in fits.
Well said, my lord. Well, you say so in bursts (in musical sections).
I have business to my lord, dear queen. My lord, will you vouchsafe me a word?
I have business with my lord, dear queen. My lord, will you grant me a word?
Nay, this shall not hedge us out. We'll hear you sing, certainly—
No, this won't shut us out. We'll hear you sing, certainly.
Well sweet queen, you are pleasant with me. But, marry, thus, my lord: my dear lord and most esteemed friend, your brother Troilus—
Well, sweet queen, you're teasing me. But, well, it's this, my lord: my dear lord and most respected friend, your brother Troilus...
Go to, sweet queen, go to—commends himself most affectionately to you—
Come on, sweet queen, come on... sends his most affectionate greetings to you...
You shall not bob us out of our melody. If you do, our melancholy upon your head!
You won't cheat us out of our song. If you do, our sadness be on your head!
Sweet queen, sweet queen; that's a sweet queen, i' faith.
Sweet queen, sweet queen; that's a sweet queen, honestly.
And to make a sweet lady sad is a sour offence.
And to make a sweet lady sad is a sour offence.

Nay, that shall not serve your turn; that shall it not, in truth, la. Nay, I care not for such words; no, no.—And, my lord, he desires you that, if the King call for him at supper, you will make his excuse.
No, that won't work; it won't, really, no. No, I don't care for such words, no, no. And, my lord, he asks that if the King calls for him at supper, you'll make his excuses.
What says my sweet queen, my very very sweet queen?
What does my sweet queen say, my very, very sweet queen?
What exploit's in hand? Where sups he tonight?
What's he up to? Where is he having supper tonight?
What says my sweet queen?—My cousin will fall out with you.
What does my sweet queen say? My niece will fall out with you.
You must not know where he sups.
You mustn't know where he's having supper.
I'll lay my life, with my disposer Cressida.
I'll bet my life it's with my disposer Cressida.
No, no, no such matter; you are wide. Come, your disposer is sick.
No, no, nothing of the kind; you're way off. Come on, your disposer is sick.
Ay, good my lord. Why should you say Cressida? / No, your poor disposer's sick.
Yes, my good lord. Why should you say Cressida? No, your poor disposer is sick.
You spy! What do you spy?—Come, give me an instrument. Now, sweet queen.
You see! What do you see? Come, give me an instrument. Now, sweet queen.
Why, this is kind of you.
My niece is horribly in love with a thing you have, sweet queen.
My niece is horribly in love with something you have, sweet queen.
She shall have it, my lord, if it be not my Lord Paris.
She can have it, my lord, as long as it isn't my Lord Paris.
He? No, she'll none of him; they two are twain.
Him? No, she wants nothing to do with him. Those two are two separate people.
Falling in, after falling out, may make them three.
Making up after falling out might make them three (a baby).
Come, come. I'll hear no more of this; I'll sing you a song now.
Come, come, I won't hear any more of this. I'll sing you a song now.
Ay, ay, prithee now. By my troth, sweet lord, thou hast a fine forehead.
Yes, yes, please do. Honestly, sweet lord, you have a fine forehead.
Let thy song be love. This love will undo us all. O Cupid, Cupid, Cupid!
Let your song be about love. This love will ruin us all. Oh Cupid, Cupid, Cupid!
Love! Ay, that it shall, i' faith.
Love! Yes, it shall be, truly.
Ay, good now, love, love, nothing but love.
Yes, please, love, love, nothing but love.
In good troth, it begins so.

Love, love, nothing but love, still love, still more! / For, oh, love's bow / Shoots buck and doe; / The shaft confounds / Not that it wounds, / But tickles still the sore. / These lovers cry, O ho, they die! / Yet that which seems the wound to kill / Doth turn O ho! to ha! ha! he! / So dying love lives still. / O ho! a while, but ha! ha! ha! / O ho! groans out for ha! ha! ha!—hey ho!

Love, love, nothing but love, always more love! Oh, love's bow shoots both buck and doe. The arrow doesn't kill by wounding, but keeps tickling the sore. These lovers cry, "Oh ho, we're dying!" Yet what seems to be the fatal wound turns "Oh ho!" into "Ha ha he!" So dying love lives on. "Oh ho!" for a while, then "Ha ha ha!" "Oh ho!" groans into "Ha ha ha!" Heigh ho!
In love, i' faith, to the very tip of the nose.
In love, truly, to the very tip of his nose.
He eats nothing but doves, love; and that breeds hot blood, and hot blood begets hot thoughts, and hot thoughts beget hot deeds, and hot deeds is love.
He eats nothing but doves, my love, and that breeds hot blood, and hot blood breeds hot thoughts, and hot thoughts breed hot deeds, and hot deeds are love.
Is this the generation of love: hot blood, hot thoughts, and hot deeds? Why, they are vipers. Is love a generation of vipers? Sweet lord, who's a-field today?
Is this how love is bred: hot blood, hot thoughts and hot deeds? Why, they are vipers. Is love a brood of vipers? Sweet lord, who's out fighting today?
Hector, Deiphobus, Helenus, Antenor, and all the gallantry of Troy. I would fain have arm'd today, but my Nell would not have it so. How chance my brother Troilus went not?
Hector, Deiphobus, Helenus, Antenor, and all the fine knights of Troy. I wanted to arm myself today, but my Nell wouldn't let me. How is it my brother Troilus didn't go?
He hangs the lip at something. You know all, Lord Pandarus.
He's sulking about something. You know everything, Lord Pandarus.
Not I, honey-sweet queen. I long to hear how they spend today. You'll remember your brother's excuse?
Not I, honey-sweet queen. I'm longing to hear how they get on today. You'll remember your brother's excuse?
Give my regards to your niece.

They're come from the field. Let us to Priam's hall / To greet the warriors. Sweet Helen, I must woo you / To help unarm our Hector. His stubborn buckles, / With these your white enchanting fingers touch'd, / Shall more obey than to the edge of steel / Or force of Greekish sinews; you shall do more / Than all the island kings—disarm great Hector.

They've come back from the battlefield. Let's go to Priam's hall to greet the warriors. Sweet Helen, I must ask you to help take off our Hector's armour. His stubborn buckles, touched by these white, enchanting fingers of yours, will give way more readily than to the edge of steel or the force of Greek muscle. You will do more than all the island kings: disarm great Hector.
'Twill make us proud to be his servant, Paris; / Yea, what he shall receive of us in duty / Gives us more palm in beauty than we have, / Yea, overshines ourself.
It will make me proud to be his servant, Paris. Yes, the duty he receives from me will give me more glory than my beauty does; yes, it will outshine me.
Sweet, above thought I love thee.
Sweet, I love you more than thought can say.
How now! Where's thy master? At my cousin Cressida's?
Hello! Where's your master? At my niece Cressida's?
No, sir; he stays for you to conduct him thither.
No, sir; he's waiting for you to take him there.
O, here he comes. How now, how now?
Oh, here he comes. Well, well?

No, Pandarus. I stalk about her door / Like a strange soul upon the Stygian banks / Staying for waftage. O, be thou my Charon, / And give me swift transportance to these fields / Where I may wallow in the lily beds / Propos'd for the deserver! O gentle Pandar, / from Cupid's shoulder pluck his painted wings, / and fly with me to Cressid!

No, Pandarus. I prowl about her door like a newly dead soul on the banks of the Styx waiting to be ferried across. Oh, be my Charon, and give me quick passage to those fields where I can roll in the lily beds promised to those who deserve them! Oh gentle Pandarus, pluck the painted wings from Cupid's shoulders and fly with me to Cressida!
Walk here i' th' orchard, I'll bring her straight.
Walk here in the orchard. I'll bring her straight away.

I am giddy; expectation whirls me round. / Th'imaginary relish is so sweet / That it enchants my sense; what will it be / When that the wat'ry palate tastes indeed / Love's thrice-repured nectar? Death, I fear me; / Sounding destruction; or some joy too fine, / Too subtle-potent, tun'd too sharp in sweetness, / For the capacity of my ruder powers. / I fear it much; and I do fear besides / That I shall lose distinction in my joys; / As doth a battle, when they charge on heaps / The enemy flying.

I'm dizzy; expectation spins me round. The imagined taste is so sweet that it enchants my senses. What will it be like when my watering mouth really tastes love's three-times-purified nectar? Death, I'm afraid; a swooning destruction; or some joy too fine, too subtly powerful, tuned too sharply sweet for my coarser senses to take in. I'm very afraid of it. And I'm also afraid that I'll lose all sense of distinction in my joys, like an army charging in a confused mass when the enemy is fleeing.

She's making her ready, she'll come straight; you must be witty now. She does so blush, and fetches her wind so short, as if she were fray'd with a sprite. I'll fetch her. It is the prettiest villain; she fetches her breath as short as a new-ta'en sparrow.

She's getting herself ready; she'll come straight away. You must be clever now. She's blushing so much, and catching her breath so short, as if she'd been frightened by a ghost. I'll fetch her. She's the prettiest little rascal; she catches her breath as short as a newly caught sparrow.
Even such a passion doth embrace my bosom. / My heart beats thicker than a feverous pulse, / And all my powers do their bestowing lose, / Like vassalage at unawares encount'ring / The eye of majesty.
Just such a passion fills my chest. My heart beats faster than a fevered pulse, and all my faculties lose their function, like subjects suddenly meeting the eye of their king.

Come, come, what need you blush? Shame's a baby. Here she is now; swear the oaths now to her that you have sworn to me.—What, are you gone again? You must be watch'd ere you be made tame, must you? Come your ways, come your ways; and you draw backward, we'll put you i' th' fills. Why do you not speak to her? Come, draw this curtain and let's see your picture. Alas the day, how loath you are to offend daylight! And 'twere dark, you'd close sooner. So, so; rub on, and kiss the mistress. How now, a kiss in fee-farm! Build there, carpenter; the air is sweet. Nay, you shall fight your hearts out ere I part you. The falcon as the tercel, for all the ducks i' th' river. Go to, go to.

Come, come, why do you need to blush? Shyness is for babies. Here she is now. Swear to her now the oaths you've sworn to me. What, are you running off again? You need to be kept awake before you're tamed, do you, like a hawk? Come along, come along. If you pull back, we'll put you in the shafts like a horse. Why don't you speak to her? Come, draw back this curtain and let's see your picture. (He lifts her veil.) Alas, how unwilling you are to offend the daylight! If it were dark, you'd come together sooner. So, so; keep going and kiss the target. Well, a kiss with a lease for life! Build there, carpenter, the air is sweet. No, you can fight till your hearts give out before I separate you. The female falcon matches the male, I'll bet all the ducks in the river. Go on, go on.
You have bereft me of all words, lady.
You have taken away all my words, lady.

Words pay no debts, give her deeds; but she'll bereave you o' th' deeds too, if she call your activity in question. What, billing again? Here's 'In witness whereof the parties interchangeably.' Come in, come in; I'll go get a fire.

Words don't pay debts; give her deeds. But she'll take away your deeds too, if she puts your energy to the test. What, kissing again? Here's "In witness of which, the parties have exchanged signatures." Come in, come in. I'll go and light a fire.
Will you walk in, my lord?
Will you come in, my lord?
O Cressid, how often have I wish'd me thus!
Oh Cressida, how often I have wished to be like this!
Wish'd, my lord! The gods grant—O my lord!
Wished, my lord! May the gods grant... oh, my lord!
What should they grant? What makes this pretty abruption? What too curious dreg espies my sweet lady in the fountain of our love?
What should they grant? Why did you break off so suddenly? What tiny speck of dirt has my sweet lady spotted in the fountain of our love?
More dregs than water, if my fears have eyes.
More dirt than water, if my fears can see.
Fears make devils of cherubins; they never see truly.
Fears turn angels into devils. They never see truly.
Blind fear, that seeing reason leads, finds safer footing than blind reason stumbling without fear. To fear the worst oft cures the worse.
Blind fear, led by clear-sighted reason, walks more safely than blind reason stumbling about without fear. Fearing the worst often cures the worst.
O, let my lady apprehend no fear! In all Cupid's pageant there is presented no monster.
Oh, let my lady not be afraid of anything! In all of Cupid's pageant there's no monster.

Nothing, but our undertakings when we vow to weep seas, live in fire, eat rocks, tame tigers; thinking it harder for our mistress to devise imposition enough than for us to undergo any difficulty imposed. This is the monstruosity in love, lady, that the will is infinite, and the execution confin'd; that the desire is boundless, and the act a slave to limit.

Nothing, except our promises, when we vow to weep oceans, live in fire, eat rocks, tame tigers, thinking it harder for our lady to think up enough tasks than for us to perform any hard task she sets. This is what is monstrous in love, lady: that the will is infinite and the performance limited; that the desire is boundless and the act a slave to its limits.

They say all lovers swear more performance than they are able, and yet reserve an ability that they never perform; vowing more than the perfection of ten, and discharging less than the tenth part of one. They that have the voice of lions and the act of hares, are they not monsters?

They say all lovers swear to perform more than they can, and yet keep back an ability they never use, vowing more than ten men could do perfectly and doing less than a tenth of what one man could. Those who have the voices of lions and the actions of hares, aren't they monsters?

Are there such? Such are not we. Praise us as we are tasted, allow us as we prove; our head shall go bare till merit crown it. No perfection in reversion shall have a praise in present. We will not name desert before his birth; and, being born, his addition shall be humble. Few words to fair faith: Troilus shall be such to Cressid as what envy can say worst shall be a mock for his truth; and what truth can speak truest not truer than Troilus.

Are there such men? We are not like that. Praise us as you find us when you've tried us; value us as we prove ourselves. We will go bareheaded until merit crowns us. No perfection still to come will get praise now. We will not name what we deserve before it is born, and once it is born, its title will be modest. A few words to true faith: Troilus will be such to Cressida that the worst that envy can say will only be a joke against his loyalty, and the truest thing truth can say will be no truer than Troilus.
Will you walk in, my lord?
Will you come in, my lord?
What, blushing still? Have you not done talking yet?
What, still blushing? Haven't you finished talking yet?
Well, uncle, what folly I commit, I dedicate to you.
Well, uncle, whatever foolishness I commit, I dedicate to you.
I thank you for that; if my lord get a boy of you, you'll give him me. Be true to my lord; if he flinch, chide me for it.
Thank you for that. If my lord gets a boy by you, you'll give him to me. Be faithful to my lord. If he backs off, blame me for it.
You know now your hostages: your uncle's word and my firm faith.
Now you know your guarantees: your uncle's word and my firm faith.
Nay, I'll give my word for her too: our kindred, though they be long ere they are wooed, they are constant being won; they are burs, I can tell you; they'll stick where they are thrown.
No, I'll give my word for her too. Our family, though they take a long time to be won over, are faithful once they're won. They're burrs, I can tell you; they stick where they're thrown.
Boldness comes to me now and brings me heart. / Prince Troilus, I have lov'd you night and day / For many weary months.
Now boldness comes to me and gives me courage. Prince Troilus, I have loved you night and day for many weary months.
Why was my Cressid then so hard to win?
Then why was my Cressida so hard to win?

Hard to seem won; but I was won, my lord, / With the first glance that ever—pardon me. / If I confess much, you will play the tyrant. / I love you now; but till now not so much / But I might master it. In faith, I lie; / My thoughts were like unbridled children, grown / Too headstrong for their mother. See, we fools! / Why have I blabb'd? Who shall be true to us, / When we are so unsecret to ourselves? / But, though I lov'd you well, I woo'd you not; / And yet, good faith, I wish'd myself a man, / Or that we women had men's privilege / Of speaking first. Sweet, bid me hold my tongue, / For in this rapture I shall surely speak / The thing I shall repent. See, see, your silence, / Cunning in dumbness, from my weakness draws / My very soul of counsel. Stop my mouth.

Hard to seem won. But I was won, my lord, with the first look that ever... forgive me. If I confess too much, you'll play the tyrant. I love you now, but until now not so much that I couldn't control it. No, honestly, I'm lying. My thoughts were like unruly children, grown too headstrong for their mother. See what fools we are! Why have I blurted it out? Who will keep our secrets when we can't keep them ourselves? But though I loved you well, I didn't woo you. And yet, honestly, I wished I were a man, or that we women had men's right to speak first. Sweet, tell me to hold my tongue, because in this rapture I'm sure to say something I'll regret. Look, look, your silence, cunning in saying nothing, draws the secrets out of my very soul in my weakness. Stop my mouth.
And shall, albeit sweet music issues thence.
And I will, even though sweet music comes from it. (He kisses her.)
My lord, I do beseech you, pardon me; / 'Twas not my purpose thus to beg a kiss. / I am asham'd. O heavens! what have I done? / For this time will I take my leave, my lord.
My lord, I beg you, forgive me. I didn't mean to beg for a kiss like that. I'm ashamed. Oh heavens! What have I done? I'll say goodbye for now, my lord.
Leave! And you take leave till tomorrow morning—
Goodbye! If you say goodbye before tomorrow morning...
Let me go and try. / I have a kind of self resides with you; / But an unkind self, that itself will leave / To be another's fool. I would be gone. / Where is my wit? I know not what I speak.
Let me go and try. I have a kind of self that lives with you, but an unkind self, that will leave itself to be another's fool. I want to go. Where are my wits? I don't know what I'm saying.
Well know they what they speak that speak so wisely.
People who speak so wisely know very well what they're saying.

Perchance, my lord, I show more craft than love; / And fell so roundly to a large confession / To angle for your thoughts; but you are wise— / Or else you love not; for to be wise and love / Exceeds man's might; that dwells with gods above.

Perhaps, my lord, I'm showing more cunning than love, and launched so readily into a full confession to fish for your thoughts. But you are wise, or else you're not in love, because to be wise and in love at once is beyond man's power; that belongs to the gods above.

O that I thought it could be in a woman— / As, if it can, I will presume in you— / To feed for aye her lamp and flames of love; / To keep her constancy in plight and youth, / Outliving beauty's outward, with a mind / That doth renew swifter than blood decays! / Or that persuasion could but thus convince me / That my integrity and truth to you / Might be affronted with the match and weight / Of such a winnowed purity in love. / How were I then uplifted! But, alas, / I am as true as truth's simplicity, / And simpler than the infancy of truth.

Oh, if only I thought a woman could (and if one can, I'll believe it of you) keep the lamp and flames of her love burning for ever, keep her faith as fresh and young as when she pledged it, outlasting her outward beauty, with a mind that renews itself faster than the body decays! Or if only I could be convinced that my loyalty and faith to you would be met with an equal measure and weight of such purified love. How lifted up I would be then! But alas, I am as true as plain truth itself, and simpler than truth in its infancy.
In that I'll war with you.

O virtuous fight, / When right with right wars who shall be most right! / True swains in love shall in the world to come / Approve their truth by Troilus, when their rhymes, / Full of protest, of oath, and big compare, / Want similes, truth tir'd with iteration— / As true as steel, as plantage to the moon, / As sun to day, as turtle to her mate, / As iron to adamant, as earth to th' centre— / Yet, after all comparisons of truth, / As truth's authentic author to be cited, / 'As true as Troilus' shall crown up the verse / And sanctify the numbers.

Oh virtuous battle, when right fights right over who will be most right! In times to come, faithful lovers will prove their faithfulness by Troilus. When their poems, full of promises, oaths and grand comparisons, run out of similes, and truth is worn out with repeating "as true as steel, as plants to the moon, as sun to day, as turtle dove to her mate, as iron to a magnet, as earth to the centre", then, after all these comparisons of truth, "as true as Troilus" will crown the verse and make the poem holy, quoted as the original authority on truth.

Prophet may you be! / If I be false, or swerve a hair from truth, / When time is old and hath forgot itself, / When waterdrops have worn the stones of Troy, / And blind oblivion swallow'd cities up, / And mighty states characterless are grated / To dusty nothing—yet let memory / From false to false, among false maids in love, / Upbraid my falsehood when th' have said 'As false / As air, as water, wind, or sandy earth, / As fox to lamb, or wolf to heifer's calf, / Pard to the hind, or stepdame to her son'— / Yea, let them say, to stick the heart of falsehood, / 'As false as Cressid.'

May you be a prophet! If I am false, or stray a hair's breadth from truth, when time is old and has forgotten itself, when drops of water have worn away the stones of Troy, and blind oblivion has swallowed up cities, and mighty states have been ground down without trace to dusty nothing, then let memory, from one false lover to the next, among unfaithful girls in love, condemn my falseness. When they have said "as false as air, as water, wind or sandy ground, as fox to lamb or wolf to calf, leopard to deer or stepmother to stepson", yes, let them say, to pierce falseness to the heart, "as false as Cressida."

Go to, a bargain made; seal it, seal it; I'll be the witness. Here I hold your hand; here my cousin's. If ever you prove false one to another, since I have taken such pains to bring you together, let all pitiful goers-between be call'd to the world's end after my name—call them all Pandars; let all constant men be Troiluses, all false women Cressids, and all brokers between Pandars. Say 'Amen.'

Go on, it's a deal. Seal it, seal it; I'll be the witness. Here I hold your hand, and here my niece's. If you ever prove false to each other, after all the trouble I've taken to bring you together, let all pitiful go-betweens be called by my name until the end of the world: call them all Pandars. Let all faithful men be Troiluses, all false women Cressidas, and all go-betweens Pandars. Say "Amen."
Amen. Whereupon I will show you a chamber and a bed; which bed, because it shall not speak of your pretty encounters, press it to death. Away!
Amen. And so I'll show you to a room with a bed, and so that the bed won't tell about your pretty encounters, press it to death. Away with you!
And Cupid grant all tongue-tied maidens here, / Bed, chamber, pander, to provide this gear!
And may Cupid give all the tongue-tied girls here a bed, a room and a go-between to provide this stuff!

Now, Princes, for the service I have done, / Th'advantage of the time prompts me aloud / To call for recompense. Appear it to your mind / That, through the sight I bear in things to come, / I have abandon'd Troy, left my possession, / Incurr'd a traitor's name, expos'd myself / From certain and possess'd conveniences / To doubtful fortunes, sequest'ring from me all / That time, acquaintance, custom, and condition, / Made tame and most familiar to my nature; / And here, to do you service, am become / As new into the world, strange, unacquainted— / I do beseech you, as in way of taste, / To give me now a little benefit / Out of those many regist'red in promise, / Which you say live to come in my behalf.

Now, Princes, for the service I have done you, the opportunity of the moment prompts me to ask out loud for my reward. Remember that, because of my power to see the future, I have abandoned Troy, left my property, earned the name of traitor, and exposed myself, leaving safe and secure comforts for an uncertain fortune. I have cut myself off from everything that time, friends, habit and position had made comfortable and familiar to me, and here, to serve you, I have become like a newborn in the world, a stranger who knows no one. I beg you, as a kind of first taste, to give me now a small reward out of the many you have promised, which you say are still to come for me.
What wouldst thou of us, Trojan? Make demand.
What do you want from us, Trojan? Ask.

You have a Trojan prisoner call'd Antenor, / Yesterday took; Troy holds him very dear. / Oft have you—often have you thanks therefore— / Desir'd my Cressid in right great exchange, / Whom Troy hath still denied; but this Antenor, / I know, is such a wrest in their affairs / That their negotiations all must slack / Wanting his manage; and they will almost / Give us a prince of blood, a son of Priam, / In change of him. Let him be sent, great Princes, / And he shall buy my daughter; and her presence / Shall quite strike off all service I have done / In most accepted pain.

You have a Trojan prisoner called Antenor, captured yesterday. Troy values him very highly. You have often (and I thank you for it) asked for my Cressida in exchange for important prisoners, and Troy has always refused. But I know this Antenor is so essential to their affairs that all their negotiations will grind to a halt without his management, and they would almost give us a royal prince, a son of Priam, in exchange for him. Let him be sent, great Princes, and he will buy my daughter back. Her presence will completely pay off all the service I have done, so willingly and so painfully.

Let Diomedes bear him, / And bring us Cressid hither. Calchas shall have / What he requests of us. Good Diomed, / Furnish you fairly for this interchange; / Withal, bring word if Hector will tomorrow / Be answer'd in his challenge. Ajax is ready.

Let Diomedes take him and bring Cressida here. Calchas shall have what he asks of us. Good Diomedes, equip yourself properly for this exchange. And bring back word whether Hector's challenge will be answered tomorrow. Ajax is ready.
This shall I undertake; and 'tis a burden / Which I am proud to bear.
I'll do this, and it's a burden I'm proud to carry.

Achilles stands i' th'entrance of his tent. / Please it our general pass strangely by him, / As if he were forgot; and, Princes all, / Lay negligent and loose regard upon him. / I will come last. 'Tis like he'll question me / Why such unplausive eyes are bent, why turn'd on him. / If so, I have derision med'cinable / To use between your strangeness and his pride, / Which his own will shall have desire to drink. / It may do good. Pride hath no other glass / To show itself but pride; for supple knees / Feed arrogance and are the proud man's fees.

Achilles is standing at the entrance of his tent. Please, general, walk past him coldly, as if he were forgotten. And, all you Princes, give him only careless, offhand looks. I will come last. He will probably ask me why such disapproving looks are turned on him. If so, I have some healing scorn to apply between your coldness and his pride, which his own will will want to drink. It may do some good. Pride has no mirror to see itself in except other people's pride, because bending knees feed arrogance and are the proud man's wages.

We'll execute your purpose, and put on / A form of strangeness as we pass along. / So do each lord; and either greet him not, / Or else disdainfully, which shall shake him more / Than if not look'd on. I will lead the way.

We'll carry out your plan and put on a show of coldness as we go past. Let each lord do the same, and either not greet him or greet him scornfully, which will shake him more than not being looked at. I'll lead the way.
What comes the general to speak with me? / You know my mind. I'll fight no more 'gainst Troy.
Is the general coming to speak to me? You know my mind. I won't fight against Troy any more.
What says Achilles? Would he aught with us?
What does Achilles say? Does he want anything from us?
Would you, my lord, aught with the general?
Do you want anything from the general, my lord?
How do you? How do you?
How are you? How are you?
What, does the cuckold scorn me?
What, does the cuckold scorn me?
Ay, and good next day too.
Yes, and good next day too.
What mean these fellows? Know they not Achilles?
What do these fellows mean? Don't they know Achilles?
They pass by strangely. They were us'd to bend, / To send their smiles before them to Achilles, / To come as humbly as they us'd to creep / To holy altars.
They pass by coldly. They used to bow, to send their smiles ahead of them to Achilles, to come as humbly as they used to creep up to holy altars.

What, am I poor of late? / 'Tis certain, greatness, once fall'n out with fortune, / Must fall out with men too. What the declin'd is, / He shall as soon read in the eyes of others / As feel in his own fall; for men, like butterflies, / Show not their mealy wings but to the summer; / And not a man for being simply man / Hath any honour, but honour for those honours / That are without him, as place, riches, and favour, / Prizes of accident, as oft as merit; / Which when they fall, as being slippery standers, / The love that lean'd on them as slippery too, / Doth one pluck down another, and together / Die in the fall. But 'tis not so with me: / Fortune and I are friends; I do enjoy / At ample point all that I did possess / Save these men's looks; who do, methinks, find out / Something not worth in me such rich beholding / As they have often given. Here is Ulysses. / I'll interrupt his reading. / How now, Ulysses!

What, have I become poor lately? It's certain that greatness, once it falls out with fortune, must fall out with men too. A fallen man will read his fall in other people's eyes as soon as he feels it himself. For men, like butterflies, only show their powdery wings in summer. And no man is honoured simply for being a man, but for honours that are outside him, like position, wealth and favour, which are prizes of chance as often as of merit. When those fall, being slippery supports, the love that leaned on them, just as slippery, falls too; one pulls the other down and they die together in the fall. But that isn't how it is with me. Fortune and I are friends. I still enjoy in full everything I had, except these men's looks. They seem, I think, to find something in me not worth the rich attention they used to give. Here is Ulysses. I'll interrupt his reading. Hello, Ulysses!

A strange fellow here / Writes me that man—how dearly ever parted, / How much in having, or without or in— / Cannot make boast to have that which he hath, / Nor feels not what he owes, but by reflection; / As when his virtues shining upon others / Heat them, and they retort that heat again / To the first giver.

A strange writer here tells me that a man, however richly gifted, however much he has inside or outside himself, cannot boast of having what he has, or feel what he owns, except by reflection, as when his virtues shine on others and warm them, and they send that warmth back to the one who first gave it.

This is not strange, Ulysses. / The beauty that is borne here in the face / The bearer knows not, but commends itself / To others' eyes; nor doth the eye itself— / That most pure spirit of sense—behold itself, / Not going from itself; but eye to eye opposed / Salutes each other with each other's form; / For speculation turns not to itself / Till it hath travell'd, and is mirror'd there / Where it may see itself. This is not strange at all.

That isn't strange, Ulysses. The beauty a person carries in his face is not known to him, but shows itself to other people's eyes. Nor does the eye itself, that purest of the senses, see itself, since it cannot go out of itself. But when two eyes face each other, each greets the other with its own image, because sight does not turn back on itself until it has travelled out and been mirrored where it can see itself. This isn't strange at all.

I do not strain at the position— / It is familiar—but at the author's drift; / Who, in his circumstance, expressly proves / That no man is the lord of anything, / Though in and of him there be much consisting, / Till he communicate his parts to others; / Nor doth he of himself know them for aught / Till he behold them formed in the applause / Where th'are extended; who, like an arch, reverb'rate / The voice again; or, like a gate of steel / Fronting the sun, receives and renders back / His figure and his heat. I was much rapt in this; / And apprehended here immediately / Th'unknown Ajax. Heavens, what a man is there! / A very horse that has he knows not what! / Nature, what things there are / Most abject in regard and dear in use! / What things again most dear in the esteem / And poor in worth! Now shall we see tomorrow— / An act that very chance doth throw upon him— / Ajax renown'd. O heavens, what some men do, / While some men leave to do! / How some men creep in skittish Fortune's hall, / Whiles others play the idiots in her eyes! / How one man eats into another's pride, / While pride is fasting in his wantonness! / To see these Grecian lords!—why, even already / They clap the lubber Ajax on the shoulder, / As if his foot were on brave Hector's breast, / And great Troy shrieking.

I don't have trouble with the idea, which is familiar, but with where the author is going with it. He argues in detail that no man is master of anything, however much there is in him and of him, until he shares his qualities with others. Nor does he know them to be worth anything himself until he sees them shaped in the applause they receive. That applause, like an arch, echoes the voice back, or, like a steel gate facing the sun, receives and reflects back its image and its heat. I was very absorbed in this, and immediately thought of the unrecognised Ajax. Heavens, what a man he is! A real horse, who has he doesn't know what! Nature, what things there are that are thought worthless and are precious in use! And other things highly valued and poor in worth! Now tomorrow we shall see, through an act that pure chance throws on him, Ajax made famous. Oh heavens, what some men do while other men leave things undone! How some men creep into fickle Fortune's hall while others play the idiot in front of her! How one man feeds on another's glory while the proud man starves in his idleness! To see these Greek lords! Why, already they're slapping that lump Ajax on the shoulder, as if his foot were on brave Hector's chest and great Troy were shrieking.
I do believe it; for they pass'd by me / As misers do by beggars, neither gave to me / Good word nor look. What, are my deeds forgot?
I believe it, because they passed me like misers passing beggars; they gave me neither a kind word nor a look. What, are my deeds forgotten?

Time hath, my lord, a wallet at his back, / Wherein he puts alms for oblivion, / A great-siz'd monster of ingratitudes. / Those scraps are good deeds past, which are devour'd / As fast as they are made, forgot as soon / As done. Perseverance, dear my lord, / Keeps honour bright. To have done is to hang / Quite out of fashion, like a rusty mail / In monumental mock'ry. Take the instant way; / For honour travels in a strait so narrow— / Where one but goes abreast. Keep then the path, / For emulation hath a thousand sons / That one by one pursue; if you give way, / Or hedge aside from the direct forthright, / Like to an ent'red tide they all rush by / And leave you hindmost; / Or, like a gallant horse fall'n in first rank, / Lie there for pavement to the abject rear, / O'er-run and trampled on. Then what they do in present, / Though less than yours in past, must o'ertop yours; / For Time is like a fashionable host, / That slightly shakes his parting guest by th'hand; / And with his arms out-stretch'd, as he would fly, / Grasps in the comer. The welcome ever smiles, / And farewell goes out sighing. O, let not virtue seek / Remuneration for the thing it was; / For beauty, wit, / High birth, vigour of bone, desert in service, / Love, friendship, charity, are subjects all / To envious and calumniating Time. / One touch of nature makes the whole world kin— / That all with one consent praise new-born gauds, / Though they are made and moulded of things past, / And give to dust that is a little gilt / More laud than gilt o'er-dusted. / The present eye praises the present object. / Then marvel not, thou great and complete man, / That all the Greeks begin to worship Ajax, / Since things in motion sooner catch the eye / Than what stirs not. The cry went once on thee, / And still it might, and yet it may again, / If thou wouldst not entomb thyself alive / And case thy reputation in thy tent, / Whose glorious deeds but in these fields of late / Made emulous missions 'mongst the gods themselves, / And drave great Mars to faction.

Time, my lord, has a bag on his back in which he puts alms for oblivion, a huge monster of ingratitude. Those scraps are past good deeds, which are devoured as soon as they are done, forgotten as soon as they are finished. Perseverance, my dear lord, keeps honour bright. To have done something is to hang completely out of fashion, like rusty armour on a monument, a mockery. Take the immediate path, because honour travels down a passage so narrow that only one can walk in it at a time. So keep to the path, because rivalry has a thousand sons who follow one after another. If you give way, or step aside from the straight road, they all rush past like a tide coming in and leave you last. Or, like a fine horse that has fallen in the front rank, you lie there as a pavement for the miserable rear, run over and trampled on. Then what they do now, though less than what you did in the past, must top yours. For Time is like a fashionable host who barely shakes his departing guest's hand, and grasps the new arrival with outstretched arms as if he wanted to fly. Welcome always smiles, and farewell goes out sighing. Oh, don't let virtue look for a reward for what it was. Beauty, wit, high birth, strength, merit in service, love, friendship, charity, are all subject to envious, slandering Time. One trait of human nature makes the whole world alike: everyone agrees in praising new-made trinkets, even though they are made and moulded out of old things, and they give more praise to dust with a little gold on it than to gold covered in dust. The eye of the present praises what is present. So don't be surprised, you great and perfect man, that all the Greeks are beginning to worship Ajax, since things that move catch the eye sooner than things that are still. The cheering was once for you, and still could be, and may be again, if you would not bury yourself alive and shut your reputation up in your tent. Your glorious deeds on these very fields only recently made the gods themselves compete and drove great Mars to take sides.
Of this my privacy / I have strong reasons.
I have strong reasons for keeping to myself.
But 'gainst your privacy / The reasons are more potent and heroical. / 'Tis known, Achilles, that you are in love / With one of Priam's daughters.
But the reasons against your keeping to yourself are stronger and more heroic. It is known, Achilles, that you are in love with one of Priam's daughters.

Is that a wonder? / The providence that's in a watchful state / Knows almost every grain of Plutus' gold; / Finds bottom in th'uncomprehensive deeps; / Keeps place with thought, and almost, like the gods, / Do thoughts unveil in their dumb cradles. / There is a mystery—with whom relation / Durst never meddle—in the soul of state, / Which hath an operation more divine / Than breath or pen can give expressure to. / All the commerce that you have had with Troy / As perfectly is ours as yours, my lord; / And better would it fit Achilles much / To throw down Hector than Polyxena. / But it must grieve young Pyrrhus now at home, / When fame shall in our island sound her trump, / And all the Greekish girls shall tripping sing / 'Great Hector's sister did Achilles win; / But our great Ajax bravely beat down him.' / Farewell, my lord. I as your lover speak. / The fool slides o'er the ice that you should break.

Is that a surprise? The foresight of a watchful state knows almost every grain of Plutus' gold, finds the bottom of unfathomable depths, keeps pace with thought, and, almost like the gods, uncovers thoughts while they are still unspoken in their cradles.
