There is a mystery in the soul of the state, which no report has ever dared to meddle with, whose workings are more divine than speech or writing can express. All the dealings you have had with Troy are as well known to us as to you, my lord. And it would suit Achilles much better to throw down Hector than Polyxena. But it must grieve young Pyrrhus, your son at home, when fame blows her trumpet in our island and all the Greek girls sing as they dance, "Great Hector's sister was won by Achilles, but our great Ajax bravely beat Hector down." Goodbye, my lord. I speak as one who loves you. The fool is sliding over the ice that you should break.

To this effect, Achilles, have I mov'd you. / A woman impudent and mannish grown / Is not more loath'd than an effeminate man / In time of action. I stand condemn'd for this; / They think my little stomach to the war / And your great love to me restrains you thus. / Sweet, rouse yourself; and the weak wanton Cupid / Shall from your neck unloose his amorous fold, / And, like a dew-drop from the lion's mane, / Be shook to air.

This is what I have urged you to do, Achilles. A shameless, mannish woman is not more hated than an effeminate man in time of war. I am blamed for this. They think my small appetite for war and your great love for me keep you back like this. Sweet, wake yourself up, and weak, playful Cupid will loosen his loving grip on your neck and be shaken off into the air like a dewdrop from a lion's mane.
Is Ajax going to fight Hector?
Ay, and perhaps receive much honour by him.
Yes, and perhaps win a lot of honour from it.
I see my reputation is at stake; / My fame is shrewdly gor'd.
I see my reputation is at stake. My fame has been badly wounded.

O, then, beware: / Those wounds heal ill that men do give themselves; / Omission to do what is necessary / Seals a commission to a blank of danger; / And danger, like an ague, subtly taints / Even then when they sit idly in the sun.

Oh, then be careful. The wounds men give themselves heal badly. Failing to do what is necessary signs a blank warrant for danger, and danger, like a fever, infects quietly, even while men sit idle in the sun.

Go call Thersites hither, sweet Patroclus. / I'll send the fool to Ajax, and desire him / T'invite the Trojan lords, after the combat, / To see us here unarm'd. I have a woman's longing, / An appetite that I am sick withal, / To see great Hector in his weeds of peace; / To talk with him, and to behold his visage, / Even to my full of view.

Go and call Thersites here, sweet Patroclus. I'll send the fool to Ajax and ask him to invite the Trojan lords, after the fight, to come and see us here unarmed. I have a woman's craving, an appetite that makes me sick, to see great Hector in his peacetime clothes, to talk with him and look at his face until I've had my fill.
Ajax goes up and down the field asking for himself.
Ajax is going up and down the field asking for himself.
He must fight singly tomorrow with Hector, and is so prophetically proud of an heroical cudgelling that he raves in saying nothing.
He has to fight Hector in single combat tomorrow, and he's so proud in advance of a heroic beating that he raves without saying a word.

Why, a' stalks up and down like a peacock—a stride and a stand; ruminates like an hostess that hath no arithmetic but her brain to set down her reckoning, bites his lip with a politic regard, as who should say 'There were wit in this head, and 'twould out'; and so there is; but it lies as coldly in him as fire in a flint, which will not show without knocking. The man's undone for ever; for if Hector break not his neck i' th' combat, he'll break't himself in vainglory. He knows not me. I said 'Good morrow, Ajax'; and he replies 'Thanks, Agamemnon.' What think you of this man that takes me for the general? He's grown a very land fish, languageless, a monster. A plague of opinion! A man may wear it on both sides, like leather jerkin.

Why, he struts up and down like a peacock, a stride and then a pause. He broods like a landlady with no arithmetic except her head to work out the bill. He bites his lip with a statesman-like look, as if to say, "There's wisdom in this head, and it will come out." And so there is, but it lies as cold in him as fire in a flint, which won't show unless it's struck. The man is ruined for ever, because if Hector doesn't break his neck in the fight, he'll break it himself with vanity. He doesn't know me. I said "Good morning, Ajax," and he replies "Thank you, Agamemnon." What do you think of a man who takes me for the general? He's become a real fish out of water, speechless, a monster. A plague on reputation! A man can wear it either way out, like a leather jacket.
Thou must be my ambassador to him, Thersites.
You must be my ambassador to him, Thersites.

Who, I? Why, he'll answer nobody; he professes not answering. Speaking is for beggars: he wears his tongue in's arms. I will put on his presence. Let Patroclus make his demands to me, you shall see the pageant of Ajax.

Who, me? Why, he won't answer anyone. He makes a profession of not answering. Speaking is for beggars; he wears his tongue in his arms. I'll put on his manner. Let Patroclus make his requests to me, and you'll see the Ajax show.

To him, Patroclus. Tell him I humbly desire the valiant Ajax to invite the most valorous Hector to come unarm'd to my tent; and to procure safe conduct for his person of the magnanimous and most illustrious six-or-seven-times-honour'd Captain General of the Grecian army, Agamemnon. Do this.

Go on, Patroclus. Tell him I humbly ask the brave Ajax to invite the most valiant Hector to come unarmed to my tent, and to get a guarantee of safe passage for him from the generous and most illustrious, six or seven times honoured Commander-in-Chief of the Greek army, Agamemnon. Go on.
I come from the worthy Achilles—
I come from the worthy Achilles...
Who most humbly desires you to invite Hector to his tent—
...who most humbly asks you to invite Hector to his tent...
And to procure safe conduct from Agamemnon.
...and to get a guarantee of safe passage from Agamemnon.
What do you say to that?
God buy you, with all my heart.
God be with you, with all my heart.
If tomorrow be a fair day, by eleven of the clock it will go one way or other. Howsoever, he shall pay for me ere he has me.
If tomorrow is a fine day, by eleven o'clock it will go one way or the other. Either way, he'll pay for me before he gets me.
Fare ye well, with all my heart.
Why, but he is not in this tune, is he?
Why, he isn't in this mood, is he?
No, but out of tune thus. What music will be in him when Hector has knock'd out his brains, I know not; but, I am sure, none; unless the fiddler Apollo get his sinews to make catlings on.
No, but out of tune like this. What music there will be in him when Hector has knocked his brains out, I don't know. None, I'm sure, unless the fiddler Apollo takes his sinews to make strings.
Come, thou shalt bear a letter to him straight.
Come on, you'll take a letter to him straight away.
Let me bear another to his horse; for that's the more capable creature.
Let me take another to his horse, because that's the more intelligent creature.
My mind is troubled, like a fountain stirr'd; / And I myself see not the bottom of it.
My mind is troubled, like a fountain that has been stirred up, and I can't see to the bottom of it myself.
Would the fountain of your mind were clear again, that I might water an ass at it. I had rather be a tick in a sheep than such a valiant ignorance.
I wish the fountain of your mind were clear again, so I could water a donkey at it. I'd rather be a tick on a sheep than such a brave ignoramus.
See, ho! Who is that there?
Is the Prince there in person? / Had I so good occasion to lie long / As you, Prince Paris, nothing but heavenly business / Should rob my bed-mate of my company.
Is the Prince here in person? If I had as good a reason to stay in bed late as you, Prince Paris, nothing but the business of heaven would rob my bedfellow of my company.
That's my mind too. Good morrow, Lord Aeneas.
I think so too. Good morning, Lord Aeneas.
A valiant Greek, Aeneas—take his hand: / Witness the process of your speech, wherein / You told how Diomed, a whole week by days, / Did haunt you in the field.
A brave Greek, Aeneas. Take his hand. You yourself said so, when you told how Diomedes chased you on the battlefield every day for a whole week.
Health to you, valiant sir, / During all question of the gentle truce; / But when I meet you arm'd, as black defiance / As heart can think or courage execute.
Good health to you, brave sir, while this gentle truce lasts. But when I meet you armed, I wish you the blackest defiance a heart can think of or courage can carry out.

The one and other Diomed embraces. / Our bloods are now in calm; and so long health! / But when contention and occasion meet, / By Jove, I'll play the hunter for thy life / With all my force, pursuit, and policy.
Diomedes welcomes both. Our blood is calm now, so long life to you! But when the quarrel and the chance meet, by Jove, I'll hunt for your life with all my strength, pursuit and cunning.

And thou shalt hunt a lion that will fly / With his face backward. In humane gentleness, / Welcome to Troy! Now, by Anchises' life, / Welcome indeed! By Venus' hand I swear / No man alive can love in such a sort / The thing he means to kill, more excellently.

And you'll be hunting a lion that runs away with its face turned back towards you. With human courtesy, welcome to Troy! Now, by my father Anchises' life, welcome indeed! I swear by Venus' hand, no man alive can love so well the thing he means to kill.

We sympathise. Jove let Aeneas live, / If to my sword his fate be not the glory, / A thousand complete courses of the sun! / But in mine emulous honour let him die / With every joint a wound, and that tomorrow!
We feel the same. May Jove let Aeneas live a thousand full years, if his death is not to bring glory to my sword! But for my competing honour, let him die with a wound in every joint, and tomorrow!
We do; and long to know each other worse.
We do, and long to know each other worse.
This is the most despiteful gentle greeting / The noblest hateful love, that e'er I heard of. / What business, lord, so early?
This is the most spiteful friendly greeting, the noblest hate-filled love, I ever heard of. What business are you on so early, lord?
I was sent for to the King; but why, I know not.
I was sent for by the King, but I don't know why.

His purpose meets you: 'twas to bring this Greek / To Calchas' house, and there to render him, / For the enfreed Antenor, the fair Cressid. / Let's have your company; or, if you please, / Haste there before us. I constantly believe— / Or rather call my thought a certain knowledge— / My brother Troilus lodges there tonight. / Rouse him and give him note of our approach, / With the whole quality wherefore; I fear / We shall be much unwelcome.

His purpose is coming to meet you: it was for you to bring this Greek to Calchas' house, and there hand over to him the fair Cressida in exchange for the freed Antenor. Come with us, or, if you prefer, hurry there ahead of us. I firmly believe (or rather, I'd call it certain knowledge) that my brother Troilus is staying there tonight. Wake him and tell him we're coming, and the whole reason why. I'm afraid we'll be very unwelcome.
That I assure you: / Troilus had rather Troy were borne to Greece / Than Cressid borne from Troy.
That I can promise you. Troilus would rather Troy were carried off to Greece than Cressida carried away from Troy.
There is no help; / The bitter disposition of the time / Will have it so. On, lord; we'll follow you.
It can't be helped. The bitter needs of the time make it so. Go on, lord; we'll follow you.
And tell me, noble Diomed, faith, tell me true, / Even in the soul of sound good-fellowship, / Who in your thoughts deserves fair Helen best, / Myself, or Menelaus?
And tell me, noble Diomedes, honestly, tell me truly, in the spirit of real friendship: who, in your opinion, deserves fair Helen more, me or Menelaus?

Both alike: / He merits well to have her that doth seek her, / Not making any scruple of her soilure, / With such a hell of pain and world of charge; / And you as well to keep her that defend her, / Not palating the taste of her dishonour, / With such a costly loss of wealth and friends. / He like a puling cuckold would drink up / The lees and dregs of a flat tamed piece; / You, like a lecher, out of whorish loins / Are pleas'd to breed out your inheritors. / Both merits pois'd, each weighs nor less nor more, / But he as he, the heavier for a whore.

Both equally. He deserves to have her, since he seeks her back without caring about her pollution, at the cost of such hellish pain and a world of expense; and you deserve to keep her, since you defend her without tasting her dishonour, at the cost of such a loss of wealth and friends. He, like a whining cuckold, would drink up the stale dregs of a flat, used-up barrel. You, like a lecher, are happy to breed your heirs from a whore's body. Weigh both claims, and neither is heavier or lighter; but each of you is weighed down by a whore.
You are too bitter to your country-woman.
You are too harsh to your countrywoman.

She's bitter to her country. Hear me, Paris: / For every false drop in her bawdy veins / A Grecian's life hath sunk; for every scruple / Of her contaminated carrion weight / A Trojan hath been slain. Since she could speak, / She hath not given so many good words breath / As for her Greeks and Trojans suff'red death.

She has been harsh to her country. Listen, Paris: for every false drop in her lustful veins, a Greek's life has gone down; for every tiny ounce of her corrupted carcass, a Trojan has been killed. Since she could first speak, she hasn't spoken as many good words as Greeks and Trojans have died for her.
Fair Diomed, you do as chapmen do, / Dispraise the thing that you desire to buy; / But we in silence hold this virtue well, / We'll not commend what we intend to sell. / Here lies our way.
Fair Diomedes, you do what dealers do, running down the thing you want to buy. But we keep quiet about this virtue: we won't praise what we don't intend to sell. This is our way.
Dear, trouble not yourself; the morn is cold.
Dear, don't trouble yourself; the morning is cold.
Then, sweet my lord, I'll call mine uncle down; / He shall unbolt the gates.
Then, my sweet lord, I'll call my uncle down. He'll unbolt the gates.
Trouble him not; / To bed, to bed! Sleep kill those pretty eyes, / And give as soft attachment to thy senses / As infants empty of all thought!
Don't trouble him. To bed, to bed! May sleep close those pretty eyes and hold your senses as softly as it holds babies who have no thoughts!
O Cressida! but that the busy day, / Wak'd by the lark, hath rous'd the ribald crows, / And dreaming night will hide our joys no longer, / I would not from thee.
Oh Cressida! If the busy day, woken by the lark, hadn't roused the noisy crows, and if dreaming night would hide our joys any longer, I wouldn't leave you.
The night has been too short.
Beshrew the witch! with venomous wights she stays / As tediously as hell, but flies the grasps of love / With wings more momentary-swift than thought. / You will catch cold, and curse me.
Curse the witch! With evil people she stays as long and wearily as hell, but she flies from the arms of love on wings faster than thought. You'll catch cold and curse me.
Prithee tarry. / You men will never tarry. / O foolish Cressid! I might have still held off, / And then you would have tarried. Hark! there's one up.
Please stay. You men never stay. Oh foolish Cressida! I could have kept holding off, and then you would have stayed. Listen! Someone's up.
[Within] What's all the doors open here?
(Offstage) Why are all the doors open here?
A pestilence on him! Now will he be mocking. / I shall have such a life!
A plague on him! Now he'll make fun of us. I'll never hear the end of it!
How now, how now! How go maidenheads? / Here, you maid! Where's my cousin Cressid?
Well, well! How are maidenheads doing? Here, you maid! Where's my niece Cressida?
Go hang yourself, you naughty mocking uncle. / You bring me to do, and then you flout me too.
Go hang yourself, you naughty, mocking uncle. You lead me into it, and then you make fun of me too.
To do what? to do what? Let her say what. / What have I brought you to do?
Into what? Into what? Let her say what. What have I led you into?
Come, come, beshrew your heart! You'll ne'er be good, nor suffer others.
Come on, curse you! You'll never be good yourself, or let others be.
Ha, ha! Alas, poor wretch! Ah, poor capocchia! Hast not slept tonight? Would he not, a naughty man, let it sleep? A bugbear take him!
Ha ha! Alas, poor thing! Ah, poor little fool! Haven't you slept tonight? Wouldn't he let it sleep, the naughty man? May a bogeyman take him!
Did not I tell you? Would he were knock'd i' th' head!
Didn't I tell you? I wish he'd be hit on the head!
Who's that at door? Good uncle, go and see. / My lord, come you again into my chamber. / You smile and mock me, as if I meant naughtily.
Who's that at the door? Good uncle, go and see. My lord, come back into my room. You're smiling and teasing me, as if I meant something naughty.
Come, you are deceiv'd, I think of no such thing.
Come on, you're wrong; I'm thinking of no such thing.
How earnestly they knock! Pray you come in: / I would not for half Troy have you seen here.
How urgently they're knocking! Please come in. I wouldn't have you seen here for half of Troy.
Who's there? What's the matter? Will you beat down the door? How now? What's the matter?
Who's there? What's the matter? Are you going to knock the door down? Well? What's the matter?
Who's there? My lord Aeneas? By my troth, / I knew you not. What news with you so early?
Who's there? My lord Aeneas? Honestly, I didn't recognise you. What news do you have so early?
Here! What should he do here?
Here! What would he be doing here?
Come, he is here, my lord; do not deny him. / It doth import him much to speak with me.
Come on, he's here, my lord; don't deny it. It's very important for him to speak with me.
Is he here, say you? It's more than I know, I'll be sworn. For my own part, I came in late. What should he do here?
Is he here, you say? That's more than I know, I swear. For my part, I came in late. What would he be doing here?
Who, nay then! Come, come, you'll do him wrong ere you are ware; you'll be so true to him to be false to him. Do not you know of him, but yet go fetch him hither; go.
Oh, come on now! Come, come, you'll do him harm before you know it; you'll be so loyal to him that you'll betray him. Pretend you don't know where he is, but go and fetch him here anyway. Go.

My lord, I scarce have leisure to salute you, / My matter is so rash. There is at hand / Paris your brother, and Deiphobus, / The Grecian Diomed, and our Antenor / Deliver'd to us; and for him forthwith, / Ere the first sacrifice, within this hour, / We must give up to Diomedes' hand / The Lady Cressida.

My lord, I hardly have time to greet you, my business is so urgent. Your brother Paris is close by, with Deiphobus, the Greek Diomedes and our Antenor, who has been handed back to us. In exchange for him, at once, before the first sacrifice of the day, within this hour, we must hand over the Lady Cressida to Diomedes.
By Priam and the general state of Troy. / They are at hand, and ready to effect it.
By Priam and the council of Troy. They are close by and ready to carry it out.
How my achievements mock me! / I will go meet them; and, my Lord Aeneas, / We met by chance; you did not find me here.
How my successes mock me! I'll go and meet them. And, my Lord Aeneas, we met by chance; you didn't find me here.
Good, good, my lord, the secrets of neighbour Pandar / Have not more gift in taciturnity.
Good, good, my lord. The secrets of nature don't keep silent better than I will.
Is't possible? No sooner got but lost? The devil take Antenor! The young prince will go mad. A plague upon Antenor! I would they had broke's neck.
Is it possible? No sooner won than lost? The devil take Antenor! The young prince will go mad. A plague on Antenor! I wish they'd broken his neck.
How now! What's the matter? Who was here?
What's happening? What's the matter? Who was here?
Why sigh you so profoundly? Where's my lord? Gone? Tell me, sweet uncle, what's the matter?
Why are you sighing so deeply? Where's my lord? Gone? Tell me, sweet uncle, what's the matter?
Would I were as deep under the earth as I am above!
I wish I were as deep under the earth as I am above it!
O the gods! What's the matter?
Pray thee get thee in. Would thou hadst ne'er been born! I knew thou wouldst be his death! O, poor gentleman! A plague upon Antenor!
Please, go inside. I wish you'd never been born! I knew you'd be the death of him! Oh, poor gentleman! A plague on Antenor!
Good uncle, I beseech you, on my knees I beseech you, what's the matter?
Good uncle, I beg you, on my knees I beg you, what's the matter?
Thou must be gone, wench, thou must be gone; thou art chang'd for Antenor; thou must to thy father, and be gone from Troilus. 'Twill be his death; 'twill be his bane; he cannot bear it.
You must go, girl, you must go. You've been exchanged for Antenor. You must go to your father and leave Troilus. It will be the death of him; it will destroy him; he can't bear it.
O you immortal gods! I will not go.
Oh you immortal gods! I won't go.

I will not, uncle. I have forgot my father; / I know no touch of consanguinity, / No kin, no love, no blood, no soul so near me / As the sweet Troilus. O you gods divine, / Make Cressid's name the very crown of falsehood, / If ever she leave Troilus! Time, force, and death, / Do to this body what extremes you can, / But the strong base and building of my love / Is as the very centre of the earth, / Drawing all things to it. I'll go in and weep—

I won't, uncle. I have forgotten my father. I feel no tie of blood, no family, no love, no blood, no soul as close to me as sweet Troilus. Oh you divine gods, make Cressida's name the very crown of falseness if she ever leaves Troilus! Time, force and death, do the worst you can to this body, but the strong foundation and building of my love is like the very centre of the earth, drawing everything towards it. I'll go in and weep...
Tear my bright hair, and scratch my praised cheeks, / Crack my clear voice with sobs and break my heart, / With sounding 'Troilus.' I will not go from Troy.
...tear my bright hair, scratch my much-praised cheeks, crack my clear voice with sobs and break my heart crying "Troilus." I will not leave Troy.
It is great morning; and the hour prefix'd / For her delivery to this valiant Greek / Comes fast upon. Good my brother Troilus, / Tell you the lady what she is to do / And haste her to the purpose.
It is broad daylight, and the hour fixed for handing her over to this brave Greek is coming fast. My good brother Troilus, tell the lady what she must do and hurry her along.
Walk into her house. / I'll bring her to the Grecian presently; / And to his hand when I deliver her, / Think it an altar, and thy brother Troilus / A priest, there off'ring to it his own heart.
Walk to her house. I'll bring her to the Greek at once. And when I hand her over to him, think of his hand as an altar, and your brother Troilus as a priest, offering his own heart on it.
I know what 'tis to love, / And would, as I shall pity, I could help! / Please you walk in, my lords?
I know what it is to love, and I wish I could help as much as I pity him! Will you walk in, my lords?

Why tell you me of moderation? / The grief is fine, full, perfect, that I taste, / And violenteth in a sense as strong / As that which causeth it. How can I moderate it? / If I could temporize with my affections / Or brew it to a weak and colder palate, / The like allayment could I give my grief. / My love admits no qualifying dross; / No more my grief, in such a precious loss.

Why do you talk to me about calming down? The grief I taste is pure, full and complete, and it rages as strongly as the thing that causes it. How can I calm it? If I could compromise with my feelings, or water them down to a weaker, colder taste, I could calm my grief in the same way. My love won't allow any mixing with impurities, and nor will my grief, at such a precious loss.
Here, here, here he comes. Ah, sweet ducks!
Here, here, here he comes. Ah, sweet ducks!

What a pair of spectacles is here! Let me embrace too. 'O heart,' as the goodly saying is,— / O heart, heavy heart, / Why sigh'st thou without breaking? / where he answers again / Because thou canst not ease thy smart / By friendship nor by speaking. / There was never a truer rhyme. Let us cast away nothing, for we may live to have need of such a verse. We see it, we see it. How now, lambs!

What a pair of spectacles this is! Let me embrace too. "Oh heart," as the good old saying goes: "Oh heart, heavy heart, why do you sigh without breaking?" And then it answers: "Because you cannot ease your pain by friendship or by speaking." There was never a truer rhyme. Let's not throw anything away, because we may live to need a verse like that. We see it, we see it. Well, lambs!
Cressid, I love thee in so strain'd a purity / That the bless'd gods, as angry with my fancy, / More bright in zeal than the devotion which / Cold lips blow to their deities, take thee from me.
Cressida, I love you with such a refined purity that the blessed gods, as if angry with my love, which burns brighter than the devotion cold lips breathe to their gods, are taking you from me.
Ay, ay, ay, ay; 'tis too plain a case.
Yes, yes, yes, yes; it's all too plain.
And is it true that I must go from Troy?
And is it true that I must leave Troy?

And suddenly; where injury of chance / Puts back leave-taking, justles roughly by / All time of pause, rudely beguiles our lips / Of all rejoindure, forcibly prevents / Our lock'd embrasures, strangles our dear vows / Even in the birth of our own labouring breath. / We two, that with so many thousand sighs / Did buy each other, must poorly sell ourselves / With the rude brevity and discharge of one. / Injurious time now with a robber's haste / Crams his rich thiev'ry up, he knows not how. / As many farewells as be stars in heaven, / With distinct breath and consign'd kisses to them, / He fumbles up into a loose adieu, / And scants us with a single famish'd kiss, / Distasted with the salt of broken tears.

And immediately, so that the injury of chance puts off our farewells, roughly shoves aside any pause, rudely cheats our lips of any reply, forcibly stops our close embraces, and strangles our dear vows in the very birth of our struggling breath. We two, who bought each other with so many thousand sighs, must sell ourselves cheaply with the rough shortness of a single one. Cruel time, with a robber's hurry, now crams his rich loot together any old how. As many farewells as there are stars in the sky, each with its own breath and the kisses that seal it, he bundles into one careless goodbye, and stints us to a single starved kiss, spoiled by the salt of broken-off tears.
[Within] My lord, is the lady ready?
(Offstage) My lord, is the lady ready?
Hark! you are call'd. Some say the Genius / Cries so to him that instantly must die. / Bid them have patience; she shall come anon.
Listen! You are being called. Some say the guardian spirit calls like this to a man who is about to die. Tell them to be patient; she'll come soon.
Where are my tears? Rain, to lay this wind, or my heart will be blown up by my throat!
Where are my tears? Rain, to calm this wind of sighs, or my heart will be blown up through my throat!
I must then to the Grecians?
So I must go to the Greeks?
A woeful Cressid 'mongst the merry Greeks! / When shall we see again?
A grieving Cressida among the merry Greeks! When shall we see each other again?
Hear me, my love. Be thou but true of heart.
Listen to me, my love. Only be faithful in your heart.
I true? How now! What wicked deem is this?
Me faithful? What! What wicked thought is this?

Nay, we must use expostulation kindly, / For it is parting from us. / I speak not 'Be thou true' as fearing thee, / For I will throw my glove to Death himself / That there's no maculation in thy heart; / But 'Be thou true' say I to fashion in / My sequent protestation: be thou true, / And I will see thee.

No, we must talk gently, because it is leaving us. I don't say "Be faithful" because I fear you, for I would throw down my glove to Death himself to defend that there is no stain in your heart. I say "Be faithful" to lead into the promise that follows: be faithful, and I will come and see you.
O! you shall be expos'd, my lord, to dangers / As infinite as imminent! But I'll be true.
Oh, you'll be exposed to dangers, my lord, as endless as they are close! But I'll be faithful.
And I'll grow friend with danger. Wear this sleeve.
And I'll make friends with danger. Wear this sleeve.
And you this glove. When shall I see you?
And you wear this glove. When shall I see you?
I will corrupt the Grecian sentinels / To give thee nightly visitation. / But yet be true.
I will bribe the Greek sentries so that I can visit you every night. But still, be faithful.

Hear why I speak it, love. / The Grecian youths are full of quality; / They're loving, well compos'd, with gifts of nature, / Flowing and swelling o'er with arts and exercise. / How novelty may move, and parts with person, / Alas, a kind of godly jealousy, / Which, I beseech you, call a virtuous sin, / Makes me afear'd.

Hear why I say it, love. The Greek young men are very accomplished. They are loving, well made, with natural gifts, overflowing with skills and training. How novelty, and talents together with good looks, may move you... alas, a kind of holy jealousy, which I beg you to call a virtuous sin, makes me afraid.
O heavens! you love me not!
Oh heavens! You don't love me!

Die I a villain then! / In this I do not call your faith in question / So mainly as my merit. I cannot sing, / Nor heel the high lavolt, nor sweeten talk, / Nor play at subtle games; fair virtues all, / To which the Grecians are most prompt and pregnant; / But I can tell that in each grace of these / There lurks a still and dumb-discoursive devil / That tempts most cunningly. But be not tempted.

Then let me die a villain! In this I don't question your faithfulness as much as my own merit. I can't sing, or dance the high lavolta, or make sweet conversation, or play clever games. They are all fine accomplishments, which the Greeks are very quick and skilled at. But I can tell you that in each of these graces there lurks a quiet devil that speaks without words and tempts most cunningly. But don't be tempted.
No. / But something may be done that we will not; / And sometimes we are devils to ourselves, / When we will tempt the frailty of our powers, / Presuming on their changeful potency.
No. But sometimes we do things we don't intend to do, and sometimes we are devils to ourselves, when we test the frailty of our powers, relying too much on their changeable strength.
Come, kiss; and let us part.
Good brother, come you hither; / And bring Aeneas and the Grecian with you.
Good brother, come here, and bring Aeneas and the Greek with you.
My lord, will you be true?
My lord, will you be faithful?

Who, I? Alas, it is my vice, my fault! / Whiles others fish with craft for great opinion, / I with great truth catch mere simplicity; / Whilst some with cunning gild their copper crowns, / With truth and plainness I do wear mine bare. / Fear not my truth: the moral of my wit / Is plain and true; there's all the reach of it.

Who, me? Alas, it is my vice, my fault! While others fish cleverly for a great reputation, I catch only a name for simplicity with my great truthfulness. While some cunningly gild their copper crowns, I wear mine bare, with truth and plainness. Don't fear my faithfulness: the whole meaning of my mind is plain and true; that's as far as it goes.

Welcome, Sir Diomed! Here is the lady / Which for Antenor we deliver you; / At the port, lord, I'll give her to thy hand, / And by the way possess thee what she is. / Entreat her fair; and, by my soul, fair Greek, / If e'er thou stand at mercy of my sword, / Name Cressid, and thy life shall be as safe / As Priam is in Ilion.

Welcome, Sir Diomedes! Here is the lady we are handing over to you in exchange for Antenor. At the city gate, lord, I'll give her into your hand, and on the way I'll tell you what she is. Treat her well. And, by my soul, fair Greek, if you are ever at the mercy of my sword, say "Cressida," and your life will be as safe as Priam is in Troy.

Fair Lady Cressid, / So please you, save the thanks this prince expects. / The lustre in your eye, heaven in your cheek, / Pleads your fair usage; and to Diomed / You shall be mistress, and command him wholly.

Fair Lady Cressida, if you please, don't bother with the thanks this prince expects. The shine in your eyes and the heaven in your cheeks plead for your good treatment, and you shall be mistress to Diomedes and command him completely.

Grecian, thou dost not use me courteously / To shame the zeal of my petition to thee / In praising her. I tell thee, lord of Greece, / She is as far high-soaring o'er thy praises / As thou unworthy to be call'd her servant. / I charge thee use her well, even for my charge; / For, by the dreadful Pluto, if thou dost not, / Though the great bulk Achilles be thy guard, / I'll cut thy throat.

Greek, you don't treat me courteously, shaming the sincerity of my request by praising her. I tell you, lord of Greece, she soars as far above your praises as you are unworthy to be called her servant. I order you to treat her well, simply because I order it. For, by dreadful Pluto, if you don't, even if great bulky Achilles is your bodyguard, I'll cut your throat.

O, be not mov'd, Prince Troilus. / Let me be privileg'd by my place and message / To be a speaker free: when I am hence / I'll answer to my lust. And know you, lord, / I'll nothing do on charge: to her own worth / She shall be priz'd. But that you say 'Be't so,' / I speak it in my spirit and honour, 'No.'

Oh, don't get upset, Prince Troilus. Let my position as an envoy give me the right to speak freely. When I am gone from here, I'll do as I please. And know this, lord: I'll do nothing because I am ordered to. She will be valued for her own worth. But when you say "Do it," I say, on my spirit and honour, "No."
Come, to the port. I'll tell thee, Diomed, / This brave shall oft make thee to hide thy head. / Lady, give me your hand; and, as we walk, / To our own selves bend we our needful talk.
Come, to the gate. I tell you, Diomedes, this boast will often make you hide your head. Lady, give me your hand, and as we walk, let's say what we need to say to each other.
How have we spent this morning! / The Prince must think me tardy and remiss, / That swore to ride before him to the field.
How we have wasted this morning! The Prince must think me late and careless, when I swore to ride ahead of him to the battlefield.
'Tis Troilus' fault. Come, come to field with him.
It's Troilus' fault. Come, come to the field with him.
Yea, with a bridegroom's fresh alacrity / Let us address to tend on Hector's heels. / The glory of our Troy doth this day lie / On his fair worth and single chivalry.
Yes, with a bridegroom's eager readiness, let's prepare to follow at Hector's heels. The glory of our Troy depends today on his fine worth and his single knighthood.

Here art thou in appointment fresh and fair, / Anticipating time with starting courage. / Give with thy trumpet a loud note to Troy, / Thou dreadful Ajax, that the appalled air / May pierce the head of the great combatant, / And hale him hither.

Here you are, fresh and splendid in your armour, ahead of time in your eager courage. Sound a loud note to Troy with your trumpet, dreadful Ajax, so that the terrified air may pierce the ears of the great fighter and drag him here.

Thou, trumpet, there's my purse. / Now crack thy lungs and split thy brazen pipe; / Blow, villain, till thy sphered bias cheek / Out-swell the colic of puff'd Aquilon. / Come, stretch thy chest, and let thy eyes spout blood: / Thou blowest for Hector.

You, trumpeter, there's my purse. Now crack your lungs and split your brass pipe. Blow, you rascal, until your round, puffed-out cheek swells bigger than the bloated north wind. Come on, stretch your chest and let your eyes spout blood. You're blowing for Hector.
Is not yond Diomed, with Calchas' daughter?
Isn't that Diomedes over there, with Calchas' daughter?
'Tis he, I ken the manner of his gait: / He rises on the toe. That spirit of his / In aspiration lifts him from the earth.
It's him; I recognise the way he walks. He rises on his toes. That spirit of his lifts him off the ground with ambition.
Most dearly welcome to the Greeks, sweet lady.
A dear welcome to the Greeks, sweet lady.
Our general doth salute you with a kiss.
Our general greets you with a kiss.
Yet is the kindness but particular; / 'Twere better she were kiss'd in general.
But that kindness is only from one person. It would be better if she were kissed by everyone.
And very courtly counsel: I'll begin. / So much for Nestor.
And very courtly advice. I'll begin. (He kisses her.) So much for Nestor.
I'll take that winter from your lips, fair lady. / Achilles bids you welcome.
I'll take that winter off your lips, fair lady. Achilles bids you welcome.
I had good argument for kissing once.
I had a good reason for kissing once.
But that's no argument for kissing now; / For thus popp'd Paris in his hardiment, / And parted thus you and your argument.
But that's no reason for kissing now, because this is how Paris boldly popped in and separated you from your reason.
O deadly gall, and theme of all our scorns! / For which we lose our heads to gild his horns.
Oh deadly bitterness, and the subject of all our scorn! We lose our heads to gild his cuckold's horns.
The first was Menelaus' kiss; this, mine: / Patroclus kisses you.
The first kiss was Menelaus'; this one is mine. Patroclus kisses you.
Paris and I kiss evermore for him.
Paris and I always do his kissing for him.
I'll have my kiss, sir. Lady, by your leave.
I'll have my kiss, sir. Lady, with your permission.
In kissing, do you render or receive?
In kissing, do you give or receive?
I'll make my match to live, / The kiss you take is better than you give; / Therefore no kiss.
I'll bet my life the kiss you take is better than the one you give. So no kiss.
I'll give you boot; I'll give you three for one.
I'll give you something extra; I'll give you three for one.
You are an odd man; give even or give none.
You're an odd man; give even or give none.
An odd man, lady! Every man is odd.
An odd man, lady! Every man is odd (single, unique).
No, Paris is not; for you know 'tis true / That you are odd, and he is even with you.
No, Paris isn't, because you know it's true that you are odd (alone), and he has got even with you.
You flick me on the head (on my horns).
It were no match, your nail against his horn. / May I, sweet lady, beg a kiss of you?
It would be an unequal match, your fingernail against his horn. May I, sweet lady, beg a kiss from you?
Why then, for Venus' sake give me a kiss / When Helen is a maid again, and his.
Why then, for Venus' sake, give me a kiss when Helen is a virgin again and his.
I am your debtor; claim it when 'tis due.
I owe it to you. Claim it when it's due.
Never's my day, and then a kiss of you.
My day will never come, and then I'll have a kiss from you.
Lady, a word. I'll bring you to your father.
Lady, a word. I'll take you to your father.
A woman with a quick wit.

Fie, fie upon her! / There's language in her eye, her cheek, her lip, / Nay, her foot speaks; her wanton spirits look out / At every joint and motive of her body. / O! these encounterers so glib of tongue / That give a coasting welcome ere it comes, / And wide unclasp the tables of their thoughts / To every tickling reader! Set them down / For sluttish spoils of opportunity, / And daughters of the game.

Shame, shame on her! There's language in her eyes, her cheeks, her lips; even her foot speaks. Her lustful spirit looks out from every joint and movement of her body. Oh, these flirts with such smooth tongues, who give a welcome before a man has even approached, and open wide the notebooks of their thoughts to every reader who tickles them! Mark them down as easy spoils for any opportunist, and daughters of the game.

Hail, all you state of Greece! What shall be done / To him that victory commands? Or do you purpose / A victor shall be known? Will you the knights / Shall to the edge of all extremity / Pursue each other, or shall be divided / By any voice or order of the field? / Hector bade ask.

Greetings, all you lords of Greece! What is to be done for the one who wins? Or do you intend that a winner should be declared? Do you want the knights to fight each other to the very end, or should they be separated by some command or rule of the contest? Hector asked me to ask.
Which way would Hector have it?
He cares not; he'll obey conditions.
He doesn't mind. He'll follow whatever terms are set.
But securely done, / A little proudly, and great deal misprising / The knight oppos'd.
But done overconfidently, a little proudly, and greatly underrating the knight he is fighting.
If not Achilles, sir, / What is your name?
If you aren't Achilles, sir, what is your name?

Therefore Achilles. But whate'er, know this: / In the extremity of great and little / Valour and pride excel themselves in Hector; / The one almost as infinite as all, / The other blank as nothing. Weigh him well, / And that which looks like pride is courtesy. / This Ajax is half made of Hector's blood; / In love whereof half Hector stays at home; / Half heart, half hand, half Hector comes to seek / This blended knight, half Trojan and half Greek.

Achilles, then. But whoever you are, know this: courage and pride are both at their extremes in Hector, one great and one small. His courage is almost infinite, and his pride is as empty as nothing. Weigh him carefully, and what looks like pride is courtesy. This Ajax is half made of Hector's blood. Out of love for that, half of Hector stays at home. Half a heart, half a hand, half of Hector comes to fight this mixed knight, half Trojan and half Greek.
A maiden battle then? O! I perceive you.
A girls' fight, then? Oh, I see what you mean.

Here is Sir Diomed. Go, gentle knight, / Stand by our Ajax. As you and Lord Aeneas / Consent upon the order of their fight, / So be it; either to the uttermost, / Or else a breath. The combatants being kin / Half stints their strife before their strokes begin. / [Ajax and Hector enter the lists]

Here is Sir Diomedes. Go, gentle knight, stand by our Ajax. Whatever you and Lord Aeneas agree about how they should fight, let it be so, either to the death or just a bout. Because the fighters are related, their quarrel is half-checked before their blows begin. (Ajax and Hector enter the fighting ground.)
They are facing each other already.
What Trojan is that same that looks so heavy?
Who is that Trojan who looks so gloomy?

The youngest son of Priam, a true knight; / Not yet mature, yet matchless; firm of word; / Speaking in deeds and deedless in his tongue; / Not soon provok'd, nor being provok'd soon calm'd; / His heart and hand both open and both free; / For what he has he gives, what thinks he shows, / Yet gives he not till judgement guide his bounty, / Nor dignifies an impure thought with breath; / Manly as Hector, but more dangerous; / For Hector in his blaze of wrath subscribes / To tender objects, but he in heat of action / Is more vindicative than jealous love. / They call him Troilus, and on him erect / A second hope as fairly built as Hector. / Thus says Aeneas, one that knows the youth / Even to his inches, and, with private soul, / Did in great Ilion thus translate him to me.

Priam's youngest son, a true knight. Not yet fully grown, yet unmatched; firm to his word; he speaks in deeds and not with his tongue. He is not quickly provoked, nor quickly calmed once provoked. His heart and hand are both open and generous, for he gives what he has and shows what he thinks; yet he doesn't give until judgement guides his generosity, nor does he honour an unworthy thought by speaking it. He is as manly as Hector, but more dangerous, because Hector, in the heat of his anger, spares those who are helpless, while he, in the heat of the fight, is more vengeful than jealous love. They call him Troilus, and build on him a second hope as fine as Hector. So says Aeneas, who knows the young man down to the last inch, and who described him to me like this, in confidence, in great Troy.
His blows are well dispos'd. There, Ajax!
His blows are well placed. There, Ajax!
Princes, that's enough, if you please.
I am not warm yet; let us fight again.
I'm not warmed up yet. Let's fight again.

Why, then will I no more. / Thou art, great lord, my father's sister's son, / A cousin-german to great Priam's seed; / The obligation of our blood forbids / A gory emulation 'twixt us twain: / Were thy commixtion Greek and Trojan so / That thou could'st say 'This hand is Grecian all, / And this is Trojan; the sinews of this leg / All Greek, and this all Troy; my mother's blood / Runs on the dexter cheek, and this sinister / Bounds in my father's; by Jove multipotent, / Thou shouldst not bear from me a Greekish member / Wherein my sword had not impressure made / Of our rank feud; but the just gods gainsay / That any drop thou borrow'dst from thy mother, / My sacred aunt, should by my mortal sword / Be drained! Let me embrace thee, Ajax. / By him that thunders, thou hast lusty arms; / Hector would have them fall upon him thus. / Cousin, all honour to thee!

Why, then I'll fight no more. Great lord, you are my father's sister's son, a first cousin to great Priam's children. The bond of our blood forbids a bloody contest between us two. If your mixture of Greek and Trojan were such that you could say, "This hand is all Greek, and this is Trojan; the muscles of this leg are all Greek and this all Trojan; my mother's blood runs in my right cheek and this left one throbs with my father's," then, by all-powerful Jove, you would not carry away from me a single Greek limb without my sword printing on it the mark of our bitter feud. But the just gods forbid that any drop of blood you got from your mother, my sacred aunt, should be drained by my deadly sword! Let me embrace you, Ajax. By the god of thunder, you have strong arms. This is how Hector would like them to fall on him. Cousin, all honour to you!
I thank thee, Hector. / Thou art too gentle and too free a man. / I came to kill thee, cousin, and bear hence / A great addition earned in thy death.
Thank you, Hector. You are too gentle and too generous a man. I came to kill you, cousin, and to carry away the great title of having won it by your death.
Not Neoptolemus so mirable, / On whose bright crest Fame with her loud'st Oyes / Cries 'This is he!' could promise to himself / A thought of added honour torn from Hector.
Not even Neoptolemus, so admirable, on whose bright helmet Fame cries out with her loudest "Oyez!", "This is the man!", could expect to win a scrap of extra honour from Hector.
There is expectance here from both the sides / What further you will do.
Both sides are waiting to see what you will do next.
We'll answer it: / The issue is embracement. Ajax, farewell.
We'll give them their answer: the result is an embrace. Ajax, goodbye.
If I might in entreaties find success, / As seld' I have the chance, I would desire / My famous cousin to our Grecian tents.
If I could succeed in asking (and I seldom get the chance), I would invite my famous cousin to our Greek tents.
'Tis Agamemnon's wish; and great Achilles / Doth long to see unarm'd the valiant Hector.
It is Agamemnon's wish, and great Achilles longs to see brave Hector without his armour.

Aeneas, call my brother Troilus to me, / And signify this loving interview / To the expecters of our Trojan part; / Desire them home. Give me thy hand, my cousin; / I will go eat with thee, and see your knights. / [Agamemnon and the rest of the Greeks come forward]

Aeneas, call my brother Troilus to me, and report this friendly meeting to those waiting on the Trojan side. Tell them to go home. Give me your hand, my cousin. I'll go and eat with you and see your knights. (Agamemnon and the other Greeks come forward.)
Great Agamemnon comes to meet us here.
Great Agamemnon is coming to meet us here.
The worthiest of them tell me name by name; / But for Achilles, my own searching eyes / Shall find him by his large and portly size.
Tell me the names of the worthiest of them, one by one. But as for Achilles, my own searching eyes will find him by his large and stately size.

Worthy all arms! as welcome as to one / That would be rid of such an enemy. / But that's no welcome. Understand more clear, / What's past and what's to come is strew'd with husks / And formless ruin of oblivion; / But in this extant moment, faith and troth, / Strain'd purely from all hollow bias-drawing, / Bids thee with most divine integrity, / From heart of very heart, great Hector, welcome.

Worthy in arms! As welcome as you can be to someone who would like to be rid of such an enemy. But that's no welcome. Let me put it more clearly: the past and the future are strewn with husks and the shapeless ruins of oblivion. But in this present moment, faith and truth, purified of all false and crooked motives, bid you, with the most divine sincerity, from the very heart of my heart, great Hector, welcome.
I thank thee, most imperious Agamemnon.
[To Troilus] My well-fam'd lord of Troy, no less to you.
(To Troilus) My famous lord of Troy, the same welcome to you.
Let me confirm my princely brother's greeting. / You brace of warlike brothers, welcome hither.
Let me confirm my royal brother's greeting. You pair of warlike brothers, welcome here.
O you, my lord? By Mars his gauntlet, thanks! / Mock not that I affect the untraded oath; / Your quondam wife swears still by Venus' glove. / She's well, but bade me not commend her to you.
Oh, you, my lord? By Mars's glove, thank you! Don't laugh that I use an unusual oath; your former wife still swears by Venus' glove. She's well, but she didn't ask me to give you her regards.
Name her not now, sir; she's a deadly theme.
Don't mention her now, sir. She's a deadly subject.
Oh, forgive me. I'm being offensive.

I have, thou gallant Trojan, seen thee oft, / Labouring for destiny, make cruel way / Through ranks of Greekish youth; and I have seen thee, / As hot as Perseus, spur thy Phrygian steed, / Despising many forfeits and subduements, / When thou hast hung thy advanced sword i' th'air, / Not letting it decline on the declined; / That I have said to some my standers-by / 'Lo, Jupiter is yonder, dealing life!' / And I have seen thee pause and take thy breath, / When that a ring of Greeks have shrap'd thee in, / Like an Olympian wrestling. This have I seen; / But this thy countenance, still lock'd in steel, / I never saw till now. I knew thy grandsire, / And once fought with him. He was a soldier good, / But, by great Mars, the captain of us all, / Never like thee. O, let an old man embrace thee; / And, worthy warrior, welcome to our tents.

I have often seen you, you gallant Trojan, working for fate, cutting a cruel path through the ranks of young Greeks. And I have seen you, as hot as Perseus, spur on your Trojan horse, scorning many who had surrendered and were at your mercy, when you held your raised sword in the air and would not let it fall on the fallen, so that I said to some who stood by me, "Look, there's Jupiter, giving out life!" And I have seen you pause and take a breath when a ring of Greeks had hemmed you in, like an Olympic wrestler. This I have seen. But this face of yours, always locked in steel, I never saw until now. I knew your grandfather, and once fought with him. He was a good soldier, but, by great Mars, the leader of us all, never like you. Oh, let an old man embrace you, and, worthy warrior, welcome to our tents.
Let me embrace thee, good old chronicle, / That hast so long walk'd hand in hand with time. / Most reverend Nestor, I am glad to clasp thee.
Let me embrace you, good old history book, who has walked so long hand in hand with time. Most reverend Nestor, I am glad to hold you.
I would my arms could match thee in contention / As they contend with thee in courtesy.
I wish my arms could match you in fighting as they compete with you in courtesy.
Ha! / By this white beard, I'd fight with thee tomorrow. / Well, welcome, welcome! I have seen the time.
Ha! By this white beard, I'd fight you tomorrow. Well, welcome, welcome! I have seen the day.
I wonder now how yonder city stands, / When we have here her base and pillar by us.
I wonder how that city over there is still standing, when we have its foundation and pillar here with us.
I know your favour, Lord Ulysses, well. / Ah, sir, there's many a Greek and Trojan dead, / Since first I saw yourself and Diomed / In Ilion on your Greekish embassy.
I know your face well, Lord Ulysses. Ah, sir, many Greeks and Trojans have died since I first saw you and Diomedes in Troy on your Greek embassy.

Sir, I foretold you then what would ensue. / My prophecy is but half his journey yet; / For yonder walls, that pertly front your town, / Yon towers, whose wanton tops do buss the clouds, / Must kiss their own feet.

Sir, I told you then what would follow. My prophecy has only gone half its journey yet, because those walls that stand so boldly in front of your town, those towers whose proud tops kiss the clouds, must kiss their own feet.

I must not believe you. / There they stand yet; and modestly I think / The fall of every Phrygian stone will cost / A drop of Grecian blood. The end crowns all; / And that old common arbitrator, Time, / Will one day end it.

I mustn't believe you. There they still stand, and I modestly think that the fall of every Trojan stone will cost a drop of Greek blood. The end crowns everything, and that old common judge, Time, will end it one day.
So to him we leave it. / Most gentle and most valiant Hector, welcome. / After the General, I beseech you next / To feast with me and see me at my tent.
Then we'll leave it to him. Most gentle and most brave Hector, welcome. After the General, I beg you to feast with me next and visit me at my tent.
I shall forestall thee, Lord Ulysses, thou! / Now, Hector, I have fed mine eyes on thee; / I have with exact view perus'd thee, Hector, / And quoted joint by joint.
I'll get in before you, Lord Ulysses, you! Now, Hector, I have fed my eyes on you. I have studied you carefully, Hector, and noted you joint by joint.
Stand fair, I pray thee; let me look on thee.
Stand still, please; let me look at you.
Thou art too brief. I will the second time, / As I would buy thee, view thee limb by limb.
You're too quick. I'll look at you a second time, limb by limb, as if I were going to buy you.
O, like a book of sport thou'lt read me o'er; / But there's more in me than thou understand'st. / Why dost thou so oppress me with thine eye?
Oh, you'll read me through like a book about hunting. But there's more in me than you understand. Why do you weigh me down so with your stare?

Tell me, you heavens, in which part of his body / Shall I destroy him? Whether there, or there, or there? / That I may give the local wound a name, / And make distinct the very breach whereout / Hector's great spirit flew. Answer me, heavens.

Tell me, you heavens, in which part of his body shall I destroy him? There, or there, or there? So that I can give the wound a name and mark out the very gap through which Hector's great spirit flew out. Answer me, heavens.

It would discredit the blest gods, proud man, / To answer such a question. Stand again. / Think'st thou to catch my life so pleasantly / As to prenominate in nice conjecture / Where thou wilt hit me dead?

It would disgrace the blessed gods, proud man, to answer such a question. Stand still again. Do you think you can take my life so easily that you can name in advance, with precise guesswork, where you will strike me dead?

Wert thou an oracle to tell me so, / I'd not believe thee. Henceforth guard thee well; / For I'll not kill thee there, nor there, nor there; / But, by the forge that stithied Mars his helm, / I'll kill thee everywhere, yea, o'er and o'er. / You wisest Grecians, pardon me this brag. / His insolence draws folly from my lips; / But I'll endeavour deeds to match these words, / Or may I never—

Even if you were an oracle telling me so, I wouldn't believe you. From now on, guard yourself well, because I won't kill you there, or there, or there; but, by the forge that hammered out Mars's helmet, I'll kill you everywhere, yes, over and over. You wisest Greeks, forgive me this boast. His insolence draws foolishness from my lips. But I'll try to make my deeds match these words, or may I never...

Do not chafe thee, cousin; / And you, Achilles, let these threats alone / Till accident or purpose bring you to't. / You may have every day enough of Hector, / If you have stomach. The general state, I fear, / Can scarce entreat you to be odd with him.

Don't get angry, cousin. And you, Achilles, leave these threats alone until chance or intention brings you to it. You can have enough of Hector every day, if you have the appetite. I'm afraid the whole Greek council can hardly persuade you to fight with him.
I pray you let us see you in the field; / We have had pelting wars since you refus'd / The Grecians' cause.
Please, let us see you on the battlefield. We've had petty wars since you refused to fight for the Greek cause.
Dost thou entreat me, Hector? / Tomorrow do I meet thee, fell as death; / Tonight all friends.
Are you begging me, Hector? Tomorrow I'll meet you, as deadly as death. Tonight, all friends.

First, all you peers of Greece, go to my tent; / There in the full convive we; afterwards, / As Hector's leisure and your bounties shall / Concur together, severally entreat him. / Beat loud the tambourines, let the trumpets blow, / That this great soldier may his welcome know.

First, all you lords of Greece, come to my tent. There we'll all feast together. Afterwards, as Hector's time and your generosity allow, invite him one by one. Beat the drums loud, let the trumpets blow, so that this great soldier knows he is welcome.
My Lord Ulysses, tell me, I beseech you, / In what place of the field doth Calchas keep?
My Lord Ulysses, tell me, please, where in the camp does Calchas stay?

At Menelaus' tent, most princely Troilus. / There Diomed doth feast with him tonight, / Who neither looks upon the heaven nor earth, / But gives all gaze and bent of amorous view / On the fair Cressid.
At Menelaus' tent, most princely Troilus. Diomedes is feasting with him there tonight, and he looks neither at heaven nor earth, but turns all his gaze and loving attention on the fair Cressida.
Shall I, sweet lord, be bound to you so much, / After we part from Agamemnon's tent, / To bring me thither?
Sweet lord, will you do me the great favour, after we leave Agamemnon's tent, of taking me there?
You shall command me, sir. / As gentle tell me of what honour was / This Cressida in Troy? Had she no lover there / That wails her absence?
You can command me, sir. In return, kindly tell me what reputation this Cressida had in Troy. Did she have no lover there who weeps at her absence?
O, sir, to such as boasting show their scars / A mock is due. Will you walk on, my lord? / She was belov'd, she lov'd; she is, and doth; / But still sweet love is food for fortune's tooth.
Oh, sir, those who show off their scars deserve to be mocked. Will you walk on, my lord? She was loved, she loved; she is, and she does. But sweet love is always food for fortune's teeth.
I'll heat his blood with Greekish wine tonight, / Which with my scimitar I'll cool tomorrow. / Patroclus, let us feast him to the height.
I'll heat his blood with Greek wine tonight, and cool it tomorrow with my curved sword. Patroclus, let's feast him to the full.
How now, thou core of envy! / Thou crusty batch of nature, what's the news?
Well, you rotten core of envy! You burnt crust of nature, what's the news?
Why, thou picture of what thou seemest, and idol of idiot worshippers, here's a letter for thee.
Why, you image of what you seem to be, and idol of idiot worshippers, here's a letter for you.
Why, thou full dish of fool, from Troy.
Why, you full dish of fool, from Troy.
Who's in the tent now? (Who's keeping to it?)
The surgeon's box or the patient's wound.
The surgeon's case or the patient's wound. (Thersites puns on "tent", a probe for wounds.)
Well said, adversity! And what needs these tricks?
Well said, you pain in the neck! And what's the point of these tricks?
Prithee, be silent, boy; I profit not by thy talk; thou art said to be Achilles' male varlet.
Please be quiet, boy. I get nothing from your talk. You're said to be Achilles' male servant.
Male varlet, you rogue! What's that?
Male servant, you rogue! What's that?

Why, his masculine whore. Now, the rotten diseases of the south, the guts-griping ruptures, catarrhs, loads o' gravel in the back, lethargies, cold palsies, raw eyes, dirt-rotten livers, wheezing lungs, bladders full of imposthume, sciaticas, lime-kilns i' th' palm, incurable bone-ache, and the rivelled fee-simple of the tetter, take and take again such preposterous discoveries!

Why, his masculine whore. Now may the rotten diseases of the south, gut-wrenching hernias, colds, loads of kidney stones, sleeping sickness, paralysis, sore eyes, livers rotten with dirt, wheezing lungs, bladders full of abscesses, sciatica, burning palms, incurable bone-ache and permanent wrinkled skin disease take, and take again, such unnatural freaks!
Why, thou damnable box of envy, thou, what meanest thou to curse thus?
Why, you damnable box of envy, you, what do you mean by cursing like this?
Why, no, you ruinous butt; you whoreson indistinguishable cur, no.
Why, no, you ruined barrel; you shapeless bastard dog, no.

No! Why art thou, then, exasperate, thou idle immaterial skein of sleave silk, thou green sarcenet flap for a sore eye, thou tassel of a prodigal's purse, thou? Ah, how the poor world is pestered with such water-flies, diminutives of nature!

No! Then why are you so annoyed, you useless, flimsy tangle of silk thread, you green silk patch for a sore eye, you tassel on a spendthrift's purse, you? Ah, how the poor world is pestered with such mayflies, nature's tiny creatures!

My sweet Patroclus, I am thwarted quite / From my great purpose in tomorrow's battle. / Here is a letter from Queen Hecuba, / A token from her daughter, my fair love, / Both taxing me and gaging me to keep / An oath that I have sworn. I will not break it. / Fall Greeks; fail fame; honour or go or stay; / My major vow lies here, this I'll obey. / Come, come, Thersites, help to trim my tent; / This night in banqueting must all be spent. / Away, Patroclus!

My sweet Patroclus, I am completely prevented from carrying out my great plan in tomorrow's battle. Here is a letter from Queen Hecuba, and a token from her daughter, my fair love, both urging me and binding me to keep an oath I have sworn. I will not break it. Let the Greeks fall, let fame fail, let honour come or go: my greater vow is here, and this I will obey. Come, come, Thersites, help to get my tent ready. This whole night must be spent banqueting. Away, Patroclus!

With too much blood and too little brain these two may run mad; but, if with too much brain and too little blood they do, I'll be a curer of madmen. Here's Agamemnon, an honest fellow enough, and one that loves quails, but he has not so much brain as ear-wax; and the goodly transformation of Jupiter there, his brother, the bull, the primitive statue and oblique memorial of cuckolds, a thrifty shoeing-horn in a chain at his brother's leg, to what form but that he is, should wit larded with malice, and malice forced with wit, turn him to? To an ass, were nothing: he is both ass and ox. To an ox, were nothing: he is both ox and ass. To be a dog, a mule, a cat, a fitchook, a toad, a lizard, an owl, a puttock, or a herring without a roe, I would not care; but to be Menelaus, I would conspire against destiny. Ask me not what I would be, if I were not Thersites; for I care not to be the louse of a lazar, so I were not Menelaus. Hey-day! sprites and fires!

With too much blood and too little brain, these two may go mad; but if they go mad with too much brain and too little blood, I'll become a doctor for madmen. Here's Agamemnon, an honest enough fellow, and one who loves quails (loose women), but he has less brain than earwax. And as for that fine transformation of Jupiter there, his brother the bull (Menelaus), the original image and crooked monument of cuckolds, a cheap shoehorn on a chain at his brother's leg: what shape could wit stuffed with malice, and malice stuffed with wit, turn him into, other than what he is? Turning him into a donkey would be nothing: he's both donkey and ox. Turning him into an ox would be nothing: he's both ox and donkey. I wouldn't mind being a dog, a mule, a cat, a polecat, a toad, a lizard, an owl, a kite or a herring without roe; but if I were Menelaus, I'd plot against fate itself. Don't ask me what I'd be if I weren't Thersites, because I wouldn't mind being the louse on a leper, as long as I weren't Menelaus. Hey there! Spirits and will-o'-the-wisps!
We go wrong, we go wrong.
We're going the wrong way, the wrong way.
No, yonder 'tis; / There, where we see the lights.
No, it's over there, where we see the lights.
Here comes himself to guide you.
Here he comes himself to show you the way.
Welcome, brave Hector; welcome, Princes all.
Welcome, brave Hector; welcome, all you Princes.
So now, fair Prince of Troy, I bid good night; / Ajax commands the guard to tend on you.
So now, fair Prince of Troy, I'll say good night. Ajax will order the guard to attend you.
Thanks, and good night to the Greeks' general.
Thank you, and good night to the Greeks' general.
Sweet draught! 'Sweet' quoth a'! / Sweet sink, sweet sewer!
Sweet toilet! "Sweet," he says! Sweet drain, sweet sewer!
Good night and welcome, both at once, to those / That go or tarry.
Good night and welcome, both at once, to those who are going or staying.
Old Nestor tarries; and you too, Diomed, / Keep Hector company an hour or two.
Old Nestor is staying; and you too, Diomedes, keep Hector company for an hour or two.
I cannot, lord; I have important business, / The tide whereof is now. Good night, great Hector.
I can't, lord. I have important business, and now's the time for it. Good night, great Hector.
[Aside to Troilus] Follow his torch; he goes to / Calchas' tent; I'll keep you company.
(Aside to Troilus) Follow his torch. He's going to Calchas' tent. I'll keep you company.
Come, come, come into my tent.

That same Diomed's a false-hearted rogue, a most unjust knave; I will no more trust him when he leers than I will a serpent when he hisses. He will spend his mouth and promise, like Brabbler the hound; but when he performs, astronomers foretell it: it is prodigious, there will come some change; the sun borrows of the moon when Diomed keeps his word. I will rather leave to see Hector than not to dog him. They say he keeps a Trojan drab, and uses the traitor Calchas' tent. I'll after. Nothing but lechery! All incontinent varlets!

That Diomedes is a false-hearted rogue, a thoroughly dishonest villain. I'll trust him no more when he leers than I trust a snake when it hisses. He'll open his mouth and promise like a yapping hound, but when he actually does something, astronomers predict it: it's a portent, some great change is coming. The sun borrows light from the moon when Diomedes keeps his word. I'd rather miss seeing Hector than miss following him. They say he keeps a Trojan whore and uses the traitor Calchas' tent. I'll go after him. Nothing but lechery! All lustful rascals!
What, are you up here, ho! Speak.
Hey, is anyone up in here? Speak.
Diomed. Calchas, I think. Where's your daughter?
Diomedes. Calchas, I think? Where's your daughter?
Stand where the torch may not discover us.
Stand where the torch won't show us.
Cressida is coming out to him.
Now, my sweet guardian! Hark, a word with you.
Now, my sweet guardian! Listen, a word with you.
She will sing any man at first sight.
She'll sing to any man at first sight (sight-read any man).
And any man may sing her, if he can take her cliff; she's noted.
And any man can sing her, if he can find her clef. She's been marked out (as loose).
Nay, but do, then; / And let your mind be coupled with your words.
No, but do it, then, and let your mind match your words.
Sweet honey Greek, tempt me no more to folly.
Sweet honey Greek, don't tempt me into foolishness any more.
Fo, fo! come, tell a pin; you are a forsworn.
Pooh, pooh! Come on, that's nothing; you're breaking your word.
In faith, I cannot. What would you have me do?
Honestly, I can't. What do you want me to do?
A juggling trick, to be secretly open.
A conjuring trick: to be secretly open (for him).
What did you swear you would bestow on me?
What did you swear you would give me?
I prithee, do not hold me to mine oath; / Bid me do anything but that, sweet Greek.
Please, don't hold me to my oath. Ask me to do anything but that, sweet Greek.
No, no, good night; I'll be your fool no more.
No, no, good night. I won't be your fool any more.
Hark! a word in your ear.
Listen! A word in your ear.
You are moved, Prince; let us depart, I pray, / Lest your displeasure should enlarge itself / To wrathful terms. This place is dangerous; / The time right deadly; I beseech you, go.
You are upset, Prince. Please, let's leave, in case your anger breaks out into furious words. This place is dangerous, and the time is deadly. I beg you, go.
Nay, good my lord, go off; / You flow to great distraction; come, my lord.
No, my good lord, come away. You're heading for great distress. Come, my lord.
I pray you, stay; by hell and all hell's torments, / I will not speak a word.
Please, stay. By hell and all hell's torments, I won't say a word.
Nay, but you part in anger.
Doth that grieve thee? O withered truth!
Does that upset you? Oh withered truth!
By Jove, I will be patient.
Pooh, pooh! Goodbye. You're playing games with me.
In faith, I do not. Come hither once again.
Honestly, I'm not. Come here once more.
You shake, my lord, at something; will you go? / You will break out.
You're shaking at something, my lord. Will you come away? You'll lose control.
Nay, stay; by Jove, I will not speak a word: / There is between my will and all offences / A guard of patience. Stay a little while.
No, stay. By Jove, I won't say a word. There is a guard of patience between my will and any violence. Stay a little while.
How the devil Luxury, with his fat rump and potato finger, tickles these together! Fry, lechery, fry!
How the devil Lust, with his fat backside and potato finger, tickles these two together! Fry, lechery, fry!
In faith, I will, la; never trust me else.
Honestly, I will, I promise. Never trust me otherwise.
Give me some token for the surety of it.
Give me some token as a guarantee.
You have sworn to be patient.
Fear me not, my lord; / I will not be myself, nor have cognition / Of what I feel. I am all patience.
Don't worry about me, my lord. I won't be myself, or know what I feel. I am all patience.
Now the pledge; now, now, now!
Now the pledge; now, now, now!
O beauty! where is thy faith?
Oh beauty! Where is your faithfulness?
I will be patient; outwardly I will.
I will be patient; outwardly I will.
You look upon that sleeve; behold it well. / He lov'd me—O false wench!—Give't me again.
You're looking at that sleeve; look at it well. He loved me... oh false girl! Give it back to me.
It is no matter, now I have't again. / I will not meet with you tomorrow night. / I prithee, Diomed, visit me no more.
It doesn't matter, now that I have it back. I won't meet you tomorrow night. Please, Diomedes, don't visit me any more.
Now she sharpens. Well said, whetstone.
Now she's sharpening his appetite. Well done, whetstone.

O all you gods! O pretty, pretty pledge! / Thy master now lies thinking on his bed / Of thee and me, and sighs, and takes my glove, / And gives memorial dainty kisses to it, / As I kiss thee. Nay, do not snatch it from me; / He that takes that doth take my heart withal.

Oh all you gods! Oh pretty, pretty pledge! Your master is lying on his bed now thinking of you and me, and sighing, and taking my glove and giving it delicate kisses in memory of me, as I kiss you. No, don't snatch it from me. Whoever takes that takes my heart along with it.
I had your heart before; this follows it.
I had your heart already; this follows it.
I did swear to be patient.
You shall not have it, Diomed; faith, you shall not; / I'll give you something else.
You shan't have it, Diomedes; honestly, you shan't. I'll give you something else.
I will have this. Whose was it?
I will have this. Whose was it?
Come, tell me whose it was.
Come on, tell me whose it was.
'Twas one's that lov'd me better than you will. / But, now you have it, take it.
It belonged to someone who loved me better than you will. But now that you have it, take it.
By all Diana's waiting women yond, / And by herself, I will not tell you whose.
By all Diana's attendants up there (the stars), and by Diana herself, I won't tell you whose.
Tomorrow will I wear it on my helm, / And grieve his spirit that dares not challenge it.
Tomorrow I'll wear it on my helmet and torment the spirit of the man who doesn't dare to challenge it.
Wert thou the devil and wor'st it on thy horn, / It should be challeng'd.
Even if you were the devil and wore it on your horn, it would be challenged.
Well, well, 'tis done, 'tis past; and yet it is not; / I will not keep my word.
Well, well, it's done, it's over. And yet it isn't. I won't keep my word.
Why, then farewell; / Thou never shalt mock Diomed again.
Why, then, goodbye. You'll never make a fool of Diomedes again.
You shall not go. One cannot speak a word / But it straight starts you.
You mustn't go. I can't say a word without it setting you off at once.
I do not like this fooling.
I don't like this fooling about.
Nor I, by Pluto; but that that likes not you / Pleases me best.
Nor do I, by Pluto; but whatever you don't like pleases me most.
What, shall I come? The hour?
What, shall I come? At what time?
Ay, come; O Jove! Do come. I shall be plagu'd.
Yes, come. Oh Jove! Do come. I'll be tormented for this.

Troilus, farewell! One eye yet looks on thee; / But with my heart the other eye doth see. / Ah, poor our sex! this fault in us I find, / The error of our eye directs our mind. / What error leads must err; O, then conclude, / Minds sway'd by eyes are full of turpitude.

Troilus, goodbye! One eye still looks at you, but the other sees with my heart. Ah, our poor sex! I find this fault in us: the error of our eyes directs our minds. What error leads must go astray. Oh then, conclude: minds ruled by eyes are full of wickedness.
A proof of strength she could not publish more, / Unless she said 'My mind is now turn'd whore.'
She couldn't have proclaimed it more strongly, unless she said, "My mind has now turned whore."

To make a recordation to my soul / Of every syllable that here was spoke. / But if I tell how these two did co-act, / Shall I not lie in publishing a truth? / Sith yet there is a credence in my heart, / An esperance so obstinately strong, / That doth invert th'attest of eyes and ears; / As if those organs had deceptious functions / Created only to calumniate. / Was Cressid here?

To make a record in my soul of every syllable that was spoken here. But if I tell how these two acted together, won't I be lying even while I tell the truth? Because there is still a belief in my heart, a hope so stubbornly strong that it overturns the evidence of my eyes and ears, as if those organs had deceptive functions created only to slander. Was Cressida here?
I can't conjure up spirits, Trojan.
Why, my negation hath no taste of madness.
Why, my denial has no taste of madness.
Nor mine, my lord. Cressid was here but now.
Nor has mine, my lord. Cressida was here just now.

Let it not be believ'd for womanhood. / Think, we had mothers; do not give advantage / To stubborn critics, apt, without a theme, / For depravation, to square the general sex / By Cressid's rule. Rather think this not Cressid.

For the sake of womanhood, don't let it be believed. Remember, we had mothers. Don't give an opening to harsh critics, who are ready to run women down even without a reason, to measure the whole sex by Cressida's standard. Rather, think this was not Cressida.
What hath she done, Prince, that can soil our mothers?
What has she done, Prince, that could stain our mothers?
Nothing at all, unless that this were she.
Nothing at all, unless this really was her.
Will he swagger himself out on's own eyes?
Is he going to bluster himself out of believing his own eyes?

This she? No; this is Diomed's Cressida. / If beauty have a soul, this is not she; / If souls guide vows, if vows be sanctimonies, / If sanctimony be the god's delight, / If there be rule in unity itself, / This was not she. O madness of discourse, / That cause sets up with and against itself! / Bi-fold authority! where reason can revolt / Without perdition, and loss assume all reason / Without revolt: this is, and is not, Cressid. / Within my soul there doth conduce a fight / Of this strange nature, that a thing inseparate / Divides more wider than the sky and earth; / And yet the spacious breadth of this division / Admits no orifice for a point as subtle / As Ariachne's broken woof to enter. / Instance, O instance! strong as Pluto's gates: / Cressid is mine, tied with the bonds of heaven. / Instance, O instance! strong as heaven itself: / The bonds of heaven are slipp'd, dissolv'd, and loos'd; / And with another knot, five-finger-tied, / The fractions of her faith, orts of her love, / The fragments, scraps, the bits, and greasy relics / Of her o'er-eaten faith, are given to Diomed.

This her? No, this is Diomedes' Cressida. If beauty has a soul, this is not her. If souls guide vows, if vows are sacred, if sacredness is the gods' delight, if there is any rule in oneness itself, this was not her. Oh madness of reasoning, which argues both for and against itself! Double authority, where reason can rebel without being lost, and loss can take on all the appearance of reason without rebelling: this is, and is not, Cressida. Inside my soul a fight of such a strange kind is going on that a thing that cannot be divided splits wider apart than the sky and the earth, and yet the vast breadth of this division leaves no opening wide enough for a point as fine as Arachne's broken thread to enter. Proof, oh proof, as strong as the gates of hell: Cressida is mine, tied with the bonds of heaven. Proof, oh proof, as strong as heaven itself: the bonds of heaven have slipped, dissolved and come loose, and with another knot, tied by five fingers, the scraps of her faith, the leftovers of her love, the fragments, crumbs, bits and greasy remains of her over-eaten faith are given to Diomedes.
May worthy Troilus be half attach'd / With that which here his passion doth express?
