Can worthy Troilus feel even half of what his passion is expressing here?

Ay, Greek; and that shall be divulged well / In characters as red as Mars his heart / Inflam'd with Venus. Never did young man fancy / With so eternal and so fix'd a soul. / Hark, Greek: as much as I do Cressid love, / So much by weight hate I her Diomed. / That sleeve is mine that he'll bear on his helm; / Were it a casque compos'd by Vulcan's skill / My sword should bite it. Not the dreadful spout / Which shipmen do the hurricano call, / Constring'd in mass by the almighty sun, / Shall dizzy with more clamour Neptune's ear / In his descent than shall my prompted sword / Falling on Diomed.

Yes, Greek, and that will be made known in letters as red as Mars's heart when Venus set it on fire. Never did a young man love with so eternal and so fixed a soul. Listen, Greek: as much as I love Cressida, I hate her Diomedes by the same weight. That sleeve he'll wear on his helmet is mine. Even if it were a helmet made by Vulcan's skill, my sword would bite it. The dreadful waterspout that sailors call a hurricane, drawn up into a mass by the almighty sun, will not deafen Neptune's ear with more noise as it falls than my eager sword will make falling on Diomedes.
He'll tickle it for his concupy.
He'll give him a good tickling for his lust.
O Cressid! O false Cressid! false, false, false! / Let all untruths stand by thy stained name, / And they'll seem glorious.
Oh Cressida! Oh false Cressida! False, false, false! Let all lies stand beside your stained name, and they will seem glorious.
O, contain yourself; / Your passion draws ears hither.
Oh, control yourself. Your passion is drawing people's ears here.
I have been seeking you this hour, my lord. / Hector, by this, is arming him in Troy; / Ajax, your guard, stays to conduct you home.
I've been looking for you for an hour, my lord. By now Hector is arming himself in Troy. Ajax, your escort, is waiting to take you home.
Have with you, Prince. My courteous lord, adieu. / Fairwell, revolted fair! and, Diomed, / Stand fast, and wear a castle on thy head.
I'm with you, Prince. My courteous lord, goodbye. Farewell, unfaithful beauty! And, Diomedes, stand firm, and wear a castle on your head.
I'll bring you to the gates.
I'll take you to the gates.
Accept the thanks of a distracted man.

Would I could meet that rogue Diomed! I would croak like a raven; I would bode, I would bode. Patroclus will give me anything for the intelligence of this whore; the parrot will not do more for an almond than he for a commodious drab. Lechery, lechery! Still wars and lechery! Nothing else holds fashion. A burning devil take them!

I wish I could meet that rogue Diomedes! I'd croak like a raven; I'd foretell disaster, I'd foretell it. Patroclus will give me anything for news of this whore. A parrot wouldn't do more for an almond than he would for an available woman. Lechery, lechery! Always wars and lechery! Nothing else stays in fashion. May a burning devil take them!
When was my lord so much ungently temper'd / To stop his ears against admonishment? / Unarm, unarm, and do not fight today.
When was my lord ever so harsh in his mood as to block his ears against advice? Take off your armour, take it off, and don't fight today.
You train me to offend you; get you in. / By all the everlasting gods, I'll go.
You're provoking me to be rude to you. Go inside. By all the everlasting gods, I will go.
My dreams will, sure, prove ominous to the day.
My dreams will surely prove to be warnings about today.

Here, sister, arm'd, and bloody in intent. / Consort with me in loud and dear petition, / Pursue we him on knees; for I have dreamt / Of bloody turbulence, and this whole night / Hath nothing been but shapes and forms of slaughter.

Here, sister, armed and set on bloodshed. Join me in loud and heartfelt pleading. Let's follow him on our knees, because I have dreamt of bloody chaos, and this whole night has been nothing but shapes and images of slaughter.
Hey! Tell my trumpeter to sound.
No notes of sally, for the heavens, sweet brother!
No signal to attack, for heaven's sake, sweet brother!
Be gone, I say. The gods have heard me swear.
Go away, I say. The gods have heard me swear.
The gods are deaf to hot and peevish vows; / They are polluted off'rings, more abhorr'd / Than spotted livers in the sacrifice.
The gods are deaf to hot-headed, stubborn vows. They are polluted offerings, more hateful than diseased livers in a sacrifice.
O, be persuaded! Do not count it holy / To hurt by being just. It is as lawful, / For we would give much, to use violent thefts / And rob in the behalf of charity.

Oh, be persuaded! Don't think it holy to do harm by keeping your word. You might as well say that because we want to give a lot to charity, it is lawful to steal violently and rob on charity's behalf.
It is the purpose that makes strong the vow; / But vows to every purpose must not hold. / Unarm, sweet Hector.
It is the purpose that makes a vow strong, but vows made for any purpose at all must not be kept. Take off your armour, sweet Hector.
Hold you still, I say. / Mine honour keeps the weather of my fate. / Life every man holds dear; but the dear man / Holds honour far more precious dear than life.
Keep quiet, I say. My honour holds the upper hand over my fate. Every man values life, but the worthy man values honour far more dearly than life.
How now, young man! Mean'st thou to fight today?
Well, young man! Do you mean to fight today?
Cassandra, call my father to persuade.
Cassandra, call my father to persuade him.

No, faith, young Troilus; doff thy harness, youth; / I am today i' th'vein of chivalry. / Let grow thy sinews till their knots be strong, / And tempt not yet the brushes of the war. / Unarm thee, go; and doubt thou not, brave boy, / I'll stand today for thee and me and Troy.

No, honestly, young Troilus, take off your armour, youth. I am in the mood for knightly deeds today. Let your muscles grow until they are strong and knotted, and don't risk the clashes of war yet. Take off your armour, go; and don't doubt it, brave boy, I'll stand up today for you and me and Troy.
Brother, you have a vice of mercy in you, / Which better fits a lion than a man.
Brother, you have a weakness for mercy, which suits a lion better than a man.
What vice is that? Good Troilus, chide me for it.
What weakness is that? Good Troilus, scold me for it.
When many times the captive Grecian falls, / Even in the fan and wind of your fair sword, / You bid them rise and live.
Many times, when a captured Greek falls just from the breeze and wind of your fine sword, you tell him to get up and live.

For th' love of all the gods, / Let's leave the hermit Pity with our mother; / And when we have our armours buckled on, / The venom'd vengeance ride upon our swords, / Spur them to ruthful work, rein them from ruth!

For the love of all the gods, let's leave pity, that hermit, at home with our mother. And when we have buckled on our armour, let poisonous vengeance ride on our swords; spur them on to pitiful work and rein them back from pity!
Troilus, I would not have you fight today.
Troilus, I don't want you to fight today.

Who should withhold me? / Not fate, obedience, nor the hand of Mars / Beckoning with fiery truncheon my retire; / Not Priamus and Hecuba on knees, / Their eyes o'er-galled with recourse of tears; / Nor you, my brother, with your true sword drawn, / Oppos'd to hinder me, should stop my way, / But by my ruin.

Who could hold me back? Not fate, not obedience, not the hand of Mars signalling my retreat with his fiery staff; not Priam and Hecuba on their knees, their eyes sore from streaming tears; nor you, my brother, with your true sword drawn against me to stop me, could block my way, except by killing me.
Lay hold upon him, Priam, hold him fast; / He is thy crutch; now if thou lose thy stay, / Thou on him leaning, and all Troy on thee, / Fall all together.
Take hold of him, Priam, hold him tight. He is your crutch. Now if you lose your support, you who lean on him, and all Troy that leans on you, will all fall together.

Come, Hector, come, go back. / Thy wife hath dreamt; thy mother hath had visions; / Cassandra doth foresee; and I myself / Am like a prophet suddenly enrapt / To tell thee that this day is ominous. / Therefore, come back.

Come, Hector, come, go back. Your wife has dreamt, your mother has had visions, Cassandra foresees it, and I myself am like a prophet suddenly seized to tell you that this day is ill-omened. So come back.
Aeneas is a-field; / And I do stand engag'd to many Greeks, / Even in the faith of valour, to appear / This morning to them.
Aeneas is on the battlefield, and I am pledged to many Greeks, on my honour as a soldier, to meet them this morning.
Ay, but thou shalt not go.
Yes, but you shall not go.

I must not break my faith. / You know me dutiful; therefore, dear sir, / Let me not shame respect; but give me leave / To take that course by your consent and voice / Which you do here forbid me, royal Priam.

I must not break my word. You know I am dutiful, so, dear sir, don't make me shame my respect for you; but give me permission, with your consent and approval, to do what you are forbidding me here, royal Priam.
O Priam, yield not to him!
Oh Priam, don't give in to him!
Andromache, I am offended with you. / Upon the love you bear me, get you in.
Andromache, I am angry with you. By the love you have for me, go inside.
This foolish, dreaming, superstitious girl / Makes all these bodements.
This foolish, dreaming, superstitious girl makes up all these omens.

O, farewell, dear Hector! / Look how thou diest. Look how thy eye turns pale. / Look how thy wounds do bleed at many vents. / Hark how Troy roars; how Hecuba cries out; / How poor Andromache shrills her dolours forth; / Behold distraction, frenzy, and amazement, / Like witless antics, one another meet, / And all cry, 'Hector! Hector's dead! O Hector!'

Oh, farewell, dear Hector! Look how you die! Look how your eyes grow pale! Look how your wounds bleed from many openings! Listen how Troy roars, how Hecuba cries out, how poor Andromache shrieks out her grief! See madness, frenzy and horror meet each other like crazed clowns, and all cry, "Hector! Hector's dead! Oh Hector!"
Farewell! yet, soft! Hector, I take my leave. / Thou dost thyself and all our Troy deceive.
Farewell! Yet wait! Hector, I say goodbye. You are deceiving yourself and all our Troy.
You are amaz'd, my liege, at her exclaim. / Go in, and cheer the town; we'll forth, and fight, / Do deeds worth praise and tell you them at night.
You are shaken by her outcry, my lord. Go in and cheer up the town. We'll go out and fight, do deeds worth praising and tell you about them tonight.
Farewell. The gods with safety stand about thee!
Farewell. May the gods stand around you and keep you safe!
They are at it, hark! Proud Diomed, believe, / I come to lose my arm or win my sleeve.
They're at it, listen! Proud Diomedes, believe me, I'm coming to lose my arm or win back my sleeve.
Do you hear, my lord? Do you hear?
Do you hear, my lord? Do you hear?
Here's a letter come from yond poor girl.
Here's a letter from that poor girl over there.

A whoreson tisick, a whoreson rascally tisick, so troubles me, and the foolish fortune of this girl, and what one thing, what another, that I shall leave you one o' these days; and I have a rheum in mine eyes too, and such an ache in my bones that unless a man were curs'd I cannot tell what to think on't. What says she there?

A damned cough, a damned rascally cough troubles me so much, and this girl's foolish luck, and one thing and another, that I'll leave you one of these days. And I have a watering in my eyes too, and such an ache in my bones that, unless a man had been cursed, I don't know what to make of it. What does she say there?
Words, words, mere words, no matter from the heart; / Th'effect doth operate another way.
Words, words, mere words, nothing from the heart. The deeds work another way.
Go, wind, to wind, there turn and change together. / My love with words and errors still she feeds, / But edifies another with her deeds.
Go, wind, to the wind, and there turn and change together. She still feeds my love with words and lies, but builds up another man with her deeds.

Now they are clapper-clawing one another; I'll go look on. That dissembling abominable varlet, Diomed, has got that same scurvy doting foolish young knave's sleeve of Troy there in his helm. I would fain see them meet, that that same young Trojan ass that loves the whore there might send that Greekish whoremasterly villain with the sleeve back to the dissembling luxurious drab of a sleeve-less errand. O' the other side, the policy of those crafty swearing rascals that stale old mouse-eaten dry cheese, Nestor, and that same dog-fox, Ulysses, is not prov'd worth a blackberry. They set me up, in policy, that mongrel cur, Ajax, against that dog of as bad a kind, Achilles; and now is the cur, Ajax prouder than the cur Achilles, and will not arm today; whereupon the Grecians begin to proclaim barbarism, and policy grows into an ill opinion.

Now they're clawing at each other; I'll go and watch. That lying, disgusting rascal Diomedes has got that scabby, doting, foolish young Trojan rogue's sleeve on his helmet there. I'd love to see them meet, so that the young Trojan donkey who loves the whore there could send that Greek whoremongering villain with the sleeve back to the lying, lustful tart on a sleeveless (pointless) errand. On the other side, the cunning of those crafty, lying rascals, that stale, old, mouse-eaten dry cheese Nestor and that dog-fox Ulysses, has turned out not to be worth a blackberry. They set up that mongrel dog Ajax, as a strategy, against that dog of just as bad a breed, Achilles. And now the dog Ajax is prouder than the dog Achilles, and won't arm himself today. So the Greeks are starting to declare themselves barbarians, and strategy is getting a bad name.
Soft! here comes sleeve, and t'other.
Wait! Here comes the sleeve, and the other one.
Fly not; for shouldst thou take the river Styx, I would swim after.
Don't run. Even if you took to the river Styx, I would swim after you.
Thou dost miscall retire. / I do not fly; but advantageous care / Withdrew me from the odds of multitude. / Have at thee!
You give my retreat the wrong name. I'm not running away; I withdrew carefully, for my own advantage, from being outnumbered. Here I come!
Hold thy whore, Grecian; now for thy whore, / Trojan! now the sleeve, now the sleeve!
Hold on to your whore, Greek! Now fight for your whore, Trojan! Now the sleeve, now the sleeve!
What art thou, Greek? Art thou for Hector's match? / Art thou of blood and honour?
Who are you, Greek? Are you a match for Hector? Are you of noble blood and honour?
No, no I am a rascal; a scurvy railing knave; a very filthy rogue.
No, no, I'm a rascal, a scabby, ranting rogue, a really filthy villain.

God-a-mercy, that thou wilt believe me; but a plague break thy neck for frighting me! What's become of the wenching rogues? I think they have swallowed one another. I would laugh at that miracle. Yet, in a sort, lechery eats itself. I'll seek them.

Thank God you believe me. But a plague break your neck for frightening me! What's become of the whoring rogues? I think they've swallowed each other. I'd laugh at that miracle. Still, in a way, lechery eats itself. I'll look for them.

Go, go, my servant, take thou Troilus' horse; / Present the fair steed to my lady Cressid. / Fellow, commend my service to her beauty; / Tell her I have chastis'd the amorous Trojan, / And am her knight by proof.

Go, go, my servant, take Troilus' horse. Present the fine horse to my lady Cressida. Fellow, give my service to her beauty. Tell her I have punished the lovesick Trojan, and I am her knight, as I have proved.

Renew, renew! The fierce Polydamas / Hath beat down Menon; bastard Margarelon / Hath Doreus prisoner, / And stands colossus-wise, waving his beam, / Upon the pashed corses of the kings / Epistrophus and Cedius. Polixenes is slain; / Amphimacus and Thoas deadly hurt; / Patroclus ta'en, or slain; and Palamedes / Sore hurt and bruis'd. The dreadful Sagittary / Appals our numbers. Haste we, Diomed, / To reinforcement, or we perish all.

Renew the attack, renew it! The fierce Polydamas has beaten down Menon. The bastard Margarelon has taken Doreus prisoner and stands like a colossus, waving his heavy spear over the battered corpses of the kings Epistrophus and Cedius. Polixenes is killed; Amphimachus and Thoas are fatally wounded; Patroclus is captured or killed; and Palamedes is badly wounded and bruised. The dreadful centaur archer terrifies our troops. Let's hurry, Diomedes, to bring reinforcements, or we'll all die.

Go, bear Patroclus' body to Achilles, / And bid the snail-pac'd Ajax arm for shame. / There is a thousand Hectors in the field; / Now here he fights on Galathe his horse, / And there lacks work; anon he's there afoot, / And there they fly or die, like scaled sculls / Before the belching whale; then is he yonder, / And there the strawy Greeks, ripe for his edge, / Fall down before him like the mower's swath. / Here, there, and everywhere, he leaves and takes; / Dexterity so obeying appetite / That what he will he does, and does so much / That proof is call'd impossibility.

Go, take Patroclus' body to Achilles, and tell the snail-paced Ajax to arm himself for shame. There are a thousand Hectors on the battlefield. Now here he fights on his horse Galathe, and soon there's no one left to fight. Next he's over there on foot, and there they run or die, like shoals of scaly fish before a spouting whale. Then he's over there, and there the Greeks fall down before him like straw, ripe for his blade, like grass before the mower. Here, there and everywhere he leaves and takes, his skill so obedient to his desire that whatever he wants to do he does, and does so much that the evidence seems impossible.

O, courage, courage, courage, Princes! Great Achilles / Is arming, weeping, cursing, vowing vengeance. / Patroclus' wounds have rous'd his drowsy blood, / Together with his mangled Myrmidons, / That noseless, handless, hack'd and chipp'd, come to him, / Crying on Hector. Ajax hath lost a friend / And foams at mouth, and he is arm'd and at it, / Roaring for Troilus; who hath done today / Mad and fantastic execution, / Engaging and redeeming of himself / With such a careless force and forceless care / As if that lust, in very spite of cunning, / Bade him win all.

Oh, courage, courage, courage, Princes! Great Achilles is arming, weeping, cursing, swearing vengeance. Patroclus' wounds have roused his drowsy blood, together with his mangled Myrmidons, who come to him noseless, handless, hacked and chipped, crying out against Hector. Ajax has lost a friend and is foaming at the mouth; he is armed and in the fight, roaring for Troilus, who has done mad and incredible slaughter today, throwing himself into danger and getting himself out again with such careless strength and effortless care, as if lust for battle, in spite of all skill, told him to win everything.
Where is this Hector? / Come, come, thou boy-queller, show thy face; / Know what it is to meet Achilles angry. / Hector! where's Hector? I will none but Hector.
Where is this Hector? Come, come, you boy-killer, show your face. Find out what it is to meet Achilles angry. Hector! Where's Hector? I want no one but Hector.
Troilus, thou coward Troilus, show thy head.
Troilus, you coward Troilus, show your head.
Were I the general, thou shouldst have my office / Ere that correction. Troilus, I say! What, Troilus!
If I were the general, you could have my position before you got to punish him. Troilus, I say! Hey, Troilus!
O traitor Diomed! Turn thy false face, thou traitor, / And pay thy life thou owest me for my horse.
Oh traitor Diomedes! Turn your false face round, you traitor, and pay me the life you owe me for my horse.
I'll fight with him alone. Stand, Diomed.
I'll fight him alone. Stand back, Diomedes.
He is my prize. I will not look upon.
He's my prize. I won't just stand and watch.
Come, both, you cogging Greeks; have at you both!
Come on, both of you, you cheating Greeks. I'll take you both on!
Yea, Troilus? O, well fought, my youngest brother!
Yes, Troilus? Oh, well fought, my youngest brother!
Now do I see thee. Ha! have at thee, Hector!
Now I see you. Ha! Here I come, Hector!
Take a rest, if you like.
I do disdain thy courtesy, proud Trojan. / Be happy that my arms are out of use; / My rest and negligence befriend thee now, / But thou anon shalt hear of me again; / Till when, go seek thy fortune.
I scorn your courtesy, proud Trojan. Be glad that my arms are out of practice. My rest and laziness are your friends now, but you'll hear from me again soon. Until then, go and look for your luck.
Fare thee well. / I would have been much more a fresher man, / Had I expected thee.
Goodbye. I would have been a much fresher man if I had been expecting you.

Ajax hath ta'en Aeneas. Shall it be? / No, by the flame of yonder glorious heaven, / He shall not carry him; I'll be ta'en too, / Or bring him off. Fate, hear me what I say: / I reck not though thou end my life today.

Ajax has captured Aeneas. Shall we allow it? No, by the flame of that glorious sky up there, he won't take him away. I'll be captured too, or rescue him. Fate, hear what I say: I don't care if you end my life today.

Stand, stand, thou Greek; thou art a goodly mark. / No? wilt thou not? I like thy armour well; / I'll frush it and unlock the rivets all / But I'll be master of it. Wilt thou not, beast, abide? / Why then, fly on; I'll hunt thee for thy hide.

Stop, stop, you Greek; you're a fine target. No? Won't you? I like your armour. I'll smash it and break open all the rivets, but I'll be its master. Won't you stay, you beast? Why then, run on; I'll hunt you for your hide.

Come here about me, you my Myrmidons; / Mark what I say. Attend me where I wheel; / Strike not a stroke, but keep yourselves in breath; / And when I have the bloody Hector found, / Empale him with your weapons round about; / In fellest manner execute your arms. / Follow me, sirs, and my proceedings eye. / It is decreed Hector the great must die.

Gather round me here, you, my Myrmidons. Listen to what I say. Follow me wherever I turn. Don't strike a blow, but save your breath, and when I have found the bloodthirsty Hector, surround him with your weapons and use them in the most savage way. Follow me, men, and watch what I do. It is decreed that great Hector must die.
The cuckold and the cuckold-maker are at it. Now, bull! Now, dog! 'Loo, Paris, 'loo! now my double-hen'd Spartan! 'loo, Paris, 'loo! The bull has the game. 'Ware horns, ho!

The cuckold and the cuckold-maker are at it. Now, bull! Now, dog! Go on, Paris, go on! Now, my Spartan with two hens (two husbands for one wife)! Go on, Paris, go on! The bull is winning. Watch out for the horns, ho!

I am a bastard too; I love bastards. I am a bastard begot, bastard instructed, bastard in mind, bastard in valour, in everything illegitimate. One bear will not bite another, and wherefore should one bastard? Take heed, the quarrel's most ominous to us: if the son of a whore fight for a whore, he tempts judgement. Farewell, bastard.

I'm a bastard too. I love bastards. I was born a bastard, educated a bastard, I'm a bastard in mind, a bastard in courage, illegitimate in everything. One bear won't bite another, so why should one bastard bite another? Be careful: the quarrel is very unlucky for us. If the son of a whore fights for a whore, he's tempting judgement. Goodbye, bastard.
Most putrified core so fair without, / Thy goodly armour thus hath cost thy life. / Now is my day's work done; I'll take my breath: / Rest, sword; thou hast thy fill of blood and death!
You rotten core, so beautiful on the outside, your fine armour has cost you your life. Now my day's work is done. I'll get my breath back. Rest, sword; you've had your fill of blood and death!
Look, Hector, how the sun begins to set, / How ugly night comes breathing at his heels; / Even with the vail and dark'ning of the sun, / To close the day up, Hector's life is done.
Look, Hector, how the sun begins to set, how ugly night comes breathing at its heels. Just as the sun goes down and darkens to close the day, Hector's life is over.
I am unarm'd; forego this vantage, Greek.
I am unarmed. Give up this advantage, Greek.
Strike, fellows, strike; this is the man I seek.
Strike, men, strike; this is the man I'm looking for.
So, Ilion, fall thou next! Now, Troy, sink down; / Here lies thy heart, thy sinews, and thy bone. / On, Myrmidons, and cry you all amain / 'Achilles hath the mighty Hector slain.'
So, Troy, fall next! Now, Troy, sink down. Here lies your heart, your muscles and your bones. On, Myrmidons, and all shout as loud as you can, "Achilles has killed the mighty Hector."
Hark! a retire upon our Grecian part.
Listen! A retreat sounded on our Greek side.
The Trojan trumpets sound the like, my lord.
The Trojan trumpets are sounding the same, my lord.
The dragon wing of night o'erspreads the earth / And, stickler-like, the armies separates. / My half-supp'd sword, that frankly would have fed, / Pleas'd with this dainty bait, thus goes to bed.
The dragon wings of night spread over the earth and separate the armies, like an umpire. My half-fed sword, which would gladly have eaten more, pleased with this tasty snack, goes to bed like this.
Come, tie his body to my horse's tail; / Along the field I will the Trojan trail.
Come, tie his body to my horse's tail. I'll drag the Trojan along the battlefield.
Hark! hark! what shout is this?
The bruit is, Hector's slain, and by Achilles.
The rumour is that Hector has been killed, and by Achilles.
If it be so, yet bragless let it be; / Great Hector was as good a man as he.
If it's true, let there be no boasting about it. Great Hector was as good a man as he is.
March patiently along. Let one be sent / To pray Achilles see us at our tent. / If in his death the gods have us befriended; / Great Troy is ours, and our sharp wars are ended.
March on steadily. Let someone be sent to ask Achilles to meet us at our tent. If the gods have done us a favour in his death, great Troy is ours and our bitter wars are over.
Stand, ho! yet are we masters of the field. / Never go home; here starve we out the night.
Halt, there! We are still masters of the field. Let's not go home; we'll last out the night here.

He's dead, and at the murderer's horse's tail, / In beastly sort, dragg'd through the shameful field. / Frown on, you heavens, effect your rage with speed. / Sit, gods, upon your thrones, and smile at Troy. / I say at once let your brief plagues be mercy, / And linger not our sure destructions on.

He's dead, and dragged like an animal through the shameful field, tied to his murderer's horse's tail. Frown on, you heavens, and carry out your anger quickly. Sit on your thrones, you gods, and smile at Troy. I say, let your quick plagues be merciful, and don't drag out our certain destruction.
My lord, you do discomfort all the host.
My lord, you are discouraging the whole army.

You understand me not that tell me so. / I do not speak of flight, of fear of death, / But dare all imminence that gods and men / Address their dangers in. Hector is gone. / Who shall tell Priam so, or Hecuba? / Let him that will a screech-owl aye be call'd / Go in to Troy, and say there 'Hector's dead.' / There is a word will Priam turn to stone; / Make wells and Niobes of the maids and wives, / Cold statues of the youth; and, in a word, / Scare Troy out of itself. But, march away; / Hector is dead; there is no more to say. / Stay yet. You vile abominable tents, / Thus proudly pight upon our Phrygian plains, / Let Titan rise as early as he dare, / I'll through and through you. And, thou great-siz'd coward, / No space of earth shall sunder our two hates; / I'll haunt thee like a wicked conscience still, / That mouldeth goblins swift as frenzy's thoughts. / Strike a free march to Troy. With comfort go; / Hope of revenge shall hide our inward woe.

You don't understand me if you say that. I'm not talking about running away or fear of death, but I dare every danger that gods and men can threaten. Hector is gone. Who will tell Priam, or Hecuba? Let whoever is willing to be called a screech owl for ever go into Troy and say there, "Hector's dead." Those words will turn Priam to stone, turn the young women and wives into wells of tears like Niobe, and the young men into cold statues; in a word, frighten Troy out of its wits. But march away. Hector is dead; there is no more to say. Wait a moment. You vile, disgusting tents, pitched so proudly on our Trojan plains, let the sun rise as early as it dares, I'll go through and through you. And you, great big coward (Achilles), no distance on earth will keep our two hatreds apart. I'll haunt you for ever like a guilty conscience, which makes up goblins as fast as a madman's thoughts. Beat a lively march back to Troy. Go with comfort: the hope of revenge will hide our inner grief.
Hence, broker-lackey. Ignominy and shame / Pursue thy life, and live aye with thy name!
Get out, you go-between, you lackey. May disgrace and shame follow you all your life, and live for ever with your name!

A goodly medicine for my aching bones! O world! world! Thus is the poor agent despis'd! O traitors and bawds, how earnestly are you set a-work, and how ill requited! Why should our endeavour be so lov'd, and the performance so loathed? What verse for it? What instance for it? Let me see— / Full merrily the humble-bee doth sing / Till he hath lost his honey and his sting; / And being once subdu'd in armed trail, / Sweet honey and sweet notes together fail. / Good traders in the flesh, set this in your painted cloths. / As many as be here of Pandar's hall, / Your eyes, half out, weep out at Pandar's fall; / Or, if you cannot weep, yet give some groans, / Though not for me, yet for your aching bones. / Brethren and sisters of the hold-door trade, / Some two months hence my will shall here be made. / It should be now, but that my fear is this, / Some galled goose of Winchester would hiss. / Till then I'll sweat and seek about for eases, / And at that time bequeath you my diseases.

A fine medicine for my aching bones! Oh world, world! This is how the poor agent is despised! Oh traitors and pimps, how eagerly you are put to work, and how badly you are paid! Why should our efforts be so wanted and the result so hated? What verse is there for it? What example? Let me see: "The bumblebee sings very merrily until he has lost his honey and his sting; and once his weapon's tail is gone, sweet honey and sweet songs both fail together." Good traders in flesh, put this on your painted wall-hangings. All of you here who belong to Pandar's hall, let your eyes, half blind already, weep at Pandar's fall. Or if you can't weep, at least give a few groans, if not for me, then for your aching bones. Brothers and sisters of the door-keeping trade, in about two months I'll make my will here. It should be now, except that I'm afraid some sore prostitute from Winchester would hiss. Until then I'll sweat and look around for remedies, and then I'll leave you my diseases in my will.
